: “perannare” is used here like the Gr. διετίζειν “to live through the year"; cf. Macrob. Sat. i 12, eodem quoque mense Martio ad Annam Perennam sacrificatum itur ut annare perennareque (al. perannareque) commode liceat. Warde Fowler (Rom. Fest. p. 51), citing these words of Macrobius, comments: "Annare perennare is to complete the circle of the year: cp. Suet. Vesp. 5. Anna Perenna herself is probably a deity manufactured out of these words and the idea they conveyed...; not exactly a deity of the year, but one whom it would be desirable to propitiate at the beginning of the year." The expression non perannavit is used erroneously in the spurious inscription, C.I.L. vi 412* and add. p. 49*, of the daughter (and not the sister) of Vespasian (see Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2730). In the form “perennare” the verb is used in poetry and post-Aug. prose, generally intrans. to last for many years,” e.g. Ov. 4.4. iii 42, arte perennat amor; in Colum. xii 19, 2: 20, 8, it is trans. "to make to last for years."

: cf. Aug. 6, locus cellae penuariae instar: Ner. 31, 1, stagnum maris instar. Suet. also uses instar for a statue or likeness (effigies, simulacrum), Iul. 61, cuius (equi) instar pro aede Veneris .. postea dedicavit; cf. Galb. 10, 2, e primoribus vel instar senatus (i.e. a miniature senate) instituit: Calig. 5, quod apud Parthos iustitii instar est (i.e. represents the Roman iustitium, is a sign of public mourning).
: see c. 1, 3.
: see on Galb. 19, 1.
: cf. Galb. 9, 2, confirmabatur cum secundissimis auspiciis et ominibus, tum virginis honestae vaticinatione: Tit. 5, 1, de imperii spe confirmatus est.
: see on Dom. 21.

div.p: § 3. aedilem: Vesp. was aedile in 38 A.D., in the reign of Gaius (Caligula); see c. 2, 3.

p.note: : part of the cura urbis which was one of the functions of the aediles (Cic. Legg. iii 3, 7, suntoque aediles curatores urbis, annonae, ludorumque sollemnium); they were responsible for the cleansing (vias verrere, purgare) repairing (reficere) and paving (sternere) of the streets; cf. Plaut. Stich. 347 sqq., where Pinacium, giving orders about cleansing the house with brooms (scopae) and watering-pots (nassiternae), is compared to an aedile.

: Dio (lix 12) mentions this occurrence and the significance which later was attached to it: πηλὸν πολὺν ἐν στενωπῷ τινι ἰδὼν (ὁ Γάιος) ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ἐς τὸ τοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ τοῦ Φλαβίου ἱμάτιον, ἀγορανομοῦντός (aedilis) τε τότε καὶ τῆς τῶν στενωπῶν καθαριότητος ἐπιμελουμένου, ἐμβληθῆναι. καὶ τοῦτο οὕτω πραχθὲν παραχρῆμα μὲν ἐν οὐδενὶ λόγῳ ὤφθη, ὕστερον δὲ τοῦ Οὐεπασιανοῦ τὰ πράγματα τεταραγμένα καὶ πεφυρμένα παραλαβόντος τε καὶ καταστησαμένου ἔδοξεν οὐκ ἀθεεὶ γεγονέναι, ἀλλ᾽ ἄντικρυς αὐτῷ τὴν πόλιν ὁ Γάιος πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν ἐγκεχειρικέναι.

: the robe of office of the curule aedile (as of other curule magistrates) was the toga praetexta, the white toga bordered with purple. Plebeian aediles could not wear the praetexta; nor had they a sella curulis, but only a subsellium.
: the same phrase occurs in Galb. 8, 2: Tit. 5, 3: Dom. 23, 2. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 306 sq.

: a place of shelter and protection; cf. Aen. ix 261, quaecumque mihi fortuna fidesque est, | in vestris pono gremiis: ib. viii 713 (of the river-god Nilus represented with a dark blue robe), pandentemque sinus et tota veste vocantem | caeruleum in gremium latebrosaque flumina victos.

div.p: § 4. prandente eo subiecit: Dio (lxvi 1) κύων, σῖτον αὐτοῦ αἱρουμένου, χεῖρα ἀνθρωπίνην ὑπὸ τὴν τράπεζαν ὑπέβαλε. See on "prandia,” Vitell. 13, 1.

p.note: : the appearance of a strange dog was regarded as an omen; cf. Ter. Phorm. 705, quot res postilla monstra evenerunt mihi! | intro iit in aedes ater alienus canis, etc. The adj. and subst. extrarius was used especially as the opp. of domesticus or ex eadem familia; e.g. Ter. Phorm. 579, hanc condicionem (“marriage proposal'") si quoi tulero extrario: Apul. Met. viii 22, servus habens ex eodem famulitio conservam coniugem, liberae cuiusdam extrariaeque mulieris flagrabat cupidine.

: refuse (purgamenta) of all kinds and, at times, dead bodies were thrown out at the cross-roads; cf. Petron. Satyr. 134, quae striges comederunt nervos tuos, aut quod purgamentum nocte calcasti in trivio aut cadaver?: Auson. Epigr. 72, abiecta in triviis inhumati glabra iacebat | testa hominis nudum iam cute calvitium. Dogs naturally frequented the trivia; cf. Phaedr. i 27, 11, canis trivio conceptus, et educatus stercore. ..
: ‘“manu humana denuntiabatur fore ut Vespasiani manu omnia regerentur. Manus nempe dextra imperii signum, cuius et instrumentum est'” (Marcilius).
: Dio (l.c.), βοῦς ἐν τῷ ἄγρῳ, ἐν ᾧ τὴν δίαιταν ὡς πλήθει ἐποιεῖτο, δειπνοῦντι προσελθὼν ὤκλασε, καὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑπέθηκε.

: cf. βοῦς ἀροτήρ (Hesiod): Ov. F. i 698, cedebat taurus arator equo. Other instances of a subst. in appos. like an adj. are intercessores tribunos (Iul. 29, 1), serpens draco (Tib. 72, 2), excubitori tribuno (Claud. 42, 1), anus matronas (Ner. 11, 1), tironem militem (Galb. 6, 3). cervicem summisit: as the Roman empire was to bow to Vespasian.

: Tac. H. ii 78, recursabant animo vetera omina: cupressus arbor in agris eius conspicua altitudine repente prociderat ac postera die eodem vestigio resurgens procera et latior virebat; grande id prosperumque consensu haruspicum et summa claritudo iuveni admodum Vespasiano promissa. Dio (l.c.), κυπάρισσός τε περιφανής πρόρριζος ὑπὸ σφοδροῦ πνεύματος ἀνατραπεῖσα, ἔπειτα τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ὑφ᾽ ἑαυτῆς ἀνέστη, καὶ ἀκμάζουσα διετέλεσε. Dio's statement about the strong gale contradicts Suetonius' words "sine ulla vi tempestatis," and Boissée proposed ὑπ᾽ οὐ σφοδροῦ. The second downfall of this cypress, signifying the overthrow of Domitian, is mentioned in Dom. 15, 2, arbor, quae privato adhuc Vespasiano eversa surrexerat, tunc rursus repente corruit.

: this is prob. the genitive; cf. arbor palmae, Aug. 94, 11. The specifying gen. with arbor is found first in Liv. xxiv 3, proceris abietis arboribus. Pliny (N.H.) uses both the nom. in appos. with arbor and also the gen.; Varro and Quintilian have the nom., Columella always the gen. In the Thes. Ling. Lat. “cupressus" here is taken as a nom., as in Tac. H. ii 78 (see preceding note).
: = in praediis Cosanis, c. 2, 1.

: Pliny (N.H. xvi 132) gives other examples of this: Est in exemplis et sine tempestate ullave causa alia quam prodigi cecidisse multas (arbores) ac sua sponte resurrexisse. Factum hoc populi Romani Quiritibus ostentum Cimbricis bellis Nuceriae in luco Iunonis ulmo, postquam etiam cacumen amputatum erat, quoniam in aram ipsam procumbebat, restituta sponte, ita ut protinus floreret, a quo deinde tempore maiestas populi Romani resurrexit, quae ante vastata cladibus fuerat. Memoratur hoc idem factum et in Philippis salice procidua atque detruncata, et Stagiris in museo populo ("poplar'") alba, omnia fausti ominis.

div.p: § 5. at: at (like δε) is often used, especially in poetry, with a weakened force as a particle of transition in passing to a fresh narration, or in an enumeration of instances, etc. (see Hand Tursell. i 422, Kühner-Stegmann ii 84); cf. Galb. 7, 2: Dom. 4, 1: 16, 1.

p.note: : when accompanying Nero on his musical tour (c. 4, 4). Dio (l.c.), καὶ παρ' ὀνείρατος ἔμαθεν ὅτι, ὅταν ὁ Καῖσαρ Νέρων ὀδόντα ἀποβάλῃ, αὐταρχήσει· καὶ τοῦτό τε τὸ κατὰ τὸν ὀδόντα τῇ ἐπιούσῃ ἡμέρᾳ συνηνέχθη.
: cf. Mart. x 56, 3, eximit aut reficit dentem Cascellius (a dentist) aegrum.

: the hall or entrance-room of the house where Nero was staying. On a journey the comites of the emperor, of whom Vespasian was one, lived with the emperor, or provision was made for their housing (Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 79). tantum quod: "only just,” vixdum (a gloss recenter has ousted the genuine reading in many of the MSS.); cf. Aug. 63, 1, tantum quod pueritiam egressus: ib. 98, 2, de navi quae tantum quod appulerat: Ner. 6, 1, tantum quod exoriente sole. The expression is found only in Cicero's Letters and in post-class. writers; cf. Cic. Fam. vii 23, 1, tantum quod ex Arpinati veneram, cum mihi litterae a te redditae sunt. Suetonius is peculiar in using it with the participle. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 272, say that tantum quod in this sense arose from tantum (= tantillum) temporis exactum est, quod. (Distinguish tantum quod = nisi quod, e.g. Cic. Verr. i 116, tantum quôd hominem non nominat, causam quidem totam perscribit).

div.p: § 6. apud Iudaeam: in the vulgar speech apud c. acc. was used instead of in c. abl. Hand (op. cit. i 414) says that in good writers it is so used only in certain formulae such as apud forum, apud villam, but in the comic writers and in late authors, especially Tac. and Suet., it is used of islands, cities, etc. Cf. Nonius 522 М. (p. 840, Lindsay): Error consuetudinis ‘‘aput’” pro ‘‘in’” utitur; itaque vitiose dicimus, cum nos in foro fuisse dicamus, aput aut ad forum fuisse, cum aput iuxta significet.

p.note: : Carmēlus was the name both of the mountain and also of the god to whom it was sacred. The mountain is a continuation of the Antilibanus range on the borders of Phoenicia and Palestine; now Jebel Mar Elyas (i.e. Elijah) or Kurmul. From remote antiquity it has been a sacred place. Scylax (Periplus 42) describes it as ἱερὸν Διός. Iamblichus (vit. Pythag. 4) says that Pythagoras dwelt for some time in solitude in a temple on Carmel. It is familiar in Scripture history from the story of Elijah's triumph over the priests of Baal. Tacitus (H. ii 78) describes Vespasian's visit to Carmel: Est Iudaeam inter Suriamque Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque. Nec simulacrum deo aut templum (sic tradidere maiores): ara tantum et reverentia. Illic sacrificanti Vespasiano, cum spes occultas versaret animo, Basilides sacerdos inspectis identidem extis: “quidquid est,” inquit, ‘“Vespasiane, quod paras, seu domum extruere seu prolatare agros sive ampliare servitia, datur tibi magna sedes, ingentes termini, multum hominum.” Has ambages et statim exceperat fama et tunc aperiebat, nec quidquam magis in ore volgi; crebriores apud ipsum sermones, quanto sperantibus plura dicuntur.

: here used in its extended sense of any kind of oracular deliverance (cf. Cic. Div. ii 56, 115: Verg. Aen. iv 346, etc.). Sortes were properly little tablets or lots on which was written some verse or proverb; these were mixed together, and one drawn at random was taken as an omen. Divination by sortes of this kind was practised at Praeneste (Suet. Tib. 63), at the Fons Aponus near Patavium (Tib. 14), and probably at the oracle of Fortuna at Antium (Calig. 57).

: cf. Sall. Iug. 63, where a soothsayer at Utica, after examining the victims offered to the gods, encourages Marius: proinde, quae animo agitabat fretus dis ageret, fortunam quam saepissume experiretur, cuncta prospere eventura.
: = successurum. This use of provenire (cf. προχωρεῖν) is common in Tac. (e.g. H. iv 18, si destinata provenissent), but occurs only here in Suet.

: the Jewish historian, who, as he tells us himself (Vita 1), was descended on his mother's side from Asmonaean princes and inherited from his father the priesthood which ranked highest. He commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee against Vespasian, and was captured at the fall of Jotapata (67 A.D., see on Vesp. 4 ad fin.). His life was spared on the intercession of Titus. He describes (Bell. Iud. iii 8) his interview with the victorious Vespasian, where he said among other things to the future emperor: “Νέρωνί με πέμπεις ; τί γάρ; οἱ μετὰ Νέρωνα μέχρι σου διάδοχοι μένουσι; σὺ Καῖσαρ, Οὐεσπασιανέ, καὶ αὐτοκράτωρ σὺ καὶ παῖς ὁ σὸς οὗτος. Δέσμει δέ με νῦν ἀσφαλέστερον, καὶ τήρει σαυτῷ. Δεσπότης μὲν γὰρ οὐ μόνον ἐμοῦ σύ, Καῖσαρ, ἀλλὰ καὶ γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης καὶ παντὸς ἀνθρώπων γένους.” Dio (lxvi 1) makes Josephus predict that his liberation by Vespasian as emperor would be in a year's time: 'Ιώσηπος δὲ ἀνὴρ Ἰουδαῖος, ἀχθείς τε ὑπ' αὐτοῦ πρότερον καὶ δεθείς, ἐγέλασε καὶ ἔφη “Νῦν μέν με δήσεις, μετ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν δὲ λύσεις αὐτοκράτωρ γενόμενος.” He was eleased when Vespasian was proclaimed emperor by the armies in Syria and Judaea, and he was with Titus at the siege of Jerusalem. He accompanied Titus to Rome in 71 and was granted Roman citizenship by Vespasian, adopting the nomen gentilicium of Flavius; he also received an annual allowance and land in Judaea which Domitian made tax-free.
: cf. Oros. vii 9, 3, maxime Iosephi Iudaeorum ducis sententia, qui captus, cum in vincula coiceretur, constantissime dixerat, sicut Suetonius refert, continuo se ab eodem sed imperatore solvendum.

div.p: § 7. Neronem monitum per quietem: cf. Dio lxvi 1, καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Νέρων ἔδοξέ ποτε ἐν τοῖς ὕπνοις τὸν τοῦ Διὸς ὄχον ἐς τὴν Οὐεσπασιανοῦ οἰκίαν εἰσαγαγεῖν. For per quietem see on c. 25.

p.note: : tensae were the sacred cars richly adorned with ivory and silver, which conveyed the statues of the gods with their decorations (exuviae) in the solemn procession (pompa) from the Capitoline to the Circus at the opening of the Ludi Circenses (Tit. 2). The statues were placed on couches (pulvinaria) during the games and afterwards borne back in the tensae to their shrines. See the illustrations in Daremberg-Saglio v 115.

: when not in use, the tensae were kept under the care of the aediles in a special building on the Capitol known as "aedes t(h)ensarum”; see Mommsen Staatsr. ii³ 500, Annali dell' Inst. 1858 p. 203: Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 52.

: the tensae were escorted (deducere) by the chief senators, who, along with pueri patrimi et matrimi (i.e. children who were ingenui and whose fathers and mothers were still alive), laid hold of the bridles and traces, or assisted in dragging the tensae by thongs (lora) attached for the purpose (Livy, v 41 ix 40, having ducere tensas). The most prob. deriv. of tensa is that of Asconius on Cic. Verr. i 59 "tensae, sacra vehicula sic dictae, quod ante eas lora tenduntur.”” In Suet. Aug. 43 we are told that even when ill Augustus accompanied the tensae in a litter (accidit votivis Circensibus, ut correptus valitudine, lectica cubans tensas deduceret). This deductio apparently became one of the duties of the emperor, and Nero's dream foretold that not he but Vespasian would in future discharge it. ...

: these words present considerable difficulty and some (e.g. Wolf) have regarded them as a gloss on non multo post. Galba, consul under Tiberius in 33 A.D., became consul for the second time on Jan. 1, 69 A.D., a few days after his arrival in Rome as emperor (Tac. H. i 1 and 11). According to Tacitus and Plutarch (see following note) the portent occurred after the death of Galba. Moreover the meaning of comitia ineunte is by no means clear. Baumg.-Cr. thinks that inire comitia in the sense of auspicari comitia may be defended by the indiscriminate use of these two verbs with bellum, proelium, militiam, etc. But if the text is sound, Ernesti and Bremi seem right in their explanation that the miraculous event took place when Galba was going into the electoral assembly of the people in the Campus Martius; the actual elections were held in the senate, but the people still assembled in the Campus Martius to hear the results announced (Dom. 10, 4, n.), and the statue of Julius Caesar on the island in the Tiber would be visible from the Campus. For the construction comitia consulatus cf. Auson. 419, 2 D 42, comitia consulatus mei (which suggests that sui may have fallen out here after consulatus). Various corrections have been proposed. Marcilius warmly approved of a reading in comitio secundum consulatum ineunte Galba, introduced by Ursinus from his alleged "codex"; Burman hazarded several conjectures, e.g. non multo post comitia secundi consulatus, ineunte Capitolium Galba, and post comitia secundum consulatum ineunte Galba; Oudendorp would read non multo post initia secundi consulatus, intereunte Galba. But in the 15 other passages where non (nec, neque, haud) multo post is used by Suetonius post is always an adv., not a prep.

: presaging the transfer of the empire from the West to the East (i.e. to Vespasian commanding in the East). Tacitus (H. i 86) mentions it among the alarming prodigia reported when Vitellius was advancing against Otho: statuam divi Iulii in insula Tiberini amnis sereno et immoto die ab Occidente in Orientem conversam. Plutarch (Oth. 4) says it happened at the time when the partizans of Vespasian were becoming openly active: τὸν ἐν μεσοποταμίᾳ νήσῳ Γαΐου Καίσαρος ἀνδριάντα μήτε σεισμοῦ γεγονότος μήτε πνεύματος ἀφ᾽ ἑσπέρας μεταστραφέντα πρὸς τὰς ἀνατολάς· ὅ φασι συμβῆναι περὶ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας ἐν αἷς οἱ περὶ Οὐεσπασιανὸν ἐμφανῶς ἤδη τῶν πραγμάτων ἀντελαμβάνοντο. acie Betriacensi: see on Oth. 9, 2.

: typifying Otho and Vitellius; cf. Aesch. Agam. 115, where two eagles typifying Agamemnon and Menelaus appear to the Greek host. The story in Tac. H. ii 50 is quite different: Die, quo Bedriaci certabatur, avem invisitata specie apud Regium Lepidum (between Parma and Modena) celebri luco consedisse incolae memorant, nec deinde coetu hominum aut circumvolitantium alitum territam pulsamve donec Otho se ipse interficeret; tum ablatam ab oculis; et tempora reputantibus initium finemque miraculi cum Othonis exitu competisse. Dio (lxiv 10) agrees with Tac.: ὅπου τέ φασι πρὸ τῆς μάχης ἄλλα τε φανῆναι σημεῖα, καί τινα ὄρνιν ἐξαίσιον, ὁποῖον οὐ πώποτε ἑωράκεσαν, ἐπὶ πολλὰς ἡμέρας ὀφθῆναι.

: typifying Vespasian, who conquered Vitellius the conqueror of Otho. Cf. the ἔφεδρος or suppositicius in boxing or wrestling contests who met the victor of a preceding round. Valerius Maximus (i 4, 6) records an earlier instance of contending eagles foreshadowing the issue of a battle: -M. Brutus cum reliquias exercitus sui adversus Caesarem et Antonium eduxisset, duae aquilae ex diversis castris advolaverunt, et edita inter se pugna, ea, quae a parte Bruti fuerat, male mulcata fugit. See Plut. Brut. 48.

div.p: § 2. Moesiaci exercitus bina milia: the province of Moesia (Vitell. 15, 1, n.) was occupied by three legions, the 3rd (Gallica), 7th (Claudia), and 8th (Augusta). Suetonius says here that it was not till after Otho's death that detachments of these legions reached Aquileia. Tacitus (H. ii 46) says that an advance guard from Moesia (praemissi e Moesia) were with Otho just after his defeat at Bedriacum and encouraged him by reporting that the Moesian legions had entered Aquileia; also in H. ii 85 Tacitus speaks of the Moesian legions as being at Aquileia, where they maltreated the messengers who brought news of Otho's death, tore the standards which displayed the name of Vitellius, and finally plundered the military chest. Spooner (on H. ii 46), following Lipsius, gratuitously accuses Suetonius of mixing up the detachments from the Moesian with those from the Pannonian legions mentioned in H. ii 11, Laeta interim Othoni principia belli, motis ad imperium eius e Dalmatia Pannoniaque exercitibus. Fuere quattuor legiones, e quibus bina milia praemissa; ipsae modicis intervallis sequebantur. Hardy (in an article "Tacitus as a military historian," J. Ph. xxxi 136) rightly defends the accuracy of Suetonius, arguing that he had probably derived his information from his father who was a tribune in the 13th legion from Pannonia which fought for Otho (see Oth. 10, 1), and that various incidents mentioned by Tacitus (H. ii 85, 96 iii 5) clearly imply that the Moesian legions could not have been at Aquileia, though detachments may have been. Furthermore the legions were certainly in Moesia in July or August, when they declared for Vespasian (H. ii 85), and Tacitus says nothing of their having been sent back there, though he gives a precise account of the Othonian legions sent back to their provinces by the victorious Vitellius (H. ii 66, 67). Suetonius is alone in his statement that it was the Moesian detachments at Aquileia who first selected Vespasian as emperor and, though checked for the time, inspired the later action of the legions in Egypt and the East. Tacitus (H. ii 85), after describing the acclamation of Vespasian by the armies in Egypt, Judaea, and Syria, mentions how the army of Illyricum (i.e. Moesia, Pannonia, Dalmatia) came over to Vespasian's side and hastened his movements by its ardour. Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 10) narrates the events in the same order. This too is a matter on which Suetonius may have had special information, though Dessau (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1. 346 n.) characterizes his account as one of his many blunders ("ein Irrtum Suetons, wie sich manche bei ihm finden'"). Dessau holds that the three legions in Moesia felt themselves compromised by the gross insubordination of their detachments sent to Italy. When these detachments had been quieted and had rejoined the main body in Moesia, the reunited legions were uneasy lest they should have to pay the penalty to the new emperor Vitellius; so they looked about for some suitable person to support against Vitellius, and decided to throw in their lot with Vespasian who had been chosen by the armies in the East.

p.note: : see Oth. 11.
: for the forms setius and sequius see on Tit. 5, 3.
: the capital of Venetia in the N.E. corner of Italy at the head of the Adriatic, mod. Aquileja or Aglar.
: in a causal sense, see on Tit. 5, 1.

: grassari "to go," "to proceed" was used especially of proceeding, or acting, with violence (e.g. grassari ferro, veneno). Cf. Aug. 67, 2, superbe avareque in provincia grassatos: Calig. 56, 1, ita bacchantem atque grassantem: Galb. 14, 2, his diverso vitiorum genere grassantibus. Sometimes with in (cf. saevire in), e.g. Ner. 36, 1, пес minore superbia in exteros grassatus est; and with adversus, e.g. Calig. 34, 1, nec minore superbia saevitiaque paene adversus omnis aevi .. 2D2 hominum genus grassatus est: Suetonius also uses grassator for "a footpad" (e.g. Aug. 43, 1) and grassatura for brigandage" (e.g. Tib. 37, 1).

: cf. Tac. (l.c.), unde metus et ex metu consilium: posse imputari Vespasiano, quae apud Vitellium excusanda erant, i.e. that acts might be made a merit of with Vespasian, which would have to be excused to Vitellius.

: cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 3, milites praedicti (i.e. of Moesia and Pannonia), postquam Othonem praetoriis, Vitellium Germanicianis legionibus factum comperere, aemuli, ut inter se solent, ne dissimiles viderentur, Vespasianum perpulere: Oros. vii 8, 3, de Hispania siquidem ilico Galba surrexerat; quo mox oppresso, Otho Romae, Vitellius in Germania, Vespasianus in Syria imperia simul atque arma rapuerunt.

: Galba was acclaimed as emperor by the 6th legion in Spain; and thus, as Tacitus (H. i 4) says, a constitutional secret was disclosed that an emperor could be appointed elsewhere than at Rome (evolgato imperii arcano, posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri). See Galb. 10.

: the praetorians, disgusted with the parsimony of Galba, offered to support Otho (Tac. H. i 23 sq.); he was saluted as Imperator by a handful of them who carried him off to the praetorian camp, the gates of which were at once thrown open and the revolution was complete (ib. 27, 36: Suet. Oth. 6). The affection and loyalty (animus fidesque) of the praetorians towards Otho are described by Suetonius (Oth. 8); and Tacitus (H. ii 46) calls them ‘“proprius Othonis miles.”

: Suetonius is the first to use this adj., applying it to the army in Germany; cf. Tib. 25, 2: Galb. 20, 1: Oth. 8, 1. It is found also in Eutrop. vii 17, x 15; Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 3. A similar formation is ‘‘urbaniciani" for the soldiers garrisoned in the city (of Rome), Spart. Carac. 4, Get. 6: Paul. Dig. iv 6, 35; “Illyricianus” occurs in Treb. Poll. Claud. 14. For the proclamation of Vitellius as emperor by the legions in Germany see Oth. 8, 1: Vitell. 8, 1.

div.p: § 3. legione tertia: the transference (in 67-68) of the 3rd (Gallica) legion from Syria to Moesia is mentioned in Tac. H. ii 74: tertiam legionem, quod e Syria in Moesiam transisset, suam ("devoted to himself'") numerabat (Vespasianus). It repulsed with great slaughter an invasion of Moesia by the Sarmatae (H. i 79). It was the first legion in Moesia to declare for Vespasian; H. ii 85, Adcelerata interim Vespasiani coepta Illyrici exercitus studio transgressi in partes. Tertia legio exemplum ceteris Moesiae legionibus praebuit. nomen eius vexillis inscripserunt: Tacitus (H. ii 85) mentions that the Moesian legions at Aquileia tore the ensigns which bore the name of Vitellius: laceratis vexillis nomen Vitellii praeferentibus. For this sign of revolt cf. H. iii 13, miles praescriptum Vespasiani nomen, proiectas Vitellii effigies aspexit: iii 31, primores castrorum nomen atque imagines Vitellii amoliuntur. Under the Empire the name of the emperor and of the corps was embroidered, probably in gold, on the vexilla which were made of cloth generally red, sometimes purple (or white). A similar practice prevailed under the Republic; cf. Dio xl 18 (speaking of the army of Crassus in Parthia in 53 Β.C.), σημεῖον δέ τι τῶν μεγάλων, τῶν τοῖς ἱστίοις ἐοικότων καὶ φοινικᾶ γράμματα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς πρὸς δήλωσιν τοῦ τε στρατοῦ καὶ τοῦ στρατηγοῦ σφων τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἐχόντων, ἐς τὸν ποταμὸν . . ἐνέπεσε.

p.note: : "detachments," also called vexillationes (Galb. 20, 1) or vexilla as serving under a vexillum instead of their proper signa; cf. Tac. H. i 6, multi numeri e Germania ac Britannia et Illyrico: id. Agr. 18, sparsi per provinciam numeri.

: a Jew, son of the alabarch in Alexandria and nephew of the writer Philo. He renounced the Jewish faith and was made procurator of Judaea by Claudius (c. 46 A.D.). He accompanied Corbulo in his Armenian campaign in 64 (Tac. A. xv 28). Under Nero he was made prefect of Egypt (67-70 A.D.). An edict issued by him as prefect is still preserved (Rhein. Mus. ii 133 sqq.), in which his name appears as Τιβέριος Ἰούλιος ᾿Αλέξανδρος. During his administration there was a riot between the Jews and Greeks in Alexandria, and 50,000 Jews were slain by the Roman legionaries. He was rewarded for his devotion to Vespasian's cause by being made lieutenant-general of the army under Titus, and he was present at the capture of Jerusalem. See Joseph. Antiq. xx 4 sq.: Bell. Iud. ii 11, 15, 18, etc.

: Alexander had been raised to the rank of eques by Claudius. The prefect of Egypt by the arrangement of Augustus must be an eques; cf. Tac. H. i 11, Aegyptum copiasque, quibus coercetur, iam inde a divo Augusto equites Romani obtinent loco regum: ita visum expedire, provinciam aditu difficilem, annonae fecundam, superstitione ac lascivia discordem et mobilem, insciam legum, ignaram magistratuum, domi retinere. Regebat tum Tiberius Alexander, eiusdem nationis. Alexander's espousal of the cause of Vespasian is referred to in Tac. H. ii 74, praefectus Aegypti Ti. Alexander consilia sociaverat.

: Tac. H. ii 79, Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui Kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. See on Galb. 11, in verba sua iurasse cognovit. =

: primus principatus dies (Tac. l.c.), usually called dies imperii; in later authors natalis imperii (e.g. Spart. vit. Hadr. 4). The dies imperii, marking the beginning of a reign, was the day on which the proconsular imperium was conferred on the new Princeps. It is a disputed point whether this imperium could legitimately be conferred by either the senate or the army, or whether the senate exclusively had the right to confer it, so that in cases where the title Imperator was conferred by the soldiers it required the formal confirmation of the senate. former view is defended by Hardy on Plin. ad Trai. 52, following Mommsen Staatsr. ii³ 842 sq.; the latter by Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. ch. ii n. E, following Herzog Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 610 sq. The

: consisting of three legions, the 5th (Macedonica), 10th (Fretensis), and 15th (Apollinaris). Cf. Vitell. 15, 1. Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 10), from a desire to claim the honour for his country, says that the proclamation of Vespasian as emperor took place in Judaea earlier than in Egypt, and that Vespasian wrote to Tiberius Alexander to ask for his support.

: i.e. the 11th of July; Tacitus, however, says that it was on the 3rd (quinto Nonas Iulias), and his statement has been generally accepted as correct. Ernesti goes so far as to substitute Nonas for Idus in our text. Tacitus also says that before the Ides (15th) of July the whole of Syria had taken the oath of allegiance to Vespasian: c. 81, ante Idus Iulias Syria omnis in eodem sacramento fuit. Fabia (Les Sources de Tacite p. 155) infers that Suetonius confused the two armies in Syria and Judaea. =

div.p: § 4. iactatum: in manibus hominum versatum. More usually Suet. has iactari in the sense of in ore hominum esse; e.g. Galb. 6, 2: 12,3: Oth. 12, 2: Vesp. 1, 4.

p.note: : the letter probably purported to convey a last charge written by the vanquished Otho in the hours before his suicide (see Oth. 10, 2); cf. Suet. vit. Horat. 1, extremis iudiciis (of a last will and testament). But extrema might also mean "most urgent." obtestatio (adjuration, solemn entreaty) cf. Tib. 40, revocante (Tiberium) assidua obtestatione populo: Vitell. 2, 3, suorum obtestatione. For

: this report was spread by Mucianus; cf. Tac. c. 80, Nihil aeque provinciam exercitumque accendit quam quod asseverabat Mucianus statuisse Vitellium, ut Germanicas legiones in Syriam ad militiam opulentam quietamque transferret; contra Syriacis legionibus Germanica hiberna caelo ac laboribus dura mutarentur.

: praeses (ἡγεμών) was a general title denoting a governor; cf. Macer Digest i 18, 1, praesidis nomen generale est, eoque et proconsules et legati Caesaris et omnes provincias regentes, licet senatores sint, praesides appellantur. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 240 n. 3) points out that praeses provinciae is not found till after the first century, when it is used by Tacitus (A. vi 41, xii 45), by the younger Pliny (Pan. 70), by Trajan (ep. ad Plin. 44) and by Suetonius (Iul. 35, 1; Aug. 23, 1; Tib. 32, 2; 41; Claud. 17, 3; Oth. 7, 1; Dom. 6, 2; 8, 2). At a later period it came to be applied particularly to the governors of the lowest class, those of equestrian rank, who had no distinguishing title; cf. Mattingly, Imp. Civ. Serv. p. 147.

: consul in 52 under Claudius, but afterwards he roused that emperor's suspicions and was forced to withdraw into a retired part of Asia "as like an exile as he was later like an emperor" (Tac. H. i 10, tam prope ab exule fuit quam postea a principe). Restored to favour by Nero he was made governor of Syria in '67 with command of four legions, while Vespasian was in Judaea in command of three. He called on Vespasian to seize the throne (H. ii 76) and proclaimed him emperor in the theatre at Antioch (ib. 80). He was appointed to act as general against Vitellius, while Vespasian and Titus remained behind in the East (ib. 82). According to Dio (lxv 8) he hoped to share the imperial power, though Vespasian bore the name of emperor: ὁ Μουκιανὸς ἰσχυρῶς προσέκειτο (instabat) ἐλπίσας τὸ μὲν ὄνομα τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐκεῖνον ἕξειν, αὐτὸς δὲ διὰ τὴν ἐπιείκειαν αὐτοῦ ἰσομοιρήσειν. For the character of Mucianus see c. 13 and notes there.

: the correct form of this name is uncertain: “Vologeses" Vologaeses” “Vologesus'” ،“Vologaesus" are all found in the MSS. of Tacitus, and "Vologesus" is a variant here. See Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 475; Furneaux on Tac. A. xii 14. Vologaesus I was king of Parthia, 51-78 A.D. He made repeated efforts to establish his brother Tiridates as king of Armenia. This brought him into conflict with the Roman forces under Corbulo, peace being ultimately made in 63 by Tiridates consenting to receive the crown of Armenia as a gift from the hands of Nero at Rome. Vespasian sent envoys to the Parthians when he was preparing for war (Tac. H. ii 82) and he was already aware of the defeat and death of Vitellius when envoys from Vologaesus arrived at Alexandria with the offer of 40,000 men (H. iv 51). Vespasian thanked the king and directed him to send ambassadors to the senate and to learn for himself that peace had been restored; this he did and secured a renewal of his alliance with Rome (Suet. Ner. 57). He sent a golden crown to Titus on the fall of Jerusalem (Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 5). His request for Roman auxiliaries, with one of Vespasian's sons as their leader, to aid him against the Alani was refused; see Dom. 2, 2.

: the initial distrust and jealousy between Mucianus and Vespasian as commanders of strong forces in neighbouring provinces was removed largely through the conciliatory agency of Vespasian's son Titus; cf. Tac. H. ii 5, Ceterum hic (Mucianus) Syriae, ille (Vespasianus) Iudaeae praepositus, vicinis provinciarum administrationibus invidia discordes, exitu demum Neronis positis odiis in medium consuluere, primum per amicos, dein praecipua concordiae fides Titus prava certamina communi utilitate aboleverat, natura atque arte compositus alliciendis etiam Muciani moribus.

: there were four legions (3rd Gallica, 4th Scythica, 6th Ferrata, 12th Fulminata) in Syria when Mucianus was appointed governor (Tac. H. і 10). The 3rd was transferred to Moesia (see on § 3). Mucianus, in urging Vespasian to strike for empire, says to him (H. ii 76): Tibi e Iudaea et Syria et Aegypto novem legiones (4 in Syria, 3 in Judaea, 2 in Egypt viz. 3rd Cyrenaica and 22nd Deiotariana) integrae, nulla acie exhaustae, non discordia corruptae, sed firmatus usu miles et belli domitor externi; classium alarum cohortium robora et fidissimi reges et tua ante omnes experientia.
: Tacitus (H. iv 51) calls them equites, the famous Parthian bowmen being cavalry.

: Mucianus was the commander of the forces which Vespasian sent ahead from the East; but Antonius Primus, without waiting for the arrival of Mucianus, advanced into Italy with the legions of Moesia, Dalmatia, and Pannonia, and defeated the Vitellians; see on Vitell. 18. Tacitus (H. ii 83) describes the troops of Mucianus and the manner of his march: Mucianus cum expedita manu, socium magis imperii quam ministrum agens, non lento itinere, ne cunctari videretur, neque tamen properans, gliscere famam ipso spatio sinebat, gnarus modicas vires sibi et maiora credi de absentibus; sed legio sexta et tredecim vexillariorum milia ingenti agmine sequebantur. The 6th legion had been stationed in Syria since the reign of Tiberius; the 13,000 vexillarii were most probably detachments of 2,600 from each of the five legions left behind, two in Syria and three in Judaea (Heraeus ad loc.).

: Dio lxv 9, τὸν μὲν Μουκιανὸν ἐς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἐπὶ τὸν Οὐιτέλλιον ἔπεμψεν, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐς τὴν Αἴγυπτον ἐκομίσθη: Oros. vii 9, 3, per Alexandriam profectus est Romam; sed cognita interfectione Vitelli paulisper Alexandriae substitit. Titus was left to carry on the war against the Jews; Tac. H. ii 82, Titum instare Iudaeae, Vespasianum obtinere claustra Aegypti placuit: sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et dux Mucianus et Vespasiani nomen ac nihil arduum fatis ("the destiny before which all difficulties vanish," Church and Brodribb).

: usually explained as Alexandria and Pelusium (cf. Hirtius, B. Alex. 26, tota Aegyptos maritimo accessu Pharo, pedestri Pelusio, velut claustris munita existimatur); but Alexandria alone may be meant, as in Liv. xlv 11 Pelusium is called claustra Aegypti, so too Philae in Luc. x 313. Braithwaite explains claustra Aegypti as "the stronghold of Egypt," Aegypti being a genitive of definition, but this interpretation finds no support in any of the uses of claustrum cited in the Thes. Ling. Lat. Vespasian argued that by controlling Egypt, the key of the corn-supply (claustra annonae), and by cutting off the revenues of the richest provinces (Syria, Asia, and Egypt), the army of Vitellius could be forced to surrender by lack of corn and pay (Tac. H. iii 8). For the vital importance of the occupation of Egypt cf. Tac. A. ii 59, Augustus .. seposuit ("kept for himself'") Aegyptum, ne fame urgueret Italiam, quisquis eam provinciam claustraque terrae ac maris quamvis levi praesidio adversum ingentes exercitus insedisset: id. H. i 11 (quoted on c. 6, 3 praefectus Aegypti).

: Tac. H. iv 82, altior inde Vespasiano cupido adeundi sacram sedem (Serapidis dei), ut super rebus imperii consuleret. The phrase capere auspicium occurs also in Apul. Met. ix 8; cf. c. augurium (Aug. 95): с. omen (Cic. Div. i 104): c. praesagia belli (Luc. vii 331).

: the splendour of this temple is described in Amm. Marc. xxii 16, 12: His accedunt altis sufflata fastigiis templa, inter quae eminet Serapeum, quod licet minuatur exilitate verborum, atriis tamen columnariis amplissimis et spirantibus signorum figmentis et reliqua operum multitudine ita est exornatum, ut post Capitolium, quo se venerabilis Roma in aeternum attollit, nihil orbis terrarum ambitiosius cernat. The worship of Serapis (or Sarapis) prevailed at Alexandria from c. 300 B.C. to c. 400 A.D. Many divergent accounts of its introduction are collected in Plut. De Is. et Osir. 28, 29 and Tac. H. iv 83, 84. Some said that Ptolemy I (323-285 в.с.) in obedience to a vision brought the colossal statue from Sinope in Pontus; others that Ptolemy III (247-222) introduced the god from Seleucia in Syria, or from Memphis in Egypt where a large Serapeum was excavated in 1850 by Mariette Bey. The Serapeum was a temple erected in connexion with the sepulchres of the dead Apis bulls, whose mummies were placed there in subterranean corridors described by Bevan, Ptolemaic Egypt p. 41. The name of the god is a blend of Osiris and Apis, the Egyptian Osir-Hapi; see Tit. 5, 3, n. Macrobius (Sat. i 7) says that the Egyptian priests of the older faith only accepted the worship of Serapis when forced to do so by the Ptolemies; but he was the principal god in the Greek and Roman towns of Egypt. identification of Serapis with various other divinities is mentioned in Tac. The (l.c.): deum ipsum multi Aesculapium, quod medeatur aegris corporibus, quidam Osirin, antiquissimum illis gentibus numen, plerique Iovem ut rerum omnium potentem, plurimi Ditem patrem (i.e. Pluto), insignibus quae in ipso manifesta, aut per ambages coniectant. The statue of Serapis at Alexandria perished when the temple was destroyed by Theodosius in 389 A.D. The worship of Serapis was introduced into Italy through Sicily and the Greek towns of Campania in the 2nd cent. B.C. For the triumph of the cults of Isis and Serapis in the Western world see Dill, Rom. Society from Nero to M. Aurelius 560 sqq.

: cf. the story as told in Tac. H. iv 82: Arceri templo cunctos iubet. Atque ingressus intentusque numini, respexit pone tergum e primoribus Aegyptiorum nomine Basiliden, quem procul Alexandria plurium dierum itinere et aegro corpore detineri haud ignorabat. Percontatur sacerdotes num illo die Basilides templum inisset; percontatur obvios num in urbe visus sit: denique missis equitibus explorat illo temporis momento octoginta milibus passuum afuisse. Tunc divinam speciem et vim responsi ex nomine Basilidis interpretatus est. This last sentence is explained by Doederlein: “Tunc agnovit illum, quem pone tergum conspexit, ipsum deum fuisse responsi loco apparentem, qui consulenti sub persona Basilidis fortunam principalem (βασιλείαν) portenderet."

: verbenae was used in the general sense of greenery of any kind (leaves, twigs, branches) employed for sacred purposes; cf. Donatus on Ter. Andr. 726: verbenae sunt omnes herbae frondesque festae. At times the term denotes more specifically rosemary, myrtle, bay, olive, and vervain itself (verbenaca, ἱερὰ βοτάνη); so Serv. on Aen. xii 120: Verbena proprie est herba sacra, ros marinus, ut multi volunt, abusive tamen verbenas iam vocamus omnes frondes sacratas, ut est laurus, oliva, et myrtus. For the various purposes (offerings, wreaths, etc.) for which verbenae were utilised see Daremberg-Saglio, v 736. ..

: panificium is used by Varro (L.L. v 105) of the process of breadmaking, by Celsus (ii 18) of the bread that is made. Here it seems to mean a sacrificial cake such as those offered to Osiris which are called popana in Juv. vi 541, tenui popano corruptus Osiris (πόπανα = πλακούντια πλατέα καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ περιφερῆ, Schol. ad Plat. Rep. v 227). So at Roman sacrifices placentae or liba were used.
: the priest consulted by Vespasian on Mount Carmel (see c. 5, 6) bore, according to Tac. H. ii 78, the same name, a name (from βασιλεύς “king") which augured well for Vespasian's hopes of empire.

: Tacitus (H. iv 82) describes Basilides as an Egyptian noble (e primoribus Aegyptiorum), and Suet. may be incorrect in his description, though his version of the story differs in other respects from that of Tac. (e.g. Tac. makes Vespasian's visit to the Serapeum a consequence of the miraculous cures which he had effected). Torrentius, Marcilius, and others regard libertus as a mere interpolation of some ‘“malus grammaticus.’” Casaubon's theory is that it may have got into the text through a dittography of the last two syllables of Basilides. Oudendorp proposed liberius; Bentley uberius. I would suggest Libye ortus. Ernesti defends libertus on the ground that Vespasian would have been familiar with the appearance of one of his own freedmen, whereas it is improbable that on his first visit to Alexandria he would have known this Egyptian noble, and that the very fact that he had given Basilides his freedom was a happy omen for his deliverance of Rome from oppression. We know of another Basilides, probably a procurator, who is mentioned as an imperial freedman (Καίσαρος ἀπελεύθερος) in a decree of the prefect of Egypt in 49 A.D. (C.I.G. 4956; Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. i 229).

: Suetonius speaks as if the news of the defeat of Vitellius (near the end of October) and of his death (near the end of December) reached Vespasian at Alexandria simultaneously. Tacitus is more precise. In H. iii 48 he says that Vespasian had not yet reached Alexandria when he got news of his victory: Vespasianum Cremonensis proelii nuntius in Aegypto adsequitur. Eo properantius Alexandriam pergit, etc.; in iv 51 he says that many Romans of every rank risked the perils of the wintry sea to bring tidings to Vespasian at Alexandria of the fall of Vitellius: ut Vespasiano post Cremonensem pugnam et prosperos undique nuntios, cecidisse Vitellium multi cuiusque ordinis, pari audacia fortunaque hibernum mare adgressi, nuntiavere.

: the two battles known as the battles of Betriacum (or Bedriacum) were fought much nearer to Cremona; see on Oth. 9, 2. Cremona was very loyal to Vitellius, and after the second battle (Oct., 69), in which the Vitellians were routed, Antonius Primus captured, sacked, and burned the city.
: as described in Vitell. 17.

div.p: § 2. auctoritas.. maiestas: similarly Dio (lxvi 8) says that Vespasian was invested with σεμνότης by the miracles which he performed at Alexandria: τὸ θεῖον τούτοις αὐτὸν ἐσέμνυνεν (his rebus numen eum venerabilem effecit); cf. Tac. iv 81, multa miracula evenere, queis caelestis favor et quaedam in Vespasianum inclinatio numinum ostenderetur.

p.note: : scilicet is quite pleonastic after ut (= utpote), and its genuineness has been suspected. Torrentius approved the reading ut solet given in one of the MSS. which he used; but ut solet is probably due to ut illic assolet a few lines above. There is another remarkable pleonasm in Tit. 7, 3, abstinuit alieno, ut si quis umquam, where see note.

: cf. Tac. (l.c.): E plebe Alexandrina quidam oculorum tabe notus genua eius advolvitur remedium caecitatis exposcens gemitu, monitu Serapidis dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit; precabaturque principem ut genas et oculorum orbes dignaretur respergere oris excremento. Alius manum aeger, eodem deo auctore, ut pede ac vestigio Caesaris calcaretur orabat.
: Tac. says manum aeger, and so Dio (lxvi 8) Οὐεσπασιανὸς τυφλόν τέ τινα, καὶ ἕτερον οὐκ ἀρτίχειρα, . . . τοῦ μὲν τὴν χεῖρα πατήσας, τοῦ δὲ τοῖν ὀφθαλμοῖν προσπτύσας, ὑγιεῖς ἀπέφηνε.

: "at the front of the tribunal," having, as it were, the tribunal behind him; cf. pro suggestu (Caes., etc.) of a speaker standing forward on the platform, and pro rostris, which is used by post-Aug. writers of speakers (e.g. Calig. 10, 1, defunctam pro rostris laudavit) and of statues, etc., on the Rostra (e.g. Vitell. 3, 1). Tenney Frank (Rivista di Filologia lii 1, 1925), discussing phrases like pro tribunali where the original meaning of pro was "before," says that tribunal originally signified the seat of the tribunes, on whom the orator turned his back; afterwards it was used to denote the fixed platform on which this seat came to be placed (Class. Quart. xx 1, 1926).

: cf. Dio (l.c.), ἐξ ὕψεως τῶν ὀνειράτων. We constantly read of dreams in connexion with Serapis: the bringing of the statue of the god from Sinope to Alexandria was due to a vision which appeared to Ptolemy per quietem (Tac. H. iv 83); cf. Cic. Div. ii 59, qui (= quo) igitur convenit aegros a coniectore ('interpreter’”) somniorum potius quam a medico petere medicinam? an Aesculapius, an Serapis potest nobis praescribere per somnium curationem valetudinis, Neptunus gubernantibus non potest?: Artemid. Oneirocr. v 92, νοσῶν τις εὔξατο τῷ Σεράπιδι, εἰ μέλλει σωθήσεσθαι, τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτῷ χεῖρα ὄναρ ἐπισείεσθαι, εἰ δὲ μή, ἀριστεράν. Sleeping in the temples of Serapis and Aesculapius (ἐγκοίμησις, incubatio) in order to get such visions was a common practice; Strabo (xvii 801) says that the most distinguished men used to sleep in the temple of Serapis at Canobus, to have cures revealed to them.

: cf. Plaut. Capt. 550, qui insputatur morbus (epilepsy, comitialis morbus). For the supposed curative effects of saliva see Plin. N.H. xxviii 7, where ophthalmia, among other diseases, is said to yield to it. Spitting was also supposed to avert the "evil eye" and to aid the effects of medicine: Plin. (l.c.), terna despuere deprecatione in omri medicina mos est atque ita effectus adiuvare. In the N.T. the healing of a deaf man and of a blind man by spittle are mentioned among the miracles, and Casaubon, in his note on our passage, says: "Agnoscis, pie lector, falsam imitationem miraculorum Christi. Sic solitus illudere hominibus & δαίμων.” David Hume in his famous sceptical Essay on Miracles adduces this miracle of Vespasian. Spartianus, vit. Hadr. 25, mentions two cases of blindness being cured by contact with the emperor Hadrian. Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, was said to have been able to cure splenetic persons by touching them with his toe (Plin. N.H. vii 20).

div.p: § 3. cum vix fides esset successuram: for the constr. see on Oth. 5, 2, haud dubia fiducia plures adfuturos.

p.note: : Tacitus (iv 81) describes how Vespasian was gradually induced to make the attempt: Vespasianus primo inridere, aspernari; atque illis instantibus modo famam vanitatis metuere, modo obsecratione ipsorum et vocibus adulantium in spem induci. Postremo aestimari a medicis iubet an talis caecitas ac debilitas ope humana superabiles forent. Medici varie disserere: huic non exesam vim luminis, et redituram si pellerentur obstantia; illi elapsos in pravum artus, si salubris vis adhibeatur, posse integrari. Id fortasse cordi deis, et divino ministerio principem electum, denique patrati remedii gloriam penes Caesarem, inriti ludibrium penes miseros fore. Igitur Vespasianus cuncta fortunae suae patere ratus nec quicquam ultra incredibile, laeto ipse voltu, erecta quae adstabat multitudine, iussa exsequitur. Statim conversa ad usum manus, ac caeco reluxit dies. Utrumque, qui interfuere, nunc quoque memorant, postquam nullum mendacio pretium.

: in front of the assembled populace, facing them; a very favourite phrase with Suet. who uses it twenty times (e.g. Galb. 17, Oth. 6, 3). For examples in Sall., Liv., and other authors see KühnerStegmann, i 514. "in contione" is constantly used in pre-class. and class. writers.

: eventus is used at times in the Latin of this period for "a successful result"; cf. Iul. 20, 5, desperans tam praecipitis consilii eventum: Tac. A. ii 26, satis iam eventuum, satis casuum: Plin. Εp. v 20, egi ego pro Vareno non sine eventu.

: Tegea (mod. Paleo-Episkopi) in Arcadia was one of the oldest towns in the Peloponnesus. It possessed a famous temple of Athena Alea, described by Pausanias (viii 45). Strabo (fl. 25 B.C.) says that while the other well-known towns of Arcadia had perished, leaving scarcely a trace behind, Tegea was still in a tolerable state of preservation: viii 388, Τεγέα δ᾽ ἔτι μετρίως συμμένει, καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τῆς ᾿Αλέας ᾿Αθηνᾶς.

: on his voyage from Alexandria Vespasian visited Rhodes and several cities in Asia Minor. He crossed from Ionia to Greece and then from Corcyra to the Iapygian promontory on the Tarentine Gulf, and was warmly welcomed by the Italian cities and by the capital. Cf. Joseph. Bell. Iud. vii 2, 4. He did not arrive at Rome before September, 70 A.D.

: it was not till June, 71 A.D., that this triumph was celebrated. The senate had decreed separate triumphs to Vespasian and Titus; Vespasian decided that one should suffice, and for the first time in its history Rome saw a father and son triumphing together (cf. Tit. 6, 1: Dom. 2, 1). The triumph as described by Josephus (vii 5, 4) was of unparalleled splendour (magnificus triumphus, Oros. vii 9, 8). Vespasian was weary of the pompous ceremony before its close, and chided himself for his folly in wanting a triumph at his age; see c. 12.

: Vespasian's first consulship was in 51 A.D. under Claudius, when he was consul suffectus for the last two months of the year. He held the office for the second time in 70 along with Titus, the senate bestowing it by decree (Tac. H. iv 3, 38); again in 71 with Nerva, and in 72, 74, 75, 76, 77, 79 with Titus (cf. Tit. 6, 1).

: Vespasian and Titus assumed the censorship in 73, probably in April. For the epigraphic evidence of this see Newton (op. cit. p. 28 sqq.) and Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2'655). According to Censorinus (de die natali 18, 14) the lustrum which closed the censorship took place in 74; but in spite of the lustrum conditum, the title of "Censor" is frequently given as an honorary title to Vespasian and Titus in inscriptions in the following years. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 350, n. 3) shows that in Plin. N.H. vii 162, census quem intra quadriennium imperatores Caesares Vespasiani pater filiusque censores egerunt, the words intra quadriennium have been usually misinterpreted as meaning "during four years (71-74)," whereas the real meaning is "four years ago," i.e. four years before the date at which Pliny was writing.

: cf. Vitell. 15, 3, iuravit.. nihil sibi antiquius quiete publica fore: Claud. 11, 1, nihil antiquius duxit quam id biduum .. memoriae eximere. The phrase aliquid (or nihil) antiquius habere, used at all periods of Lat., is exactly the Gr. πρεσβύτερόν τι (οr οὐδὲν) ἔχειν.

div.p: § 2. ignominiae: the “humiliating defeat" of the Vitellians at Betriacum (or Cremona, see c. 7, 1). For this sense of “ignominia’” cf. Oth. 9, 3, ne victis quidem adeo afflictis ut non in ultionem ignominiae quidvis discriminis subirent: Ner. 39, 1, ignominia ad Orientem legionibus in Armenia sub iugum missis: Aug. 23, graves ignominias cladesque duas accepit. civitates liberae: these free states or cities "although geographically, were not juristically within a province at all" (Greenidge, Roman Public Life p. 317). Under the Republic they were free from Roman taxation and enjoyed complete autonomy. They were outside the jurisdiction of the governor, who could only enter a civitas libera as its guest. Under the Empire, however, their libertas no longer conferred immunity from Roman taxation (Greenidge, p. 428; cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 654 sqq., Marquardt, Staatsv. i² 71 sqq.). nec non et see on Tit. 5, 2.

p.note: : client kingdoms on the frontiers of the Empire (such as Commagene, mentioned below in § 4), ruled by kings in alliance with Rome (reges socii), each bound by terms of his special treaty (valid only during his lifetime), but all under an obligation to furnish troops if required.

: exauctorare (= ab auctoramento, id est obligatione militari, et iuramento solvere) was at times used of an honorable discharge (see on "missio,” Vitell. 15, 1), but more often of a summary and dishonorable dismissal (cf. Vitell. 10, 1). Tacitus (H. iv 46) describes the steps taken by Mucianus, before Vespasian's arrival at Rome, to reinstate the praetorians who had been dismissed by Vitellius and had then sided with Vespasian, and to get rid of the 16 praetorian cohorts formed by Vitellius from the Germanic legions. These cohorts could not safely be disbanded all at once, and Mucianus was forced to proceed very gradually: quibus aetas et iusta stipendia, dimissi cum honore, alii ob culpam, sed carptim ac singuli. Vespasian restored the old number of 9 praetorian cohorts. The legions with which Vespasian dealt drastically were those of which merely detachments had fought for Vitellius at the second battle of Betriacum (Vitell. 15, 2, n.), but of which the main body had remained in Germany and taken part in the revolt of Civilis (69-70 A.D., see Tac. H. iv 12 sqq.; not mentioned by Suet.). Three of them (i Germanica, iv Macedonica, xvi Gallica) were disbanded; apparently also xv Primigenia which surrendered to Civilis at Castra Vetera (H. iv 23, 60) and is not mentioned after 70 A.D. (see Dessau Inscr. 2275 n.). It is a disputed point whether v Alaudae was disbanded by Vespasian or was annihilated either in 86 by the Dacians or in 92 by the Sarmatians (Dom. '6, 1). See the articles "Legio" by Cagnat in Daremberg-Saglio and by Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa; also Parker, The Roman Legions, 107 sqq.

: the only special payment which we know was made to Vespasian's victorious soldiers was one by Mucianus of 100 sesterces each (Dio lxv 22). Vespasian had resolutely refused to promise the usual lavish donativa (see on Dom. 2, 3); cf. Tac. H. ii 82, donativum militi neque Mucianus nisi modice ostenderat, ne Vespasianus quidem plus civili bello obtulit quam alii in pace, egregie firmus adversus militarem largitionem eoque exercitu meliore. For adeo nihil ut (= tantum abest ut .., ut) cf. c. 12 adeo nihil appetivit, ut; it occurs from Livy on (Hand Tursell. i 141).

: praemia is frequently used by Suetonius for the bounties (commoda, see on Vitell. 15, 1) to which time-expired soldiers were entitled on their discharge; cf. Iul. 70, missionem et praemia flagitantes: Aug. 15, promissa veteranis praemia: ib. 49, 2, quicquid ubique militum esset, ad certam stipendiorum (i.e. service-time) praemiorumque formulam astrinxit. So‘commoda praemiorum” in Aug. 24, 1: (legiones) immodeste missionem postulantes citra ("without") commoda emeritorum praemiorum exauctoravit.

div.p: § 3. fragrantem unguento: fragrare is a poetic word, not found earlier in prose (see Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb.); it is used either with the abl. as here (cf. Catull. 6, 8) or with the acc. (e.g. Apul. Met. vi 11, Venus balsama fragrans).

p.note: : the command of an ala or squadron of auxiliary cavalry (see on Galb. 10, 2), one of the posts held by a young Roman qualifying in the army with a view to obtaining office at Rome and admission to the senate; cf. Aug. 38, 2, liberis senatorum militiam auspicantibus non tribunatum modo legionum, sed et praefecturas alarum dedit; ac ne qui expers castrorum esset, binos plerumque laticlavios praeposuit singulis alis.

: “aspernari est averti, non solum corpore, sed etiam animo” (Donat. on Ter. Phorm. 371). nutus is used here of drawing back or tossing back the head in disgust; cf. nutare in Plaut. Mil. 208, capite nutat: non placet quod repperit, where Ussing comments “non adnuens, sed renuens, nutu aspernatus, ut ait Sueton.”

: so in Plaut. Most. 39, oboluisti alium. The acc. was freely used with olere and its compounds; e.g. Varr. Men. 63, alium ac caepe olere: Cic. Phil. ii 63, redolere vinum (Kühner-Stegmann, i 277). alium “garlic survives in the Romance languages: Ital. aglio, Fr. ail, Span. ajo. On the forms alium and allium (given here by QR) Vollmer (Thes. Ling. Lat.) says: “proba scriptura est ‘alium' firmata titulo Pompeiano Corp. iv 2070 et codicibus melioribus (ut Ambr. Plaut. Poen. 1314 ali[i] ); tamen iam primo post Chr. saeculo scribebant “allium” (Inscr. Pompei. p. 1620, 15) quae scriptio fere regnat apud librarios recentiores." = litteras: "letters patent,” “commission," dati officii codicillos (Claud. 29, 1, suppositos aut etiam palam immutatos datorum officiorum codicillos). For "litterae" used of official ordinances cf. Cic. Verr. v 56, cedo mihi eiusdem praetoris litteras et rerum decretarum et frumenti imperati.
: revocare in the sense of rescindere is not used in class. prose; it occurs in Sen., Tac., etc.

: Ostia (at the mouth of the Tiber, 16 miles from Rome) and Puteoli (on the coast of Campania) were two of the squadron-stations of the main Roman fleet at Misenum. In Claud. 25, 2 Suetonius mentions that Claudius stationed cohorts at Ostia and Puteoli to guard against the danger of fires (Puteolis et Ostiae singulas cohortes ad arcendos incendiorum casus collocavit). It is not definitely known whether those cohorts consisted of classiarii “marines” (so Daremberg-Saglio, i 1222), or were two of the cohortes urbanae (so Smilda ad loc., following Mommsen, Hermes xvi 645). See also on Oth. 8, 2.

: sc. argenti "shoe-money"; cf. Digest ii 15, 8, 14, de calciario quoque arbitrio praetoris transigendum est: xxxiv 1, 21, neque vestiarium neque calciarium deberi palam est. Similarly clavarium “shoenail-money," Тас. Н. iii 50, seditiosae militum voces .. clavarium (donativi nomen est) flagitantium. See Parker, Rom. Legions 223.
: see on c. 4, 3.
: cf. Calig. 29, 1, Monenti Antoniae aviae tamquam parum esset non oboedire: “Memento,” ait, “omnia mihi et in omnes licere.'"

: here, as in other writers, excalciare has a personal object; contrast Vitell. 2, 5, petit ut sibi pedes praeberet excalciandos. Varro (ap. Non. 478 M.) has excalciari as a deponent: ad Herculis, ut introeat, nemo se excalciatur. Suetonius also uses discalciatus "unshod" "barefooted" (Ner. 51).
: these classiarii seem to have been used as couriers (cursores); see Hirschfeld, Kaiserl. Verwaltungsb.2 228, 3.

div.p: § 4. Achaiam: Augustus assigned the province of Achaia to the senate and it was governed by a proconsul (Dio liii 12). In 16 A.D. Tiberius made it an imperial province (Tac. A. i 76), but Claudius gave it back to the senate (Claud. 25). Nero abolished the province and proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games in 67 (Ner. 24: Plut. Flamin. 12: Dio lxiii 11). Vespasian declared the Greeks incapable of freedom and restored the senatorial province with a yearly tribute (Paus. vii 17).

p.note: : the cities-league of Lycia (Λυκίων τὸ κοινόν) was a civitas libera et foederata from the Sullan period on. It suffered much under Cassius in 43 B.C., but its freedom was recognised a second time by M. Antonius and it continued to enjoy it till 43 A.D. when Claudius took it away (Claud. 25, Lyciis ob exitiabiles inter se discordias libertatem ademit). Dio (lx 17) says that Claudius added Lycia to the praefectura of Pamphylia, but from the evidence available it seems to have been first formed into a province along with Pamphylia under Vespasian in 74. They formed an imperial province under the governorship of a praetorius legatus Augusti pro praetore. See Marquardt, Staatsv. i² 374 sqq.

: Rhodes had been made a civitas foederata for its staunch support of Rome in the Macedonian and Mithridatic wars (Appian Bell. Civ. iv 66 sqq.). It lost its freedom in 44 A.D. for crucifying some Roman citizens (Dio lx 24), but recovered it in 53, Nero pleading its cause before Claudius (Suet. Claud. 25 libertatem Rhodiis ob paenitentiam veterum delictorum reddidit: Tac. A. xii 58, reddita Rhodiis libertas, adempta saepe aut firmata, prout bellis externis meruerant aut domi seditione deliquerant). Presumably Rhodes and Samos (see below) were brought into the province of Asia by Vespasian. Marquardt (op. cit. 348) points out that this was the origin of the mistaken statement in Sextus Rufus Brev. 10, sub Vespasiano principe Insularum provincia facta est. The Insularum provincia, ἐπαρχία νήσων (κυκλάδων), is first mentioned in the reign of Diocletian, 284-305 A.D. (C.I.L. iii 450).

: Byzantium became a civitas foederata as a reward for its services to Rome in the war with the pseudo-Philip of Macedon (c. 150 в.с.). Later it became a civitas libera with freedom revocable by Rome at pleasure, whereas the freedom of a civitas foederata was guaranteed by a definite foedus. In Cic. Prov. Cons, 4, 6 it is mentioned as a civitas libera which had been outrageously plundered by the proconsul L. Piso. In the time of Claudius it was no longer immunis, for envoys appeared before the senate in 53 A.D. asking for relief, and Claudius helped them to secure a remission of tribute for 5 years on account of their losses in recent Thracian wars (Tac. A. xii 62). Pliny, N.H. iv 11, speaks of it as an oppidum liberae condicionis, but Vespasian took away its freedom. For its relation to the province of Macedonia, and later to that of Bithynia, where the younger Pliny was governor, see Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 43.

: the island of Samos was united to the province of Asia in 84 B.C. Augustus wintered at Samos in 20-19 в.с. and bestowed freedom on the islanders as a reward for their hospitality (Dio liv 7, 9). It is mentioned as a free state in Plin. N.H. v 37 (Pliny's work was dedicated to Titus in 77 A.D.).

: the reading of all the better MSS. is thraciam, which was corrected by Turnebus to Tracheam and by Bentley to Trachiam (found in Ⅱ), both these forms representing the Gr. Τραχεῖαν, and the adoption of either correction is necessary. Thraciam (retained by Roth and Preud'homme) is meaningless, for Thrace had been already made a province under a procurator in 46 A.D., and only Cilicia Trachia, not Cilicia generally, could be described in the words of Suet. “dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus.” The mountainous western part of Cilicia was known as τραχεῖα aspera, the eastern plainland as πεδιάς campestris, the boundary being the city of Soli. When the province of Cilicia (first constituted in 102 B.C.) was re-organised in 64 B.c., the mountainous parts were left to tributary native princes. M. Antonius gave Cilicia Trachia to Cleopatra in 36 B.C. Later it was held by Amyntas, king of Galatia. On his death in 25 B.c. it was given by Augustus to Archelaus of Cappadocia and after his death in 17 A.D., when Cappadocia became a province, his family seem to have remained in possession of Cilicia Trachia until Caligula gave it along with Commagene to Antiochus IV (Dio lix 8). Caligula later deposed Antiochus, but Claudius restored him (Dio lx 8) and he ruled Cilicia Trachia until Vespasian finally attached it to the province of Cilicia in 74. See Marquardt, op. cit. i² 313, who points out that the same confusion of Trachia and Thracia occurs in the repetition of the words of Suet. by Eutrop. (vii 19), Aur. Vict. (Epit. 9), and Hieron. (Eusebii Chron. p. 159 Schoene).

: this district lay between Cappadocia on the N. and Syria on the S.; it was bounded on the E. by the Euphrates, and on the W. by Cilicia. For over a hundred years it had its own kings connected with the family of the Seleucidae in Syria. In 17 A.D., on the death of Antiochus III, it was made a Roman province by Tiberius, but was given back by Caligula in 38 to Antiochus IV, a son of the late king. In 72 the governor of Syria deposed him, by command of Vespasian, for intriguing with Parthia, and Commagene was made part of the province of Syria; its capital Samosata received the additional name of Flavia.

: cf. Eutrop. vii 19; Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Epit. 9; Oros. vii 9. Similar punishments by deprivation of freedom were inflicted by Augustus (Aug. 47, urbium quasdam foederatas sed ad exitium licentia praecipites libertate privavit, these cities being Cyzicus, which was shortly after reinstated, Tyre, and Sidon); by Tiberius on Cyzicus (Tib. 37); by Claudius on Rhodes and Lycia (Claud. 25); by Septimius Severus in 196 on Byzantium, which must have recovered the freedom taken from it by Vespasian (Dio lxxiv 14). For the technical expression in formam provinciae redigere” to denote the subjection of a community to Rome by placing it under a Roman governor see Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 1166.

: in 15 A.D. Tiberius, out of pique for a want of respect shown to him when staying at Rhodes, treacherously invited Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, to Rome and kept him there till his death in 17, when his kingdom was made a Roman province (Tac. A. ii 42, 56; Dio lvii 17; Strab. xii 534). From that time on it was governed by procurators (Tac. A. xii 49) until Vespasian gave it a consular governor with a legionary force. The evidence of inscriptions shows that Vespasian joined Cappadocia (with Lesser Armenia, etc.) to Galatia in one vast administrative sphere, and that this arrangement continued till the later years of Trajan, who made Galatia and Cappadocia separate provinces with separate governors. See Brandis in Pauly-Wissowa vii 552; Henderson, Five Rom. Emperors p. 60.

: cf. Tac. H. ii 81, inermes legati regebant (the Asiatic provinces in 69) nondum additis Cappadociae legionibus. One of the legions was the 12th Fulminata, and the other (as von Domaszewski suggests) was probably the 16th Flavia, a new legion organised by Vesp. in place of the disbanded 16th Gallica. Josephus (Bell. Iud. vii 1, 3) says the 12th legion was sent to Melitene in Cappadocia late in 70, so the consular legatus must have been appointed by that time (Marquardt, p. 367).

: Dio (lvii 17) mentions that Tiberius gave the administration of Cappadocia to an eques: κακ τούτου (i.e. from 17 A.D.) ἡ Καππαδοκία τῶν τε ῾Ρωμαίων ἐγένετο καὶ ἱππεῖ ἐπετράπη. Such personal agents of Caesar (procuratores Caesaris pro legato) governed the less important outlying districts which were reckoned under the imperial provinces.

div.p: § 5. deformis urbs: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, Romam deformem incendiis veteribus ac ruinis, permissa, si domini deessent, volentibus aedificandi copia, Capitolium, aedem Pacis, Claudii monumenta reparavit multaque nova instituit. In addition to his restorations and constructions of buildings in Rome, Vespasian repaired at his own expense the streets which were in a sorry condition; cf. the senate's decree of thanks in the latter part of 71 (C.I.L. vi 931, Newton 113): Imp. Caesari Vespasiano Aug., pont. max., tr. pot. iii, imp. iix, p.p., cos. iii, des. iiii, s.c., quod vias urbis neglegentia superior. tempor. corruptas inpensa sua restituit.

p.note: : the great fire at Rome in '64 A.D., which Suetonius (Ner. 38) attributes to Nero himself, and the burning of the Capitol by the Vitellians (see Vitell. 15, 3). 2E .. sine

: area meant a vacant space (cf. Paul. Fest. 11, area proprie dicitur locus vacuus: Digest 1 16, 211, locus aedificio in urbe area, rure ager appellatur), and so a building-site; e.g. Iul. 26, 2, Forum . . incohavit, cuius area super sestertium milies constitit : Hor. Ep. i 10, 13, ponendaeque domo quaerenda est area primum. For aedificare with acc. of the site cf. Varro L.L. v 147, aedificatus locus: Liv. i 35, 10, privatis aedificanda divisa sunt loca. In Digest xli 4, 13, aream emit et aedificare coepit, most probably aedificare is to be taken absolutely, as it may be in our passage.
: see on Galb. 4, 3. ..

: the same account is given in Dio lxvi 10, τόν τε νεὼν τὸν ἐν τῷ Καπιτωλίῳ εὐθὺς οἰκοδομεῖν ἤρξατο, αὐτός τε τοῦ χοῦ πρῶτος ἐκφορήσας, καὶ δηλονότι καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις τοῖς ἐπιφανεστάτοις τὸ αὐτὸ τοῦτο κελεύσας, ἵνα καὶ τῷ λοιπῷ πλήθει ἀπαραίτητον τὸ διακόνημα γένηται. The difficulty is that Vesp. did not arrive in Italy and Rome till the late summer of 70, and Tacitus (who was probably an eyewitness) in describing the ceremonies at the dedication of the site and the laying of the foundation-stone of the new temple on June 21 does not mention the emperor as taking part, but says that he commissioned Vestinus to supervise the work: H. iv 53, curam restituendi Capitolii in Lucium Vestinum confert, equestris ordinis virum, sed auctoritate famaque inter proceres. Weynand (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2648) tries to get over the difficulty by assuming that Vesp., when he arrived later at Rome, helped to clear away the débris.

: rubbish from the buildings which had been destroyed by fire; cf. Aug. 30, 1, alveum Tiberis laxavit ac repurgavit, completum olim ruderibus et aedificiorum prolationibus (‘extensions") coartatum: Ner. 38, 3 (of Nero after the great fire at Rome), pollicitus cadaverum et ruderum gratuitam egestionem: Tac. A. xv 43 (referring to the same), ruderi accipiendo Ostienses paludes destinabat, utique naves, quae frumentum Tiberi subvectavissent, onustae rudere decurrerent. The more usual meaning of rudus is a kind of concrete made from broken stones mixed with lime and used for building purposes.

: similarly Nero, to stimulate the praetorians at the attempt to dig through the Isthmus of Corinth, ‘primus rastello ('mattock') humum effodit et corbulae ('basket') congestam umeris extulit” (Ner. 19, 2). Germanicus, at the construction of a mound over the bones of the legions of Varus, "primum extruendo tumulo caespitem posuit'' (Tac. A. i 62).

: cf. Apul. Met. ix 7, calamitosus faber collo suo gerens dolium: Luc. i 603, Salius laeto portans ancilia collo: Catull. 10, 23, fractum qui veteris pedem grabati | in collo sibi collocare posset. aerearum tabularum: all engagements entered into by Rome with foreigners, whether international treaties or privileges conferred on individuals, were engraved on bronze tablets and affixed to the walls of public buildings and temples, more especially in the immediate neighbourhood of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. Polybius (iii 26) saw the old trade treaties between Rome and Carthage ἐν χαλκώμασι παρὰ τὸν Δία τὸν Καπετώλιον ἐν τῷ τῶν ἀγορανόμων ταμιείῳ (‘"the archives of the aediles''). Cf. also Appian Syr. 39 (on the treaty with Antiochus in 189 в.с.), ταῦτα συγγραψάμενοί τε καὶ ἐς τὸ Καπιτώλιον ἐς δέλτους χαλκᾶς ἀναθέντες, οὗ καὶ τὰς ἄλλας συνθήκας ἀνατιθέασιν : Cic. Phil. ii 36, toto Capitolio tabulae figebantur, neque solum singulis venibant immunitates, sed etiam populis universis; civitas non iam singillatim, sed provinciis totis dabatur unum egregium de rege Deiotaro, populi R. amicissimo, decretum in Capitolio fixum. See Mommsen, Staatsr. i3 257; Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 52. Tacitus (H. iv 40) says that the senate before the arrival of Vesp. had appointed a commission “qui aera legum vetustate delapsa noscerent figerentque." It is uncertain whether this was another version of what Suet. says, or whether Vesp. supplemented the labours of this commission (see Spooner ad loc.).

: cf. Dom. 20, exemplaribus undique petitis (when Domitian was restoring the libraries consumed by fire at Rome). The copies (exemplaria) used by Vespasian were such as are mentioned in Liv. xxvi 24, 14, haec convenerunt conscriptaque biennio post Olympiae ab Aetolis, in Capitolio ab Romanis, ut testata sacris monumentis essent, sunt posita: C.I.G. 2485 (an alliance between Rome and Astypalaea in 105 B.c., a copy of which was to be preserved on bronze at the temple of Athena in Astypalaea).

: in apposition with aerearum milia. The word is used here of an official record; cf. Calig. 8, 5, sequenda est publici instrumenti (i.e. the acta publica or acta diurna) auctoritas: Quintil. xii 8, 12, opus est intueri omne litis instrumentum (i.e. every document connected with the case): Digest xxiv 1, 58, emptionum instrumenta suo nomine confecit. Lawyers use "instrument" for a writing acknowledging or certifying to a claim, or recording the terms of a contract, deed, or grant.

: e.g. the decree (78 B.c.) granting friendship and privileges to Asclepiades of Clazomenae, Polystratus of Carystus, and Meniscus of Miletus, three naval captains who had rendered services to Rome in 90-89 during the Italian revolt (C.I.L. i 203; Bruns, Fontes Iuris Rom. p. 176; Wordsworth, Frag. and Spec. p. 205). A similar grant of privileges was decreed by the senate to Onesimus a Macedonian for services rendered by his father to Rome in the war against Perseus (Liv. xliv 16). As M has the reading consultam, Bentley would insert ac (or et) after consulta.

: e.g. the Lex Antonia de Termessibus (71 B.c.) confirming the autonomy granted to Termessus, a town in Pisidia (C.I.L. i 204; Bruns, p. 92; Wordsworth, p. 209). This measure was introduced by the tribune C. Antonius “de s(enatus) s(ententia)," i.e. with the sanction of the senate, in accordance with Sulla's ordinance (88 B.c.) requiring such sanction for any measure brought before the plebeian assembly; but in 70 B.C. the Lex Pompeia restored the unrestricted legislative validity secured for plebi scita by the Lex Hortensia in 287. =

: in class. Lat. privilegium meant a special ordinance, an exceptional measure in favour of or directed against an individual (privus singulus), which in Republican times was illegal. It was under the Caesars that the word first acquired the sense of a prerogative or "privilege” granted by a special ordinance; class. writers express this by beneficium, ius praecipuum, etc. (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb.).
: see on Galb. 4, 3. 2E2

: the inscriptions bearing on the building activity of the reigns of Vespasian and Titus, not merely in Rome but also in Italy and the provinces, are collected by Newton, op. cit. 46 sqq. Among these inscriptions are C.I.L. iii 6702, 11194-11196; vi 301, 369, 814, 934 (where Vesp. is described as restitutor aedium sacrarum), 935, 936, 939, 940 (where there is mention of a collegium subrutorum whose work, according to Mommsen, ad loc., was to dig out the ruins of buildings destroyed by fire, etc.); x 1406, 1481; xi 598; xiv 3485.

: cf. Dio lxvi 15, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἕκτον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Τίτου τέταρτον ἀρχόντων (75 A.D.) τὸ τῆς Εἰρήνης τέμενος καθιερώθη : Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Romae Capitolium, quod conflagravisse supra memoravimus, aedes Pacis, Claudii monumenta, amphitheatri tanta vis multaque alia ac forum coepta seu patrata. Josephus (Bell. Iud. vii 5) says of the building of this temple: “ταχὺ δὲ δὴ μάλα, καὶ πάσης ἀνθρωπίνης κρεῖττον ἐπινοίας ἐτετελείωτο,” and describes its ornaments which included vessels of gold and silver from the Temple in Jerusalem. Pliny (N.H. xxxvi 102) ranks it among the "pulcherrima operum quae umquam vidit orbis," and mentions several famous statues and pictures in it (xxxiv 84, xxxv 74, 109, 122). Domitian may have added some finishing touches to it, and he seems, in characteristic fashion (see Dom. 5), to have claimed the credit for the whole, which is given to him by the court poet Statius (Silv. iv 3, 17, qui Pacem propria domo reponit). The temple was burned down shortly before the death of Commodus (192 A.D.), but was soon restored. It seems to have been reduced to ruins by an earthquake in 408 A.D. Newton (p. 46, n. 7) points out that no inscription of this temple has been found, but no divinity was so frequently inserted by Vespasian on his coins as Pax (see Eckhel, vi p. 334) and there are several dedications to the "Pax Vespasiani'' in inscriptions, e.g. C.I.L. vi 200, Paci aeternae domus Imp. Vespasiani Caesaris Aug. liberorumq. eius sacrum.

: the Forum Romanum, to the N. of which the temple stood. The temple was built in an enclosed space, like the temple of Venus Genetrix in Caesar's forum and that of Mars Ultor in the forum of Augustus, and in the period after Constantine we find this space called forum Pacis (φόρον Εἰρήνης), e.g. in Amm. Marc. xvi 10, Procop. Bell. Goth. iv 21. Domitian connected the forum Augusti with the templum Pacis or forum Pacis by the forum Transitorium (see Dom. 5). (templum) Divi Claudi: cf. Claud. 45, funeratus est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum ("neglected") abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum. A portico surrounding it is probably that mentioned in Mart. Spect. 2, 9: Claudia diffusas ubi porticus explicat umbras | ultima pars aulae deficientis erat (i.e. the end of the Golden House of Nero was on this part of the Caelian mount). The temple is mentioned by Frontinus, de Aquaed. 20, 76, in connexion with the Aqua Claudia; also in C.I.L. vi 10251 a, T. Flavio Aug. lib. Trophimo constitutori collegi numinis dominorum quod est sup templo divi Claudi. There are still remains, not of the temple, but of the massive substructions; see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 232: Burn, Rome and the Campagna p. 221.

: between the Aventine and Esquiline, now the Lateran Mount; originally called Mons Querquetulanus from the oak-trees on it, it received the name Caelius from the Etruscan chief Caeles Vibenna (Etrusc. Kaile Fipne); under Tiberius the name was changed for a short time to Mons Augustus to commemorate the munificence of Tiberius in restoring it when devastated by fire (Suet. Tib. 48, Tac. A. iv 64). the Caelian were chapels of Dea Carna (Macrob. Sat. i 12), Minerva Capta (Ov. F. iii 837), and Diana (Cic. Har. Resp. 15); also a temple of Isis (Trebell. Poll. trig. tyrann. 24).
: see on c. 4, 2. On

: Platner-Ashby (Topogr. Dict. Rome p. 120) would account for this destruction partly by the construction of the distributing station of the Aqua Claudia, which Nero extended to the Caelian, and partly by the construction of the Domus Aurea.

: the vast Flavian amphitheatre, known as the Colosseum since about 1000 A.D. (Platner-Ashby, p. 6), was built in the valley between the Esquiline and Caelian on the site of the stagnum Neronis, i.e. the great pleasure lake of Nero's Golden House; cf. Mart. Spect. 2, 5, Hic ubi conspicui venerabilis amphitheatri | erigitur moles, stagna Neronis erant. It was begun by Vespasian in 72, continued and dedicated by Titus in 80, and completed by Domitian in 823; further additions were made by Alexander Severus (ob. 235) and Gordianus (ob. 238). The building was about a third of a mile in circumference, and could accommodate over 50,000 spectators. The magnificent remains attest the truth of Martial's lines (Spect. 1, 7): Omnis Caesareo cedit labor amphitheatro, | unum pro cunctis fama loquetur opus. See Jordan-Huelsen, op. cit. i 3, 282 sqq. Coins of Vesp. and Titus which depict the Flavian amphitheatre under different aspects are described by Eckhel, vi pp. 357- 359, 375, vii 271, 315; Cohen, i² p. 461, etc.

: we do not read elsewhere of this design of Augustus to build an amphitheatre in the heart of the city. The first stone amphitheatre was constructed by Statilius Taurus in the reign of Augustus (29 B.C.; cf. Suet. Aug. 29, Tac. A. iii 72, Dio li 23). It was in the Campus Martius. In the record of his reign contained in the Monumentum Ancyranum Augustus says (c. 22): Venationes bestiarum Africanarum meo nomine aut filiorum meorum et nepotum in circo aut in foro aut in amphitheatris populo dedi sexiens et viciens. Mommsen, Mon. Anc.² 94, commenting on the pl. amphitheatris, says that the word, first found here, was originally a plural “cum essent amphitheatra tanquam theatra duo," and that Aug. is referring only to the new amphitheatre of Taurus and not to other temporary wooden structures. But more probably amphitheatrum meant a building in which the θέατρον (i.e. the space for spectators, Zuschauerraum) ran round in a ring; see Meier in Pauly-Wissowa, i 1959.

div.p: § 2. amplissimos ordines: the ordo senatorius and ordo equester. The title amplissimus ordo was applied especially to the senate (see on c. 2, 3), but Cicero had already used amplissimi ordines to include senatores, equites, and tribuni aerarii, from all of whom the iudices were drawn at the time (e.g. Sull. 5, 15: Mil. 2, 4, where see Clark's note).
