Lipsius needlessly proposed to alter amplissimos to amplissimum, attaching it to the preceding sentence as an epithet of amphitheatrum, and Casaubon would either accept this change or read ambos ordines.

p.note: : a precedent for this "purgation" was that effected by Augustus; cf. Aug. 35, 1, Senatorum affluentem numerum deformi et incondita turba - erant enim super mille, et quidem indignissimi et post necem Caesaris per gratiam et praemium adlecti, quos orcinos (i.e. slaves set free by their master's will) vulgus vocabat - ad modum pristinum et splendorem redegit duabus lectionibus (these two lectiones or “revisions" were in 29 and 18 в.с.). supplevit: Aur. Vict. (Caes. 9) says that there were barely 200 gentes when Vesp. came to the throne, and that he raised the number to 1000: censu more veterum exercito, senatu motus probrosior quisque, ac lectis undique optimis viris, mille gentes compositae, cum ducentas aegerrime repperisset, exstinctis saevitia tyrannorum plerisque.

: Augustus established an annual probatio equitum (ἐξέτασις τῶν ἱππέων, Dio lv 31) combining the old annual travectio, or parade of those equites who had the equus publicus, and the recognitio equitum which had been held periodically by the censors. Before the parade, the emperor aided by ten senators held a strict investigation into the life of each of the equites and those who were proved unworthy were either degraded or reprimanded with varying degrees of severity; see Aug. 38 and 39 with Shuckburgh's notes. Suetonius also mentions the recognitio equitum by Caligula and Claudius: Calig. 16, 2, Equites R. severe curioseque nec sine moderatione recognovit, palam adempto equo quibus aut probri aliquid aut ignominiae inesset, eorum qui minore culpa tenerentur nominibus modo in recitatione praeteritis: Claud. 16, 1, Recognitione equitum iuvenem probri plenum, sed quem pater probatissimum sibi affirmabat, sine ignominia dimisit, habere dicens censorem suum, etc.
: in the case of senators movere senatu (or senatorio loco) was the usual expression for expulsion; cf. Dom. 8, 3. Tacitus

: cf. Aug. 35, 1 (quoted above on purgavit). tells of Tiberius expelling senators “prodigos et ob flagitia egentes” (A. ii 48, cf. Suet. Vitell. 2, 2) and another "quod in acta d. Augusti non iuraverat” (A. iv 42). Claudius enforced the resignation of those who were "famosi probris” (A. xi 25). Domitian expelled an ex-quaestor “quod gesticulandi saltandique studio teneretur” (Suet. Dom. 8, 3). Among those expelled by Vespasian was Palfurius Sura; see on Dom. 13, 1. sed

: cf. Tac. A. iii 55, novi homines e типіcipiis et coloniis (terms denoting the towns of Italy) atque etiam provinciis in senatum crebro adsumpti domesticam parsimoniam intulerunt praecipuus adstricti moris auctor Vespasianus fuit, antiquo ipse cultu victuque. Vespasian himself was a novus homo from Reate. Claudius, in his speech (partly preserved on a bronze tablet at Lugdunum, cf. Tac. A. xi 24) successfully advocating the admission of Gallic senators, says that Tiberius had freely enrolled senators from Italian towns. The first Paelignian senator was admitted under Augustus (C.I.L. ix 3306). Julius c, 9, 2.] Caesar had introduced some Gallic senators, who were received with bitter hostility at Rome (Iul. 76, 80). Otho, in 69 A.D., describes the senate as "caput imperii et decora omnium provinciarum” (Tac. H. i 84). A full account of the gradual admission of provincials to the senate is given by Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 107 sqq. In recruiting the equestrian order from the whole Roman empire Vespasian was following the example of Caligula of whom Dio (lix 9) says: τοῦ τε τέλους (ordinis) τοῦ τῶν ἱππέων ὀλιγαν - δροῦντος, τοὺς πρώτους ἐξ ἁπάσης καὶ τῆς ἔξω ἀρχῆς τοῖς τε γένεσι καὶ ταῖς περιουσίαις μεταπεμψάμενος κατελέξατο. See also on c. 3 supr.

: legere in senatum was the phrase used under the Republic of the censors retaining the names of old senators or admitting those newly qualified; adlectio is the tech. term under the Empire for the admission to the senate by imperial favour of those not regularly qualified. These adlecti were given varying rank among those senators who had been quaestors, praetors, etc. (adlecti inter quaestorios, aedilicios, tribunicios, praetorios, and, from the 3rd cent. A.D., consulares). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 939 sqq.; Willems, Le Sénat Romain i 626 sqq. Examples of those who were adlecti inter tribunicios or praetorios by Vespasian and Titus as censors are to be found in C.I.L. ii 4130, iii 335, vi 1359, viii 7057, ix 5533 (see Vesp. 13, note on Salvium Liberalem), xi 1834, xiv 2925; Plin. Ep. i 14. New patricians also were created in their censorship; see note on Oth. 1, 3, adlectum inter patricios. Among them were Annius Verus, grandfather of the emperor Marcus Aurelius (Capitol. Marc. Antonin. Philos. 1), and Agricola (Tac. Agr. 9). Two of the equites created by Vespasian were Hormus, one of his freedmen (Tac. H. iv 39), and Claudius (father of Claudius Etruscus, Stat. S. iii 3, 145), a freedman of Tiberius, who was a rationibus under Nero and still held that post under Domitian.
: the compound remaledicere (= ἀντιλοιδορεῖν) is first found here, and occurs later in Tertull. Idol. 21, Hieron. Ep. 69, 9. ..

: conduct befitting a true citizen living on terms of mutual respect with his fellow-citizens, neither submitting to insults nor insulting others. civilis (κοινός, δημοκρατικός) is repeatedly used by Suetonius of rulers who behave unassumingly, avoiding tyrannical arrogance (ὕβρις) and respecting the rights of those under their authority; e.g. Vesp. 12, ceteris in rebus civilis ac clemens: Claud. 12, 1, in semet augendo parcus atque civilis: Tib. 11, 1, genus vitae civile admodum instituit: Tib. 26, 1, civilem admodum ac paulo minus quam privatum egit: Calig. 3, 2, domi forisque civilis: Claud. 1, 4, fuisse creditur civilis animi: Dom. 12, 3, minime civilis animi: Tit. 6, 1, praefecturam praetorii egit aliquanto incivilius et violentius. So civilitas for moderation, constitutional conduct; Claud. 35, 1, primis imperii diebus iactator civilitatis : Aug. 51, 1, clementiae civilitatisque eius multa et magna documenta sunt. This use of civilis is not found before the Aug. period (Ov., Liv.). It is frequent in Tacitus; e.g. in H. iv 3, describing Vespasian's letter to the senate, he says: ut princeps loquebatur, civilia de se et rei publicae egregia.
: the very rare pl. series occurs earlier in the same phrase in Vell. Pat. ii 118, simulantes fictas litium series.
: excrescere is not found in class. Lat.; Suetonius uses it in Galb. 21 of a morbid excrescence on the body.

: Fest. p. 111 M., intercapedo, tempus interceptum, сит scilicet mora est ad capiendum. Cf. Aug. 38, 3, post longam intercapedinem reducto more travectionis: Plin. Εp. iv 9, 11, dicentis calor.. continuatione servatur, intercapedine et quasi remissione languescit: Cic. Fin. i 18, 61, in eorum vita nulla est miseriae intercapedo: Cic. Fam. xvi 21, non paenitebat intercapedinem scribendi ("a break in our correspondence") fecisse. The law courts had been suspended at Rome during the turmoil of civil strife in 69-70, and the rights of property must have been ruthlessly ignored in the armed violence which prevailed.

: Tac. H. iv 40, tum sorte ducti per quos redderentur bello rapta (Tacitus mentions this among the measures passed by the senate before the return of Vespasian). These special commissioners would be reciperatores (see on c. 3), and reciperatores were usually chosen by lot by the praetor urbanus when the case was between cives, by the praetor peregrinus when the case was between a civis and a peregrinus.

: it is doubtful whether the centumviral court is to be traced back to Servius Tullius or was established after the time (?241 B.C.) when the number of tribes was raised to 35. Festus says that the centumviri were nominated by the praetor, three from each of the 35 tribes. At some time under the early Empire the number was raised to 180, four panels of 45, each of which might hear separate cases, or two might sit together, or the whole four in important trials. The decemviri stlitibus iudicandis seem to have controlled the court; later, ex-quaestors; and finally Augustus reinstated the decemviri, acting under the superintendence of the praetor, who was styled hastarius or ad hastas, because the hasta as the symbol of dominium or ownership was planted in the ground before the place where the court was sitting. The centumviri dealt with questions of status, inheritance, dominium ex iure Quiritium, iura in re aliena such as rights of way, usufruct, etc. They originally sat in the Forum, but under the Empire in the Basilica Iulia. Most of the speeches of the younger Pliny were delivered in this court.

: cf. Cod. Iust. iii 1, 13, properandum nobis visum est, ne lites fiant paene immortales et vitae hominum modum excedant. Justinian introduced various changes in legal procedure, to ensure that justice be administered in a reasonable time. Complaints of the law's delays are frequent in Latin writers. Martial (vii 65) refers to a case dragging on for 20 years: Lis te bis decimae numerantem frigora brumae | conterit una tribus, Gargiliane, foris; cf. Juv. xvi 42, Expectandus erit qui lites incohet annus | totius populi. Sed tum quoque mille ferenda | taedia, mille morae. Suetonius tells of ordinances of Augustus (Aug. 32), Claudius (Claud. 23), and Galba (Galb. 14, 3) to increase the number of days available for legal business. For a discussion of the number of these dies iudiciarii (opp. to dies feriati) see the article "Actus rerum” in Pauly-Wissowa, i 331 sqq. ut

: these commissioners were empowered to take the most pressing cases first, so that each case had not to wait its turn for a prolonged hearing before the centumviri. For “extra ordinem” cf. Tac. A. xiii 51, edixit Romae praetor, per provincias qui pro praetore aut consule essent iura adversus publicanos extra ordinem redderent: Sen. Ep. 106, 2, dubitavi utrum differrem te an ius tibi extra ordinem dicerem. A defendant whose case could claim precedence was called extraordinarius reus (Cic. Fam. viii 8). Under the Roman legal system of formulae (Vitell. 7, 2, n.) there were certain cases which the praetor himself decided without sending them to a iudex. In such cases the praetor was said extra ordinem cognoscere, and the proceedings were termed extra ordinem cognitiones, iudicia, or actiones. See also on Dom. 8, 1.

: Vespasian frequently attended the meetings of the senate and consulted them on his proposals; Dio lxvi 10, ἔς τε τὸ συνέδριον διὰ παντὸς ἐφοίτα καὶ περὶ πάντων αὐτοῖς ἐπεκοίνου. A special ius referendi (ad senatum) was granted to Augustus in 23 B.C., giving him the right of making the first relatio at each meeting of the senate (Dio liii 32), and subsequent emperors had the same privilege; cf. the Sc. de imperio Vespasiani (Bruns, Fontes p. 202), utique ei senatum habere, relationem facere, remittere, senatus consulta per relationem discessionemque facere liceat. Later we read of the emperors making 4 or 5 relationes before the ordinary business of the senate (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 898). At first they made them in person, but more usually they sent them in the form of letters (litterae, epistulae) or speeches (orationes) to be read by the consuls or quaestors. Sometimes Titus read Vespasian's speeches in the senate; see Tit. 6, 1. ut.

: Vespasian re-enacted with modifications the senatus consultum Claudianum which is often mentioned by Roman jurists. The emperor Claudius got this passed by the senate in 52 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. xii 53, Inter quae refert ad patres de poena feminarum quae servis coniungerentur; statuiturque, ut ignaro domino ad id prolapsae in servitute, sin consensisset pro libertis haberentur. See also Gaius Inst. i 84-91 on which Poste says: "The Sc. Claudianum introduced some special enactments respecting the intercourse of freewomen with slaves, which, however, were subsequently abolished. (a) If a freewoman had intercourse with a slave with the consent of his proprietor she retained her freedom, though degraded to the class of a freedwoman, but her issue was the slave of the proprietor. The slavery of this issue was abolished by Hadrian. (b) If a freewoman persisted in intercourse with the slave of another person against the will and in spite of the prohibition of the proprietor, after three denunciations on his part she was awarded to him by the magistrate as a slave, and her issue, whether born before or after the adjudication, became slaves of the same person, who also acquired her estate by a species of universal succession. This terroristic law, which, from the minuteness with which the details are developed (Paulus 2, 21), appears to have been often applied, was not abrogated till the time of Justinian, Inst. 3, 12, 1. (c) If a freeman had intercourse with a slave whom he supposed to be free, her male children were born into freedom. This relief of error was abolished by Vespasian as anomalous (inelegans, Gaius § 85)." Vespasian in this last case declared that the offspring, male or female, should be slaves and the property of the mother's owner.

: a filius- or filia-familias was a male or female descendant in the power (potestas) of a pater-familias. On the legal position of filii familiarum see Roby, Rom. Priv. Law i '64 sqq. Their position was in some respects similar to that of slaves. In law they had no property; their father might allow them a peculium, but this was like a slave's peculium which legally was the master's property; cf. Suet. Tib. 15 (when Tiberius aged 44 was adopted as a son by Augustus in 2 A.D.), Nec quicquam postea pro patre familias egit aut ius, quod amiserat, ex ulla parte retinuit. Nam neque donavit neque manumisit, ne hereditatem quidem aut legata percepit ulla aliter quam ut peculio referret accepta (i.e. to place them to the credit of the peculium which he held with the permission of Augustus).

: Vespasian was only re-enacting, after the confusion of the civil wars, a measure of Claudius to stop money-lenders advancing money to youths on the post-obit system by which either the capital plus the interest, or the capital, was to be paid up after the father's death; cf. Tac. A. xi 13, lege lata saevitiam creditorum coercuit ne in mortem parentum pecunias filiis familiarum faenori darent. The Roman jurists mention a decree of the senate dealing with a usurer of this kind named Macedo; cf. Ulp. Dig. xiv 6, 1, Verba senatus consulti Macedoniani haec sunt: “Cum inter ceteras sceleris causas Macedo, quas illi natura administrabat, etiam aes alienum adhibuisset, et saepe materiam peccandi malis moribus praestaret, qui pecuniam, ne quid amplius diceretur, incertis nominibus (i.e. doubtful payers) crederet: placere, ne cui, qui filio familias mutuam pecuniam dedisset, etiam post mortem parentis eius, cuius in potestate fuisset, actio petitioque daretur: ut scirent qui pessimo exemplo faenerarent, nullius posse filii familias bonum nomen exspectata patris morte fieri.” (Cf. also Cod. Iust. iv 28). This Sc. Macedonianum is probably to be identified with that of Vespasian, though some regard it as that of Claudius; see Bruns, Fontes p. 203. Horace (Sat. i 2, 14) refers to the lending of money to tirones who had just donned the toga of manhood: Quinas hic capiti mercedes exsecat atque, | quanto perditior quisque est, tanto acrius urget; | nomina sectatur modo sumpta veste virili | sub patribus duris tironum. The Lex Plaetoria (c. 186 B.c.) enacted that contracts with minores (under 25 years of age) were only legally binding when entered into in the presence of a curator appointed by the praetor (Plaut. Rud. 1381, Pseud. 303; Cic. N.D. iii 30, 74: Off. iii 15, 61).

: Burman, Oudendorp, and others suspect that these words have got into the text through a gloss on umquam. Lipsius would omit at least hoc est. See on Dom. 17, 1, quando et quomodo, id est, lavantemne an cenantem, aggrederentur.

: cf. Dio lxvi 11, τό τε σύμπαν, τῇ προνοίᾳ τῶν κοινῶν, αὐτοκράτωρ ἐνομίζετο· ἐς δὲ δὴ τἄλλα πάντα κοινὸς καὶ ἰσοδίαιτός σφισιν ἦν: Eutrop. vii 19, Romae se in imperio moderatissime gessit. For civilis see on c. 9, 2.

: = conditionem mediocrem vel tenuem (Baumg.-Cr.). Cf. Tac. A. xiv '60, (vulgus) cui minor sapientia et ex mediocritate fortunae pauciora pericula sunt, where med. fort. means their humble or insignificant position. Suetonius uses mediocris frequently, but mediocritas in only one other passage, Aug. 101, 3, excusata rei familiaris mediocritate, i.e. the small amount of his property was urged as an excuse.

: this sequence is very exceptional and only post-classical; cf. Tac. Agr. 10, Apul. Met. iii 3, x 14. neque (nec) . que (Tib. 11, 5: 51, 2) is Ciceronian (e.g. Fin. i 48, Lael. 104) but rare. neque (nec) et is common at all periods. Kühner-Stegmann, ii 48. ..

: similarly the flatterers of Pallas, the notorious freedman of Claudius, said that he was "regibus Arcadiae ortus," i.e. descended from Pallas the mythical ancestor of Evander (Tac. A. xii 53). The Julian family traced their line back to Venus (Suet. Iul. 6); Galba claimed descent from Jupiter and Pasiphaë (Galb. 2); the Vitellii were said to be sprung from Faunus king of the Aborigines and a goddess Vitellia (Vitell. 1, 2). The fondness of the Romans for such mythical pedigrees is fully illustrated by Friedlaender, Sitteng. i¹º 120.

: there is no definite tradition of the foundation of Reate (c. 1, 2, n.), but various legends refer it to a remote antiquity and connect it with the Aborigines and Pelasgi (Dion. Hal. i 14, 15, ii 49; Varr. L.L. v 53). See Pauly-Wissowa, I.A. 346. comitem Herculis: presumably at the time when Hercules passed through Italy on his return from Spain with the captured oxen of Geryon (Aen. vii '662, viii 201 sqq.). We do not read elsewhere of any companions of Hercules on that occasion, nor is there any other mention of the monument on the Via Salaria. Pitiscus follows Lipsius in assuming that the flatterers of Vespasian gave to this companion of Hercules the name of Flavus (Xanthus ?) and included him among the founders of Reate where Vespasian was born. Two of the great Roman families, the Fabii and Antonii, claimed to be descended from Hercules. On his return journey from Spain Hercules himself was said to have founded the cities of Alesia and Nemausus in Gaul. A cult of Hercules at Reate is mentioned in C.I.L. ix 4672, 4673.

: this road ran north-east from Rome to Reate in the Sabine territory and Asculum in Picenum. It was said to have derived its name from being the route by which salt was conveyed into the interior of Italy from the salt-pits near Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber. The Colline gate of Rome from which it started was earlier known as the Porta Salaria. adeo nihil, ..
: see on c. 8, 2.
: his joint triumph with Titus for their victories over the Jews; see c. 8, 1.
: cf. Phaedr. i 31, 13, merito plectimur: Cic. Off. ii 8, 28, iure igitur plectimur: Nep. Att. 11, qui cavit ne qua in re iure plecteretur.

: Vespasian was born in 9 A.D. (c. 2, 1) and the triumph was celebrated in June, 71. The fact that he was 60 years of age was taken into account by him in considering his prospects in a conflict with Vitellius in 69; cf. Tac. H. ii 74, Vespasianus modo in spem erectus, aliquando adversa reputabat: quis ille dies foret, quo sexaginta aetatis annos et duos filios iuvenes bello permitteret?

: on Dec. 22, 69 A.D. the senate decreed to Vespasian “cuncta principibus solita" (Tac. H. iv 3) which included the tribunicia potestas (cf. H. i 47, decernitur Othoni tribunicia potestas et nomen Augusti et omnes principum honores). The position of the Princeps seems to have rested on (a) the proconsulare imperium, (b) the tribunicia potestas, (c) a special law investing him with miscellaneous prerogatives not given to him by (a) and (b); a large part of the lex de imperio conferring these prerogatives on Vespasian is still extant (C.I.L. vi 930, Newton 2, Bruns Fontes p. 202, Bury Stud. Rom. Emp. c. ii n. D.). The tribunicia potestas, granted for life, was formally assumed afresh every year, and the Princeps reckoned the years of his reign as the years of his tribunician power. It was conferred by a rogatio (following a decree of the senate) which was brought before the people in the Comitia. An interval (trinum nundinum) elapsed between the senate's decree and the Comitia and so the assumption of the tribunicia potestas came some time after the dies imperii (see on c. 6, 3). This interval in the case of Nero was 53 days, of Otho 45, of Domitian 17, of Vitellius 12. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 875, explains our corrupt passage as referring to an unusually long interval in the case of Vespasian (cf. Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2635). This explanation is not satisfactory, for though the reading here is uncertain, the general sense seems clearly to be that Vespasian did not accept the tribunicia potestas for some time after it was formally conferred upon him (cf. Vitell. 8, 2, cognomen Germanici delatum ab omnibus cupide recepit, Augusti distulit, Caesaris in perpetuum recusavit). Bury (op. cit. p. 377), following Herzog (Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 288 sq.), says: "Vespasian made no alteration in the constitution of the Principate; but he attempted to introduce some innovations in practice. He seems to have laid less stress than his predecessors on the tribunicia potestas, and to have even intended to discontinue the official counting of the years of his reign as tribunician years. He seems to have contemplated a return to the first system of Augustus (27-23 B.C.) which based the position of the Princeps mainly on the consulate. He was ordinary consul himself in every year of his reign except two (73 and 78 A.D.), and his son and consort Titus was generally his colleague." Tacitus does not mention any delay in Vespasian's receiving the tribunicia potestas, and in a military diploma of March 6, 70 A.D. (C.I.L. iii 849, Newton 30) we find “Imp. Vespasianus Caesar August., tribunic. potest., cos. II"; so on a milestone in Sardinia (C.I.L. x 8005, Newton 125), dating between January and July, 70 A.D., he is described as “pont. max., tr[ib. po]t., cos. II, i[mp] desig. III, p.p. (i.e. pater patriae)." Vespasian's tribunicia potestas was ... reckoned from July 1, 69 A.D. (his dies imperii, c. 6, 3) and not from Jan. 70, as is shown by a diploma of Dec. 2, 76 (C.I.L. iii p. 853, Newton 35) with tr. p. VIII (not VII).

: there is a hiatus between potestatem and patris patriae in all the principal MSS. except & which has nec patris patriae; some of the later have et patris or patrisque. Roth suggested aut, which is ably defended by Alexander (op. cit. p. 10 sq.) who tabulates the connectives, adversatives, and disjunctives which follow ne quidem in Suetonius, and shows that aut is used almost exclusively in cases where nouns in their various relations are to be brought together (e.g. Vitell. 13, 3, ne in sacrificio quidem umquam aut itinere ullo temperavit). Hirschfeld and others would insert statim after potestatem, assuming that it was lost through haplography; Bücheler statim пес.

: Vespasian does not bear this title in the diploma of March 6, 70 A.D., though he does on the Sardinian milestone of the same period (see above on tribuniciam potestatem); it is found in inscriptions of 71 and subsequent years (e.g. diploma of Apr. 5, 71, C.I.L. x 897, Newton 31). The title of pater (or parens) patriae is applied by Livy to Romulus and Camillus; by Cicero to Marius; Cicero himself was so saluted in the senate by Catulus (cf. Juv. viii 244, Roma patrem patriae Ciceronem libera dixit, with Mayor's note). The dictator Caesar received it by decree shortly before his death. In 2 B.C. the "senate, knights, and people" named Augustus pater patriae (Mon. Ancyr. 6, 24: Suet. Aug. 58), and his successors (except Galba, Otho, and Vitellius) received this title some time after their accession. The first offer of it was often refused, e.g. by Nero (Ner. 8), Vespasian, and Hadrian (Spart. Hadr. 6); Tiberius definitely declined it (Tib. 26, 67: Tac. A. i 72, ii 87). Pertinax (192 A.D.) was the first who received the title on his accession (Capitol. Pert. 5, primus sane omnium ea die qua Augustus est appellatus etiam patris patriae nomen accepit). Dio (liii 18) says that though the title might seem to invest the emperors with the patria postestas over their subjects, yet it was originally only given as an honour and an admonition (ἔς τε τιμὴν καὶ ἐς παραίνεσιν) that they should love their subjects as they would their children, and that their subjects should revere them as they would their fathers (cf. Sen. Clem. i 14, 2). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 779 sqq.

: Kraffert's conjecture iam is needless. nam is used here (as in c. 14, Tit. 1, Dom. 4, 1, etc.) elliptically, the connecting thought having to be supplied (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 116). It was not surprising that Vespasian did not hedge himself about with state and cared little for triumphs or imperial titles, for he was careless even about taking the customary precautions to secure an emperor's safety.

: the danger of assassination led to the introduction of this scrutatio by Augustus when he was "purging” the senate; cf. Aug. 35, 2, ne admissum quidem tunc quemquam senatorum nisi solum et praetemptato sinu (i.e. the fold of the toga where weapons might be concealed). Under Claudius the examination of callers (salutatores) was very thorough (Claud. 35, 1, salutatoribus scrutatores semper apposuit, et quidem omnibus et acerbissimos); men, women, and children were rigorously searched, and the cases for pens and styles (calamariae et graphiariae thecae) were taken from every man's attendant or scribe. Senatorial envoys to Septimius Severus on his march to Rome (193 A.D.) were searched: Spart. Sev. 6, legati senatus excussi ne quid ferri haberent. We read of scrutatores employed by the Eastern kings: Justin xxxviii 1, scrutator ab Ariarathe regio more missus. Plutarch (Dion 19) says that Plato was the only person allowed into the presence of Dionysius without being searched (ἀδιερεύνητος), and he also tells (Timol. 15) how when this younger Dionysius was living at Corinth, having lost the tyranny at Syracuse, some one visited him and jestingly shook out his robe when he entered his apartment as is customary when persons approach a tyrant, whereupon Dionysius bade him "do the same when he went out, that he might not carry off some of the moveables."
: Dio lx 3, ἡ ἔρευνα ἡ διὰ πάντων ἐπὶ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἐπαύσατο.

: cf. (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, ferebat patienter amicorum motus, contumeliis eorum, ut erat facetissimus, iocularibus respondens. Tacitus (Dial. 8) describes Vesp. as patientissimus veri. For libertas in the sense of παρρησία ‘"freedom of speech" cf. Aug. 54, nec ideo libertas aut contumacia fraudi cuiquam fuit: Ov. Her. 15, 68, hoc mihi libertas, hoc pia lingua dedit; it is mainly post-Aug., especially frequent in Quintilian (see Bonnell, Lex. Quintil.), e.g. iii 8, 48, quae in aliis libertas est, in aliis licentia vocatur: ix 2, 27, quid minus figuratum quam vera libertas?

: Eutrop. vii 20, convicia a causidicis et philosophis in se dicta leniter tulit (Vespasianus). The term causidicus (= causarum actor) was most frequently used in a contemptuous sense; see Wilkins on Cic. de or. i 202, non enim causidicum nescio quem neque clamatorem aut rabulam..conquirimus. The causidicus, like our barristers, was instructed by a solicitor (pragmaticus), who provided the pleader with "weapons" (Quintil. xii 3, 4, qui tela agentibus subministrant). The abusive tactics and malpractices of Roman pleaders at this period are often referred to; see Quintil. xii 9, 8 and 10: Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 186. =

: obliqua dicta, indirect attacks, veiled sarcasms, innuendoes (ὑπόνοιαι); cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, Sed quid mirum in amicis, cum etiam causidicorum obliqua dicta, et philosophorum contumaciam contemneret? Quintilian (ix 1, 14) says that figura (σχήμα) was limited by recent rhetoricians to cases where aliud simulatur dici quam dicitur; and again (ix 2, 65): genus... in quo per quandam suspicionem quod non dicimus accipi volumus, non utique contrarium, ut in εἰρωνείᾳ, sed aliud latens et auditori quasi inveniendum. Quod iam fere solum schema a nostris vocatur ... Eius triplex usus est: unus si dicere palam parum tutum est, alter si non decet, tertius qui venustatis modo gratia adhibetur, etc. Cf. Macrob. Sat. vii 3, loedoriam (λοιδορίαν) exprobrationem esse ac directam contumeliam: scomma (σκῶμμα) enim paene dixerim morsum figuratum, quia saepe fraude vel urbanitate tegitur, ut aliud sonet, aliud intellegas: Plut. 631 E, ὀνειδισμὸς γάρ ἐστι τῆς ἁμαρτίας παρεσχηματισμένος τὸ σκῶμμα: Spart. Sev. 14, damnabantur plerique, cur iocati essent, alii, cur tacuissent, alii, cur pleraque figurata (i.e. with double meanings) dixissent, ut “ecce imperator vere nominis sui, vere Pertinax, vere Severus.” For other examples of dicta figurata see Suet. Dom. 10.

: Vespasian was forced to banish these Stoic and Cynic philosophers when they fomented sedition: Dio lxvi 13, ὡς δ' οὖν καὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ ἐκ τῶν στωικῶν καλουμένων λόγων προαχθέντες (excitati), μεθ᾽ ὧν καὶ Δημήτριος ὁ κυνικός, συχνὰ καὶ οὐκ ἐπιτήδεια τοῖς παροῦσι δημοσίᾳ, τῷ τῆς φιλοσοφίας προσχήματι καταχρώμενοι, διελέγοντο, κἀκ τούτου καὶ ὑποδιέφθειρόν τινας, ἔπεισεν ὁ Μουκιανὸς τὸν Οὐεσπασιανὸν πάντας τοὺς τοιούτους ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἐκβαλεῖν . . καὶ πάντας αὐτίκα τοὺς φιλοσόφους ὁ Οὐεσπασιανός, πλὴν τοῦ Μουσωνίου (i.e. Musonius Rufus, the Stoic), ἐκ τῆς ῾Ρώμης ἐξέβαλε, τὸν δὲ δὴ Δημήτριον καὶ τὸν Ὁστιλιανὸν καὶ ἐς νήσους κατέκλεισε. The leader of the Stoic opposition to Vespasian was Helvidius Priscus (see below c. 15). Philosophers were again expelled from Rome by Domitian in 93 A.D. (Dom. 10, 3).

: see on c. 6, 4. Tacitus describes his character, H. i 10: Luxuria industria, comitate adrogantia, malis bonisque artibus mixtus. Nimiae voluptates, cum vacaret: quotiens expedierat (i.e. when on service), magnae virtutes. Palam laudares: secreta male audiebant (i.e. his private life was in bad repute). Sed apud subiectos, apud proximos, apud collegas variis illecebris potens, et cui expeditius fuerit tradere imperium quam obtinere. In H. ii 5 Tac. says that if his faults and those of Vespasian were removed and their virtues were united in one man, such a man would have made an excellent emperor: egregium principatus temperamentum, si demptis utriusque vitiis solae virtutes miscerentur. In an arrogant letter to the senate (H. iv 4) Mucianus boasted that he had the imperial power in his hands, and made a present of it to Vespasian: Id vero erga rem publicam superbum, erga principem contumeliosum, quod in manu sua fuisse imperium donatumque Vespasiano iactabat.

: ‘‘impudicitia de flagitiis contra naturam commissis sive stupro marium, atque ita opponitur libidinibus et adulteriis” (Baumg.- Cr.); cf. Iul. 52, 3, et impudicitiae eum et adulteriorum flagrasse infamia: Aug. 71, 1, infamiam impudicitiae facillime refutavit (though not free from libidines). ,

: the use of hactenus. ut to express a limited amount or degree occurs also in Ner. 31, 2, domum hactenus comprobavit, ut se diceret quasi hominem tandem habitare coepisse: ib. 34, 1: 40, 4: Gramm. 2; cf. Cic. de or. ii 27, 119, artem quidem et praecepta dumtaxat hactenus requirunt, ut certis dicendi luminibus ornentur. For other uses of hactenus in Suet. see on Dom. 16, 2.

: a compound not found elsewhere. The post-Aug. taxare (connected with tangere) means (1) to touch sharply (2) to twit or censure (3) to appraise or value a thing by feeling it, and so, generally, to assess. For (2) cf. Aug. 4, 2, non tantum ut pistoris, sed etiam ut nummulari nepotem taxat Augustum: Dom. 10, 43; for (3) cf. Calig. 38, 3, taxato prius modo summae: Aug. 41, 1, senatorum censum ampliavit ac pro octingentorum milium summa duodecies sestertium (i.e. 1,200,000 sesterces) taxavit. ..

: a correction by Duker of clausulae, the reading of all MSS. clausula was used for the concluding words of a speech, letter, story, poem, or play; cf. Aug. 99, 1, (Augustus) percontatus, ecquid eis videretur mimum vitae commode transegisse, adiecit et clausulam : εἰ δέ τι | ἔχοι καλῶς τὸ παίγνιον, κρότον δότε, κ.τ.λ.: Ner. 39, 3, Atellanarum histrio . in novissima clausula "Orcus vobis ducit pedes” senatum gestu notarat: Cic. de or. ii 240, a te ipso ficta narratio; addidisti clausulam: Val. Max. v 10, 2, hanc adiciendo clausulam (orationi).

: cf. [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, namque Licinium Mucianum, quo adiutore ad imperium provenerat, fiducia meritorum insolentem flectebat, adhibito aliquo utrique familiari, id unum dicens: “nosti me virum esse.'' Vespasian used vir as the opposite of impudicus or muliebria passus; cf. Verg. E. iii 7, parcius ista viris tamen obicienda memento (Damoetas warns the debauched Menalcas not to bring charges of theft against him).

: C. Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus, four times quinquennalis of Urbs Salvia in Picenum and patronus of the same colonia, was admitted to the senate by Vespasian and Titus when censors (see on c. 9, 2) at first inter tribunicios and later inter praetorios. His distinctions are given in C.I.L. ix 5533 (Dessau 1011): [C. Salv]io C. f. Vel. Liberali [Nonio] Basso cos., procos. provin[ciae Macedoniae, legato Augustorum [iuridi]c. Britann., legato leg. V Maced., [fratri A]rvali, allecto ab divo Vespasiano [et divo Ti]to inter tribunicios, ab isdem [allecto] inter praetorios, quinq. IIII, p.c. Hic sorte [procos. fac]tus provinciae Asiae se excusavit. He was famous as an eloquent pleader at Rome. Under Domitian he was brought to trial (Plin. Ep. iii 9, 23) and probably banished (relegatus), but in the reign of Trajan we find him defending Marius Priscus, governor of Africa, who was accused by Pliny and Tacitus (Plin. Ep. ii 11, 17, dixit pro Mario Salvius Liberalis, vir subtilis, dispositus, acer, disertus) and in the same year (100 A.D.) he also appeared for Caecilius Classicus who was indicted by the provincials of Baetica in Spain, their case being conducted by Pliny (Ep. iii 9, 36).

: an example of the causidicorum figurae mentioned above, the implication being that the avaricious Vespasian might wish to have Hipparchus unjustly condemned in order to seize his vast wealth. For the formula “quid (sc. attinet) ad?'' cf. Plaut. Men. 722, quid id ad me?: Cic. Verr. ii 45, 116, quid id ad praetorem uter possessor sit?

: this may have been (Ti. Claudius) Hipparchus (falsely called Plutarchus by Suidas s.v. Ηρώδης). He was condemned for treason and his property was confiscated (Philostrat. vit. soph. ii 1 p. 56 Kayser; cf. C.I.A. iii 38, τὰ Ἱππάρχου χωρία τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ φίσκου πραθέντα). His son was Ti. Cl. Atticus Herodes, consul under Trajan and again under Hadrian.
: i.e. milies centena milia sestertium, 100,000,000 sesterces, about £850,000.

: this antimonarchical champion of Cynic independence was banished to an island by Vespasian in 71 (Dio lxvi 13). He had been equally defiant of Nero; Epictetus (Dissert. i 25, 22) cites him as saying to Nero: ἀπειλεῖς μοι θάνατον, σοὶ δ᾽ ἡ φύσις (Tu mihi mortem minitaris, natura tibi). Caligula had tried to win him over by an offer of 200,000 sesterces, which was rejected with scorn (Sen. Ben. vii 11). Tacitus mentions him in A. xvi 34 as being present during the last hours of the doomed Thrasea Paetus (66 A.D.) and discussing with him the immortality of the soul; again in H. iv 40 as incurring ill-repute for defending Egnatius Celer who was accused by the Stoic Musonius Rufus in 70 A.D. Seneca bestows enthusiastic praise on his friend Demetrius ('Demetrius noster," Dial. i 3, 3; Ep. 20,9; 62, 3; 67, 14; 91, 19); in Ben. vii 8 he says "Huic non dubito quin providentia et talem vitam et talem dicendi facultatem dederit, ne aut exemplum saeculo nostro aut convicium deesset.” Philostratus in his fantastic Life of Apollonius of Tyana says that Demetrius (whom he describes as ἀνὴρ συνειληφὼς πᾶν τὸ ἐν Κυνικῇ κράτος) was a friend and would-be disciple of Apollonius, whom. he met at Corinth (iv 25) and later at Athens (v 19). He also mentions that Tigellinus had Demetrius banished from Rome under Nero (iv 42); that Apollonius recommended Demetrius to Titus at Antioch to teach him how to rule (vi 31); and that Demetrius was living at Puteoli in the reign of Domitian (vii 10).

: a usual mark of respect; cf. Aug. 56, 2, eisdem, praetextatis adhuc, assurrectum ab universis in theatro: Claud. 6, 1, spectaculis advenienti assurgere.. solebant: Iul. 78, 1: Tib. 31, 2: Cic. Inv. i 30, 48, ut maioribus natu assurgatur. So in Hom. Il. i 533, θεοὶ δ᾽ ἅμα πάντες ἀνέσταν.

: this compound is used (with dat., acc., or absol.) in post-Aug. writers to describe snarling abuse; e.g. Sil. Ital. viii 249, infima dum vulgi fovet, oblatratque senatum: Sen. Ira iii 43, quid illum oblatrantem tibi exterrere viribus tuis tentas? Dio (lxvi 13) tells the story about Demetrius differently. He says that when Demetrius, even after being sentenced to exile, kept on provoking the emperor by insults, Vespasian sent a message to him to say that even though Demetrius courted death he would not put to death a mere barking dog: Σὺ μὲν πάντα ποιεῖς ἵνα σε ἀποκτείνω, ἐγὼ δὲ κύνα ὑλακτοῦντα οὐ φονεύω.

: canis (like κύων) was used of Cynic philosophers; cf. Varr. Men. 516, Menippus ille nobilis canis: Mart. iv 53, 8, non est hic Cynicus, Cosme, quid ergo? canis: Auson. Epitaph. 31 (on the tomb of Diogenes the Cynic with the emblem of a dog upon it), Dic, canis, hic cuius tumulus? Canis. At canis hic quis? | Diogenes. Obiit? Non obiit, sed abit. It is doubtful whether the Cynics (Kuvικοί) derived their name from the gymnasium called Κυνόσαργες at Athens where their founder Antisthenes taught, or from their filthy doglike (κυνικός) mode of life.

: Eutrop. vii 20, offensarum et inimicitiarum immemor fuit; [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, huius inter cetera bona illud singulare fuit, inimicitias oblivisci, adeo ut Vitellii hostis sui filiam locupletissime dotatam splendidissimo coniungeret viro. This forgiving spirit was not shown by Vespasian in the case of Julius Sabinus; see note on “coniurationes,” c. 25 infr. executor: a rare post-Aug. subst.; no other instance is cited of its use in the sense of ultor, punitor, though exequi in the sense of ulcisci, punire, is found from Livy on; e.g. Suet. Iul. 67, 1, delicta neque observabat omnia, neque pro modo exequebatur. .. Vitellii filiam. maritavit: this daughter of Vitellius by Galeria Fundana (see Vitell. 6) had been betrothed to P. Valerius Asiaticus, governor of Gallia Belgica, who took the side of Vitellius at the beginning of 69 A.D.; Tac. H. i 59, accessere partibus (Vitellii) Valerius Asiaticus 2F Belgicae provinciae legatus, quem mox Vitellius generum adscivit, etc. On the overthrow of Vitellius he came to terms with Vespasian's generals and was designated consul towards the end of 69 (H. iv 4), but died shortly afterwards; cf. C.I.L. vi 1528, Dis Manibus D. [Valeri] Asiatici consulis designati. Subsequently Vespasian arranged another match for the daughter of Vitellius, but the name of the bridegroom is unknown. See Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 353.

: instruere was the word used of providing a bride with outfit or equipment including trousseau, trinkets, attendants, etc.; Plin. Ep. νί 32, debet, secundum condicionem mariti ("in keeping with her husband's position'"), veste, comitatu (quibus non quidem augetur dignitas, ornatur tamen) instrui: Plaut. Mil. 981, aurum atque ornamenta, quae illi instruxti mulieri.
: in consequence of the offence he had given by his behaviour when a comes of Nero on his musical tour in Greece; see c. 4, 4. ΤΕ

: Dio (lxvi 11) gives his name as Phoebus: τοῦ Φοίβου προσελθόντος αὐτῷ καὶ ἀπολογουμένου, ὅτι ἐπὶ τοῦ Νέρωνος ἐσκυθρωπακότα ποτε αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ θεάτρου ἐν τῇ Ἑλλάδι, ἐφ᾽ οἷς ἀσχημονοῦντα ἑώρα τὸν αὐτοκράτορα, ἐκέλευσε πρὸς ὀργὴν ἀπελθεῖν, τοῦ δὲ ἐρομένου ὅποι, “ ἐς κόρακας” εἶπεν, ὑπὲρ τούτου οὖν ἀπολογουμένου τοῦ Φοίβου, οὔτε τι κακὸν αὐτὸν εἰργάσατο, οὔτε ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτῷ ἄλλο οὐδὲν πλὴν αὐτὸ τοῦτο ὅτι “ ἐς κόρακας ἄπελθε.” The same name occurs in Tac. A. xvi 5 quoted on c. 4, 4. =

: ex ministris, quibus officium admittendi homines ad Principem; cf. vit. Horat. 6, Augustus epistularum ei officium optulit (offered him the post of secretary, ab epistulis). The control of the entrée to the imperial receptions (salutationes) was a special office (officium admissionis); those who held it were called Augusti liberti or servi ab admissione, or ab officiis et admissione, and in later times admissionales, and they acted under the direction of a magister admissionum. The callers who enjoyed the right of prima admissio were distinguished as primi amici, cohors primae (as opp. to secundae) admissionis, and were received either singly or in small groups in the private apartments; less important visitors merely defiled before the emperor in the atrium; cf. Sen. Ben. vi 33, non sunt isti amici, qui in primas et secundas admissiones digeruntur. Trajan is praised by Pliny (Paneg. 47) for dispensing with the ceremonies of admissio; so too Alexander Severus by Lampridius (Alex. Sev. 4). See Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 93; Daremberg-Saglio, i 71, iv 1061. ... It

: this phrase (= abire in malam crucem) does not occur elsewhere. Morbovia may be coined from morbus and via (Bremi), or the termination may be like that in Gergovia, a town in Gaul. seems to mean "Plague-town"; I have translated it by "Pest," an alternative name of Budapest; Lewis and Short render it "Sickdom' 'Sickdom"; Otto (Sprichwörter der Röm.) gives as the German equivalent "ins Pfefferland." Marcilius Most of the older editors regard Morboviam as corrupt. suggested Μακαρίαν, from the Greek euphemism ἄπαγ᾽ ἐς Μακαρίαν (Ar. Eq. 1151): Barth Corvoniam (cf. ἐς κόρακας in Dio, quoted above) : Baumg.-Cr. would eject Morboviam and substitute ἐς κόρακας.

: cf. Ner. 40, 4, hactenus excanduit, ut malum iis qui descissent minaretur. The constr. in aliquem excandescere is post-Aug.; e.g. Colum. vii 12, 5, ut semper excandescant in exteros; so exardescere in, of passionate love or anger, Tac. A. xi 12, H. i 58.
: see on c. 12. و.

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, monentibus amicis ut caveret a Metio Pompusiano, de quo sermo percrebruerat regnaturum, consulem fecit, alludens tali cavillo: ‘‘quandoque memor erit tanti beneficii'': Dio lxvii 12, Μέτιος Πομπουσιανός ὃν ὁ μὲν Οὐεσπασιανὸς μαθὼν ἐκ φήμης τινὸς ὅτι μοναρχήσει, οὐδὲν κακὸν εἰργάσατο, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἐτίμα, λέγων ὅτι Πάντως μου μνημονεύσει καὶ πάντως με ἀντιτιμήσει. Domitian dealt severely with Mettius, first banishing him and then putting him to death; see Dom. 10, 3. He is probably to be identified with the L. Pompusius Mettius mentioned (C.I.L. vi 1495) as praefectus aerarii Saturni for four years (c. 76-80 A.D.).
: i.e. he had a "nativity" or horoscope cast by the astrologers, which foretold that one day he would be emperor. See note on “genitura,” Tit. 9, 2.

: i.e. when Mettius became emperor, he would gratefully remember Vespasian who had given him his first step by making him consul. In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9 Vespasian is rightly said to be speaking with scoffing irony (alludens cavillo). Beroaldus thinks that he took the same view which M. Antoninus afterwards expressed to Verus when warned by him to beware of Avidius Cassius: “si Cassio divinitus debetur imperium, non poterimus interficere, etiam si velimus; scis enim proavi tui (i.e. Trajan) dictum: Successorem suum nullus occidit'' (Vulc. Gall. Avid. Cass. c. 2). Vespasian, relying on his own horoscope and those of his family, was confident that his sons would succeed him; see c. 25.

: = vix; see on Tit. 6, 2. For the leniency of Vespasian cf. Eutrop. vii 19, placidissimae lenitatis, ut qui maiestatis quoque contra se reos non facile puniret ultra exilii poenam: Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, Satellites tyrannidis, nisi qui forte atrocius longe processerant, flectere potius maluit quam excruciatos delere; prudentissime ratus nefaria ministeria a pluribus metu curari. Dein coniurationum multas scelere inulto abscedere patiebatur; comiter, uti erat, stultitiae arguens, qui ignorarent quanta moles molestiaque imperio inesset.

: before Vespasian arrived at Rome from Alexandria, Mucianus, who was all-powerful, had put to death Calpurnius Galerianus (the innocent son of Calpurnius Piso who had headed the conspiracy against Nero in 65 A.D.), L. Piso (proconsul of Africa), and the young son of Vitellius (Tac. H. iv 11, 49, 80). ..

: Tacitus (H. iv 5) sketches the character of this remarkable man. In his youth he had devoted himself to the study of the Stoic philosophy, “non ut plerique, ut nomine magnifico segne otium velaret, sed quo firmior adversus fortuita rem publicam capesseret civis, senator, maritus, gener, amicus, cunctis vitae officiis aequabilis, opum contemptor, recti pervicax, constans adversus metus. Erant quibus adpetentior famae videretur, quando etiam sapientibus cupido gloriae novissima exuitur.'" He married Fannia, daughter of Thrasea Paetus (cf. Plin. 2F2 Ep. vii 19), and like his father-in-law cherished vain republican ideals and celebrated the birthdays of Brutus and Cassius (Juv. v 36). Thrasea was put to death by Nero, and Priscus was banished (66 A.D.) but returned under Galba and carried on a bitter warfare with Eprius Marcellus the accuser of Thrasea (Tac. H. iv 6-9). By his meaningless and persistent defiance of Vespasian, who in his eyes was as bad as Nero, he drove the emperor into ordering first his banishment and shortly afterwards (in 73) his execution. Dio (lxvi 12) attributes Vespasian's hatred of him to his revolutionary denunciations of imperial power: ὅτι ταραχώδης τε ἦν, καὶ τῷ ὄχλῳ προσέκειτο, βασιλείας τε ἀεὶ κατηγόρει, καὶ δημοκρατίαν ἐπῄνει, καὶ ἔπραττεν ἀκόλουθα τούτοις, καὶ συνίστη τινάς, ὥσπερ που φιλοσοφίας ἔργον ὂν τό τε τοὺς κρατοῦντας προπηλακίζειν, καὶ τὸ τὰ πλήθη ταράττειν, τό τε τὰ καθεστηκότα συγχεῖν, καὶ τὸ νεώτερα αὐτοῖς πράγματα ἐπεισάγειν. ..

: this is one of the passages where the reflexive (referring to the subject of the principal clause) is used in a subordinate clause which is not oblique; cf. Ner. 35, 3, Poppaeam ictu calcis occidit quod se reversum conviciis incesserat (where, as Bagge says, one would expect either eum incesserat or se incessisset): Galb. 12, 1, quod civitates, quae cunctantius sibi accesserant, punisset: Tit. 4, 3, altero equo inscenso, cuius rector circa se dimicans occubuerat: Iul. 74, 1, Philemonem, qui necem suam per venenum inimicis promiserat, non gravius quam simplici morte puniit. For examples of this in other writers see Kühner-Stegmann, i 613; Draeger, Hist. Synt. p. 75.

: without using any of the titles of respect such as “Auguste,” “Caesar,” “Imperator.” Cf. Sen. de Const. 18, Gaius Caligula iratus fuit Herennio Macro, quod illum Gaium salutaverat: nec impune cessit primipilario quod Caligulam dixerat.

: Priscus was praetor in 70 A.D. and dedicated the site of the new Capitol (Tac. H. iv 53). As praetor designate he resisted proposals brought forward in the senate to please the emperor, maintaining (1) that financial retrenchment should be undertaken by the senate and not left to the emperor; (2) that the Capitol should be restored at the public expense, and that Vespasian should only be asked to assist (H. iv 9).

: the emperor's name and titles of honour should have appeared in the praescriptio at the head of the praetor's edict as of other official documents; cf. Tac. H. ii 65, where Cluvius Rufus was accused of aiming at empire because ‘‘diplomatibus nullum principem praescripsisset.” Some think that honore refers to prayers for the emperor's health and prosperity, such as were customary in the concluding formula (subscriptio) of magistrates' letters to him; see Tib. 32,2: Dio lvii 11. The use of transmittere in the sense of praetermittere ‘‘to pass over, say nothing about" is post-Aug.; cf. Calig. 10, 2, quae ipse pateretur incredibili dissimulatione transmittens: Tac. H. iv 9, eam sententiam modestissimus quisque silentio, deinde oblivio transmisit.

: altercationes in the law courts meant disputes or interchanges between opposing counsel, as distinct from a set speech (perpetua oratio) and the examination of witnesses (interrogatio testium); so too in the senate it meant "word-fights" between magistrates, e.g. between the consuls and tribunes (Liv. xxviii 45, xxxiii 22: Cic. Fam. i 2, Att. i 16, iv 13), between the praetors and the proconsul Caesar (Suet. Iul. 23, 1, triduo per irritas altercationes absumpto). See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 947. The Stoic Epictetus (Dissert. i 2, 19-22) mentions with approval an interchange between Priscus and Vespasian when the emperor sent a message to him to absent himself from the senate: Προσπέμψαντος γὰρ αὐτῷ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ, ἵνα μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς τὴν σύγκλητον (senatum), ἀπεκρίνατο· ᾿Ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι μὴ ἐᾶσαί με εἶναι συγκλητικόν· μέχρι δ᾽ ἂν ὦ, δεῖ μ᾽ εἰσέρχεσθαι. ῎Αγε, ἀλλ᾽ εἰσελθών, φησί, σιώπησον. Μή μ' ἐξέταζε (ne me roga sententiam), καὶ σιωπήσω. ᾿Αλλὰ δεῖ με ἐξετάσαι. Κἀμὲ εἰπεῖν τὸ φαινόμενον δίκαιον. ᾿Αλλ᾽ ἐὰν εἴπῃς, ἀποκτενῶ σε. Πότε οὖν σοι εἶπον ὅτι ἀθάνατός εἰμι; καὶ σὺ τὸ σὸν ποιήσεις, κἀγὼ τὸ ἐμόν. Σόν ἐστιν, ἀποκτεῖναι· ἐμόν, ἀποθανεῖν μὴ τρέμοντα· σόν, φυγαδεῦσαι (relegare)· ἐμόν, ἐξελθεῖν μὴ λυπούμενον.

: Dio (lxvi 12) says that Vespasian once went out of the senate-house in tears after Priscus had been so insolent that the tribunes arrested him: Πρίσκος Ἑλουίδιος . τοῖς Στωικοῖς δόγμασιν ἐντραφείς, καὶ τὴν τοῦ Θρασέου παρρησίαν οὐ σὺν καιρῷ μιμούμενος, στρατηγῶν (i.e. being praetor) δὲ τηνικαῦτα, οὔτε τι πρὸς τιμὴν τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος ἔδρα, καὶ προσέτι καὶ βλασφημῶν αὐτὸν οὐκ ἐπαύετο. Καί ποτε διὰ τοῦτο οἱ δήμαρχοι (tribunes) συλλαβόντες αὐτὸν τοῖς ὑπηρέταις παρέδοσαν. Συνεχύθη τε ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς καὶ δακρύσας ἐκ τοῦ βουλευτηρίου ἐξῆλθε, τοσοῦτον μόνον εἰπὼν ὅτι “ ἐμὲ μὲν υἱὸς διαδέξεται, ἢ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος” (for these words see Vesp. 25).

: in ordinem cogere (less frequently redigere, cf. Plin. Ep. ii 6, 5) was properly a military phrase for reducing an officer to the ranks, and it became a technical expression for treating a magistrate as if he were an ordinary private citizen (Liv. iii 35, 6) and thwarting and resisting him in the exercise of his legal functions (Liv. iii 51, 13: vi 38, 12) especially in the exercise of tribunician powers (Liv. xxv 3, 9: xliii 16, 10: Plin. Ep. i 23, 1). See Mommsen, Staatsr. i 139. The emperor Claudius used the phrase of himself when disrespectfully treated by the people of Ostia; Claud. 38, 1, Ostiensibus, quia sibi subeunti Tiberim scaphas obviam non miserint, graviter correptis eaque cum invidia (i.e. in such reproachful terms) ut in ordinem se coactum conscriberet, repente tantum non satis facientis modo veniam dedit. For ante quam with the participle see on Galb. 11, prius
: see on Vitell. 4. quam.. oppressis. There

: we are not told what form his banishment took; he may have been sent to an island. When first banished by Nero in 66, he went to Apollonia in Macedonia. relegatio was a milder penalty than exilium and did not necessarily involve a loss of civil or personal rights. were two forms of it: (1) the condemned person was forbidden to live at Rome, or at any other specified place; (2) he was compelled to live on an island or within some other limited area. Either form might be temporary or permanent. The relegatus retained his civitas, and forfeiture of his property, either total or partial, could only be directed by the judge in cases of perpetua relegatio (Ulp. Dig. xlviii 22, 7, etc.). See also on Tit. 8, 5, in asperrimas insularum avehi. In Plin. Ep. vii 19 and Tac. H. i 3 (contrast Ann. xvi 35) exilium is loosely used of Priscus' banishment.

: executioners were often sent to despatch exiles; cf. Calig. 28, misit circum insulas, qui universos (exules) contrucidarent: Tac. H. i 2, plenum exiliis mare, infecti caedibus scopuli: ib. 46, Laco praefectus, tamquam in insulam seponeretur, ab evocato, quem ad caedem eius Otho praemiserat, confossus.
: cf. Tac. A. xi 37, where Claudius softens towards Messalina and sends to save her, but Narcissus hurries on her death before the reprieve arrives. ... = =

: laetatus is found only in some late MSS., its omission in the earlier being partly due to the similarity of its last syll. to the first of the following iustis. O. Rossbach suggested gavisus (not used by Suet.), but cf. Tib. 75, 1, morte eius ita laetatus est populus. The difficulty of the sentence lies in neque, which is generally regarded as an isolated instance in Suetonius of the very rare use of neque non, for which see Kühner-Stegmann, i 817. Some cite as parallel Dom. 20, where nec is usually explained as non, but see note there. More probably some words have been lost here; the original reading may have been <neque nece > neque caede cuiusquam . . laetatus, cf. Tib. 62, 1, neque tormentis neque supplicio cuiusquam pepercit. This then would be another of the places where Suetonius couples synonymous words; e.g. Oth. 11, 1, discedere et abire; see on Vitell. 14, 1, necem atque supplicium. He uses both nex and caedes in the sense of mors violenta; forced suicide is sometimes denoted by nex (e.g. Ner. 35, 5, Senecam ad necem compulit). Other conjectures are: laetatus est et iustis (Roth): laetatus est et quamvis iustis (Bücheler): laetatus est et quamquam iustis (Alexander).

: Vespasian seems to have been of a strangely emotional nature. Dio (lxvi 12 and 16) mentions his being moved to tears by the insults of Helvidius Priscus (see above) and also when the wife of Julius Sabinus made a piteous but fruitless appeal to the emperor to spare the lives of her husband and herself (see on c. 25). Titus resembled his father in this respect (see Tit. 9, 3; 10, 1).

: so Tacitus, H. ii 5: prorsus, si avaritia abesset, antiquis ducibus par. On the other hand, Aur. Vict. (Caes. 9) says: infirmus tamen, uti quidam prave putant, adversus pecuniam, cum satis constet aerarii inopia ac labe urbium novas eum neque aliquamdiu postea habitas vestigalium pensiones exquisivisse; after enumerating the public works which Vespasian executed, Victor adds: quae tot tantaque brevi confecta prudentiam magis quam avaritiam probavere. Eutropius (vii 9, 2) qualifies the charge of avarice with praise for scrupulousness and generosity: pecuniae tantum avidior fuit, ita tamen ut eam nulli iniuste auferret; quam cum omni diligentiae provisione colligeret, tamen studiosissime largiebatur, praecipue indigentibus; nec facile ante eum cuiusquam principis vel maior est libertas comperta vel iustior. Suidas follows Eutropius: eἰς δὲ τὴν ἡγεμονίαν παρελθών, μετρίως τε καὶ σωφρόνως τὴν ἀρχὴν διῴκητο, ἐπιθυμητικῶς μὲν δοκῶν ἔχειν χρημάτων· οὐ μὴν ὥστε παρὰ δίκην ἀφαιρεῖσθαί τινα τῶν οἰκείων. καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον οὐκ ἐς τὰς ἡδονάς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐς τὰς δημοσίας χρείας ἐποιεῖτο. οὔκουν εὕροι τις ἂν ἕτερον πρὸ τοῦδε βασιλέα οὔτε δαψιλέστερον, οὔτε πρὸς τὸ ἴσον τε καὶ δίκαιον ἐξητασμένον τὴν πρὸς τὰς δωρεὰς ἐλευθεριότητα. Dio (lxvi 2) says that it was Mucianus who set the example and encouraged Vespasian in exacting money for the treasury, his maxim being that money forms the sinews of empire (νεῦρα τῆς ἡγεμονίας τὰ χρήματα). Modern historians take the view that Vespasian incurred undeserved odium for avaritia through his statesmanlike measures to put the shattered finances of the empire on a sound footing: see Duruy, Histoire des Romains iv² 653 sqq.: Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit i 514 sqq.: Bury, Stud. Rom. Emp. 378 sqq.

: Dio (lxvi 8) says that Vespasian at Alexandria renewed taxes which had been dropped, increased existing taxes, and introduced fresh ones: πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τέλη (vectigalia), τὰ μέν τινα ἐκλελειμμένα ἀνενεώσατο, τὰ δὲ καὶ νομιζόμενα προσεπηύξησε, καινά τε ἕτερα προσκατεστήσατο. Dio adds that he adopted the same course later in the rest of the subject territory, in Italy, and in Rome itself. Cf. von Domaszewski, Gesch. röm. Kaiser ii³ 149.

: the only tax which we know was abolished by Galba was one of 24 per cent., quadrage(n)suma, of an unspecified nature (Schiller, op. cit. i 368); cf. the coins of Galba with the words quadragensuma remissa; quadragens, remissae; xxxx remissae (Eckhel, vi p. 296). Hofstee (on Galb. 15) thinks that this tax was the quadragesima Galliarum (see on Vesp. 1, 2), which Galba abolished as a reward to the Gauls who had supported Vindex. Tacitus (H. i 51) mentions that Galba remitted of the tribute paid by the Gauls. Under the head of vectigalia were included decumae, tithes for the occupation of state-domains in Italy or the provinces; scriptura for grazing cattle on public pastures; customsduties (portoria); 5 per cent. on manumissions and inheritances (vicesima manumissionum et hereditatum); 4 per cent. on the sale of slaves (quinta et vicesima mancipiorum venalium); 1 per cent. on sales of other kinds (centesima rerum venalium); etc.
: e.g. the vectigal urinae (c. 23, 3) and the fiscus Iudaicus (Dom. 12, 2).

: tribute paid by the provinces was of different kinds: (a) decumae, tithes of the produce of the land; (b) stipendium, a tax of fixed amount, either a land tax (tributum soli) or a poll tax (tributum capitis); (c) annona, the supply of corn, etc., either for the officials and army of occupation (annona militaris) or for Rome (annona civica), this latter coming from Africa and Egypt. The fiscus Alexandrinus, assigned to Vespasian's reign, was probably connected with this corn-supply; see Hirschfeld, Verwaltungsb. 370.

: the locus classicus for Roman views on trades, etc., unbecoming a gentleman is Cic. Off. i 42, where quaestus liberales are distinguished from quaestus inliberales et sordidi, the latter including the occupations of faeneratores, portitores, mercenarii, opifices, and all retail traders, “sordidi etiam putandi qui mercantur a mercatoribus quod statim vendant; nihil enim proficiant, nisi admodum mentiantur, nec vero est quicquam turpius vanitate (misrepresentation).'" The only honourable occupation for senators was husbandry (agri cultura). Vespasian had trading experience before he became emperor; see c. 4, 3.

: "carried on”; cf. Aug. 4, 2, modo unguentariam tabernam modo pistrinum exercuisse: Vitell. 2, 1, Antiochi furnariam exercentis filia: Gramm. 23, 2, cum et officinas promercalium vestium exerceret. See also on Vesp. 1, 3, faenus exercuit. =

: divenderet. This special use of distrahere (rem in venditione) “to sell piecemeal" is found first in Tac. A. vi 17, copiam vendendi secuta vilitate aegrius distrahebant (agros); cf. Suet. Calig. ... 39, 2, cui instrumento ("furniture'') distrahendo nihil non fraudis ac lenocinii (“cajolery") adhibuit. In later writers distrahere was used simply in the sense of vendere, e.g. Apul. Met. xi 28, veste mea quamvis parvulo distracta, sufficientem conrasi summulam.

div.p: § 2. honores absolutiones venditare: Dio (lxvi 14) says this trafficking was carried on through Caenis (see c. 3) Vespasian's concubine: Πλεῖστόν τε ... ἴσχυσε (ἡ Καινίς), καὶ πλοῦτον ἀμύθητον ἤθροισεν, ὥστε καὶ νομισθῆναι ὅτι δι' αὐτῆς ἐκείνης ἐχρηματίζετο. πάμπολλα γὰρ παρὰ πολλῶν ἐλάμβανε, τοῖς μὲν ἀρχάς, τοῖς δὲ ἐπιτροπείας, στρατείας, ἱερωσύνας, ἤδη δέ τισι καὶ ἀποφάσεις αὐτοῦ (responsa principis) πιπράσκουσα. ἀπέκτεινε μὲν γὰρ ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς χρημάτων ἕνεκεν οὐδένα, ἔσωσε δὲ πολλοὺς τῶν διδόντων. καὶ ἡ μὲν λαμβάνουσα ἐκείνη ἦν, ὑπωπτεύετο δὲ ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς ἑκὼν αὐτῇ ἐπιτρέπειν τοῦτο ποιεῖν, ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων ὧν ἔπραττεν.

p.note: : these would be more especially the procuratores Caesaris who managed the finances in the imperial provinces, and also those in charge of the imperial fiscus at Rome; the title procurator was, however, applied to a vast multitude of officials under the Empire (see Daremberg-Saglio, iv 662 sqq.; Hirschfeld, 410 sqq.).

: with this has been compared a saying of the Cynic Diogenes; when he was asked how Dionysius (the younger, tyrant of Syracuse) used his friends, he said, "Like bags; those which are full he hangs up, and those which are empty he throws away" (Diog. Laert. vi 2, 6, ᾿Ερωτηθεὶς πῶς χρῆται Διονύσιος τοῖς φίλοις; ἔφη, ὡς θυλάκοις, τοὺς μὲν πλήρεις κρημνῶν, τοὺς δὲ κενοὺς ῥίπτων). The process of making peculators of public money disgorge (in the literal sense) their plunder is described by Demos in Aristoph. Eq. 1145 sqq., τηρῶ γὰρ ἑκάστοτ᾽ αὐ- | τοὺς οὐδὲ δοκῶν ὁρᾶν | κλέπτοντας· ἔπειτ᾿ ἀναγ- | κάζω πάλιν ἐξεμεῖν | ἅττ᾽ ἂν κεκλόφωσί μου | κημῷ καταμηλῶν.

: for the squeezing of moisture out of sponges cf. Plaut. Rud. 1008, Iam ego te hic, itidem quasi peniculus (= spongia) novos exurgeri solet, | ni hunc amittis, exurgebo quidquid umoris est tibi. Martial (xiii 47) compares the swelling of bread in milk to a sponge absorbing water: Picentina Ceres (i.e. bread of Picenum) niveo sic nectare crescit, | ut levis accepta spongia turget aqua.

div.p: § 3. negata gratuita libertate: this herdsman had no savings (peculium) wherewith to buy his freedom (cf. Sen. Ep. 80, peculium suum, quod comparaverunt ventre fraudato, pro capite numerant); so he had to fear the fate which, according to Plutarch (Cato 4), befell the age-worn herdsmen and other slaves of the elder Cato, viz. of being sold for a trifle as useless encumbrances, a practice which Plut. strongly condemns. buying of freedom by farmslaves is referred to in Verg. E. i 32; cf. also Tac. A. xiv 42, Pedanium Secundum servus ipsius interfecit, seu negata libertate cui pretium pepigerat, etc. The

p.note: : orare with two accusatives is not class., unless the acc. of the thing is a neut. pron. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 299). See on “flagitassent,” Vitell. 14, 2.

: cf. Paul. Diac. (Migne 20 col. 715) Sed vulpecula fuit semper fraudibus studens: ingenium suum mutare nescit. The Greeks had the same proverb of the wolf: ὁ λύκος τὴν τρίχα, οὐ τὴν γνώμην ἀλλάττει. Otto (Sprichwörter der Röm.) gives as the German proverb "Der Fuchs wechselt den Balg und bleibt ein Schalk." Cf. also Pindar, Ol. x 20 : τὸ γὰρ ἐμφυὲς οὔτ᾽ αἴθων ἀλώπηξ | οὔτ᾽ ἐρίβρομοι λέοντες διαλλάξαιντο ἦθος. A. A. Howard (Harv. Stud. x 28) suggests that there may have been some fable in the style and metre (iambic senarii) of Phaedrus in which were the words [Fabula haec] Vulpem pilum mutare non mores [docet], or in a direct form Vulpes pilum mutare non mores [potest].

: in ordinary speech, especially under the Empire, manubiae was often a mere synonym of praeda either in the sense of booty taken in war, or in the figurative sense of spoil or plunder of any kind. In the latter sense Suet. uses it also in Calig. 41, 1, ne quod non manubiarum genus experiretur, lupanar in Palatio constituit: Ner. 38, 3, ne non hinc (i.e. from the burning of Rome) quoque quantum posset praedae et manubiarum invaderet. When used of booty taken in war, manubiae and praeda were originally distinct. Gellius (xiii 25, 26) says that manubiae meant money obtained from the sale of booty (praeda): nam praeda dicitur corpora ipsa rerum quae capta sunt, manubiae vero appellatae sunt pecunia a quaestore ex venditione praedae redacta. More probably, however, Asconius (on Cic. Verr. ii 1, 154) is right in saying that manubiae meant the general's share of the praeda: Manubiae sunt praeda imperatoris pro portione de hostibus capta. The booty was divided between the Roman treasury, the soldiers, and the general. The general usually devoted his share to public buildings; e.g. Suet. Iul. 26, 2, Forum de manubiis incohavit: Tib. 20, Dedicavit et Concordiae aedem, item Pollucis et Castoris ... de manubiis: Aug. 30, 1, vias triumphalibus viris ex manubiali pecunia sternendas distribuit. See Daremberg-Saglio, iii 1582.
: for the combination of two or more necessitate compulsum ablatives in Suet. see App. i. § 3. D. f.

: fiscus originally denoted a basket in which money was stored in the public treasury, as opposed to cista a private money-chest. Under the principate the title fiscus or fiscus Caesaris (see on Vitell. 2, 2) was given to the emperor's own treasury or privy purse, supplied mainly by the revenues from the imperial provinces, certain dues from the senatorial provinces, the confiscated goods of condemned criminals (bona damnatorum) and lapsed inheritances (bona vacantia); out of it were met the costs of provincial administration, the army and navy, the corn-supply, etc. Distinct from the fiscus was the aerarium (or aerarium Saturni from its old office in the temple of Saturn in the Forum); this was the public treasury, which in theory was controlled by the senate but in practice by the emperor (Dio liii 16, λόγῳ μὲν γὰρ τὰ δημόσια ἀπὸ τῶν ἐκείνου ἀπεκέκριτο, ἔργῳ δὲ καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὴν γνώμην αὐτοῦ ἀνηλίσκετο). The aerarium paid for public worship, public festivals, public buildings, roads, etc. There was a third treasury, the aerarium militare which supplied army pensions; it was instituted by Augustus and received the imposts on inheritances (vicesima hereditatum) and on sales (centesima rerum venalium). See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii3 998 sqq. =

: sc. centena milia sestertium, 40,000,000,000 sesterces, about £340,000,000. Budaeus would reduce this colossal sum by reading quadragies, which is approved by Oudendorp and others. Mommsen (op. cit. ii³ 1010) also suspects some corruption in the figures. Humbert (Les Finances chez les Romains i 211, 287) holds that this vast amount was not a capital debt but an annual deficit in the revenue required to meet the necessary expenses of the State. On the other hand, Marquardt (Staatsv. ii² 297) regards it not as an annual revenue but as a sum required once for all to stabilize the finances: "Eine jährliche Einnahme scheint auch hier nicht gemeint zu sein, da der ganze Schatz, den Tiberius nach einer habsüchtigen Regierung zurückliess, nur 2700 Mill. HS betrug (Suet. Calig. 37), sondern eine Summe, die ein für allemal nöthig war, um die Finanzen zu reguliren." Schiller (l.c.) summarizes the calculations on which Vesp. based his estimate: "Natürlich war hierunter nicht nur der laufende Bedarf und die Ansammlung eines Staatsschatzes mit gerechnet, sondern namentlich die kostspieligen Bauherstellungen von Tempeln und öffentlichen Bauten, die Ergänzung der öffentlichen Dienerschaft, die enormen Ausgaben für Magazin- und Fuhrwesen, welches für die Getreideversorgung Italiens nötig war, aber auch die grossen Summen, welche für militärische Zwecke, Strassen-, Festungs- und Flottenbauten, Verabscheidung und Neuerrichtung von Legionen aufzuwenden waren." See also Herzog, Röm. Staatsverfassung ii 296.

: for this use of stare (opp. to cadere, concidere, ruere, corruere) cf. Oth. 5, 1, neque enim dissimulabat, nisi principem se stare non posse, nihilque referre ab hoste in acie an in Foro sub creditoribus caderet: Cic. Cat. ii 10, 21, qui in vetere aere alieno vacillant si stare non possunt, corruant: Cic. Phil. ii 10, quae si valuissent, res publica staret, tu tuis flagitiis concidisses: Liv. xxiii 48, nisi fide staret res publica, opibus non staturam (i.e. if the State were not supported by credit, it would not be able to support itself by its present resources).

: apart from the indef. si quando (4 instances) Suetonius uses quando in a temporal sense only twice: Galb. 15, 1 (as a conjunction), Dom. 17, 1 (as an interrog. adv.). He uses it 15 times (excluding quotations) in a causal sense; 10 times with the subjunctive, 5 times with the indicative. This causal sense is frequent in Livy; otherwise mostly poet. and post-Aug.

: cf. the old proverb, Naev. Trag. 54 (Ribb.), male parta male dilabuntur, “ill got, ill spent": Plaut. Poen. 844, male partum male disperit: Liv. ix, 9, male partam victoriam male perdiderunt. Ausonius (Caes. x) says of Vespasian: Quaerendi adtentus, moderato commodus usu, | auget nec reprimit Vespasianus opes "Set upor gathering, in reasonable spending generous, Vespasian increased his wealth, not straitened it" (H. E. White).

: so, too, Augustus ‘liberalitatem omnibus ordinibus per occasiones frequenter exhibuit'' (Aug. 41, 1). Cf. the use of liberalitas in Tac. and Suet. (Galb. 15, 1) in the concrete sense of a gift bestowed by imperial favour.

: under the Republic no property qualification was legally necessary for a senator, but wealth was taken into consideration in elections to the senate (cf. Willems, Le Sénat i 189 sqq.; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii³ 876; Tyrrell and Purser on Cic. Fam. xiii 5). Augustus made a definite census or property qualification legally necessary. According to Suet. (Aug. 41), he fixed it first at 800,000 sesterces (double the qualification of an eques), and later at 1,200,000; he also made up the amount for those who did not possess it (supplevitque non habentibus). Dio (liv 17) says he raised it from 400,000 to 1,000,000. Mommsen (i3 498) thinks Dio's statement the more accurate with regard to the higher figure (1,000,000 not 1,200,000), but considers it improbable that Augustus had ever fixed the sum so low as 400,000, which would have equalised the qualifications of senators and equites. Tacitus (A. ii 37) mentions that Augustus presented Hortensius Hortalus, a grandson of the orator, with 1,000,000 sesterces to enable him to keep up senatorial rank, and Tiberius gave the same amount to Propertius Celer for the same purpose (A. i 75). Hadrian's generosity enabled certain bankrupt (decoctores) senators to resume their position: Spart. Hadr. 7, senatoribus qui non vitio suo decoxerant, patrimonium pro liberorum modo senatoriae professionis explevit. For similar aid given by Antoninus Pius see Capitol. Anton. Pius 9; Fronto ad L. Verum, 6. Other instances in Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 134 sqq.

: Vespasian was following the example of Nero in making these annual allowances; cf. Ner. 10, 1, senatorum nobilissimo cuique, sed a re familiari destituto, annua salaria et quibusdam quingena constituit: Tac. A. xiii 34, sed nobili familiae honor auctus est oblatis in singulos annos quingenis sestertiis, quibus Messala paupertatem innoxiam sustentaret. Aurelio quoque Cottae et Haterio Antonino annuam pecuniam statuit princeps (Nero), quamvis per luxum avitas opes dissipassent.

: Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, per omnes terras, qua ius Romanum est, renovatae urbes cultu egregio. The names of the cities restored by Vespasian are not recorded. There are only a few inscriptions which mention buildings of his in the provinces, e.g. one at Seleucia in Syria (C.I.L. iii 6702, Newton, 103) and one at Patara in Lycia (Le Bas 1265, Newton 14). A considerable number of inscriptions, principally on milestones, show that he constructed roads and bridges throughout the provinces; see Newton p. 57 sqq., Pauly-Wissowa vi 2690.

: we only know that Vespasian restored the temple of Rhea, Mother of the Gods, at Herculaneum after that town, together with Pompeii, had been partly destroyed by an earthquake either in 62 (Tac. 4. xv 22) or '63 (Sen. N.Q. vi 1, 2); cf. C.I.L. x 1406, Newton 100: Imp. Caesar Vespasianus Aug., pontif. max., trib. pot. vii, imp. xvii, p.p., cos. vii, design. viii, templum Matris Deum, terrae motu conlapsum, restituit (this was found at Herculaneum in Campania; its date is MarchJune, 76). In 79 an earthquake destroyed three cities in Cyprus; cf. Euseb.-Hieron. Chron., p. 159 Schoene, Tres civitates Cypri terrae motu conruerunt. Earthquakes, especially in Asia Minor, occurred with great frequency in the first two centuries of the Empire; see Friedlaender, Sitteng. iii¹º 29. Augustus (Mon. Ancyr. vi 4) mentions that he had given countless gifts (dona innumerabilia) to cities in Italy and the provinces destroyed by fire and earthquake. In 17 A.D. a great earthquake wrecked twelve famous cities in Asia Minor and Tiberius gave generous grants to restore them; cf. A. ii 47: Suet. Tib. 48, 2, Ne provincias quidem liberalitate ulla sublevavit, excepta Asia, disiectis terrae motu civitatibus. Examples of grants made to cities destroyed by fire are that of 10 million sesterces to Bononia (Bologna) in 53 A.D. under Claudius (Tac. A. xii 58), and that of 4 million sesterces to Lugdunum (Lyons) in 65 under Nero (4. xvi 13).

: Augustus had set the example; cf. Aug. 89, 3, ingenia saeculi sui omnibus modis fovit. For ingenia (= homines ingeniosi) cf. Tac. Agr. 2, monumenta clarissimorum ingeniorum in comitio urerentur: Sen. Suas. vi 22, candidissimus omnium magnorum ingeniorum aestimator T. Livius: Verg. G. ii 382, praemiaque ingeniis pagos et compita circum | Thesidae posuere. Among the successors of Vespasian who fostered the liberal arts were Hadrian (Spart. Hadr. 16), Antoninus Pius (Capitol. Anton. 11), and Alexander Severus (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 44); see Dill, Rom. Society from Nero to M. Aurelius p. 148.
: see on c. 16, 3.

: Quintilian was the first to fill the Chair of Latin Rhetoric endowed by Vespasian at Rome; he may have held it from 72-92 A.D., the period of his greatest fame being 85-89 (Petersen, Quintil. x, Introd. p. viii). By the middle of the 2nd cent. not only the large cities but also many of the smaller towns in Italy and the provinces had such professors appointed by the communities (Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii10 192; Marquardt, Privatl.2 111, Staatsv. ii² 106). Rhetoric at Rome was originally taught by Greeks and in Greek. There was a strong conservative prejudice against Latin rhetores teaching in Latin, and they were sternly discountenanced by an edict of the censors in 92 B.c. (Gell. xv 11, 2; Suet. Rhet. 1). Gradually, however, from the time of Cicero's youth they succeeded in establishing themselves, and both Latin and Greek teachers of rhetoric were numerous at Rome in the 1st cent. of the Empire.

: annuum as a subst. (= quod praestatur quotannis or salarium) is found first in Sen. Ben. i 9, 4, alienae uxori annuum praestat; cf. Suet. Gramm. 23, quanquam ex schola quadringena annua caperet: Juv. vi 480, sunt quae tortoribus annua praestent: Plin. Ep. x 40, publici servi annua accipiunt.
: sc. sestertia, 100,000 sesterces, about £850.

: e.g. the poet Saleius Bassus; cf. Tac. Dial. 9, laudavimus nuper, ut miram et eximiam, Vespasiani libéralitatem, quod quingenta sestertia Basso donasset. For eulogies and invocations of Vespasian by poets see Sil. Ital. Pun. iii 594 sqq., Val. Flacc. Arg. i 8 sqq. The unprofitable nature of poetical pursuits at Rome and the liberality of the emperors to poets are discussed by Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 234 sqq.

: this brilliant emendation of the corruptions coevenerit, coemerit, coemit, is due to Graevius. It is uncertain whether Suetonius is referring to a picture or a statue. The "Aphrodite Anadyomene" of Apelles (ft. 336-323 в.с.), the most celebrated of Grecian painters, was originally in the temple of Aesculapius at Cos, and was brought to Rome to adorn the temple of Julius Caesar by Augustus, who in return remitted 100 talents of Coan tribute (Strab. xiv p. 657). Pliny (N.H. xxxv 91) says that when the lower part was injured no one could be found to restore (reficere) it, and when in course of time the panel of the picture fell into decay, Nero substituted for it a copy made by Dorotheos (aliam pro ea substituit Nero Dorothei manu); E. Sellers (The Elder Pliny's Chapters on the History of Art, p. 128) comments on this: "substituit may be an exaggeration, as the picture of Apelles seems still to have been in existence under Vespasian, when Suetonius speaks of its being again restored." Pliny goes on to mention that Apelles had begun another Aphrodite at Cos, intending to surpass even the fame of his earlier work, but at his death no one was found to finish the outlines already traced. Graevius thought that Suetonius is referring to this incomplete picture. Oudendorp and Baumg.-Cr. are more probably right in holding that the restoration mentioned here was of the statue of Venus, by an unknown sculptor, which was placed by Vesp. in his temple of Peace. Pliny (xxxvi 5) says: Ignoratur artifex eius quoque Veneris, quam Vespasianus Imperator in operibus Pacis suae dicavit, antiquorum dignam fama. If this view is correct, we must assume that the statue came from Cos. Other readings which have been suggested are scenae (to be taken with artifices), Lipsius; coronavit, Böttiger.

: this colossal statue of Nero by Zenodorus was 120 feet in height, and stood originally in the vestibule of Nero's Aurea Domus (see on Oth. 7, 1); it was removed by Vespasian to the Via Sacra; later Hadrian placed it to the N.W. of the Colosseum, where the base is still preserved. It was converted into a statue of the Sun (Plin. N.H. xxxiv 45), apparently by Vespasian (see Friedlaender on Mart. Spect. 2, 1, Hic ubi sidereus propius videt astra colossus). Spartianus (Hadr. 19) says that it was Hadrian who consecrated it to the Sun after removing the features of Nero, while Lampridius (Commod. 17) states that Commodus replaced. the head of Nero by his own. See also Dio lxvi 15, lxxii 22.

: a congiarium (from congius a measure of about 6 pints) was originally a distribution of free oil or wine among the plebs. Under the Empire we find it used of a largess of money to the people, while donativum meant a similar gift to the soldiers; e.g. Ner. 7, 2, populo congiarium, militi donativum proposuit. The word was also used in a general sense for a gift, especially of money, as here and in Iul. 27, 1, vel invitatos vel sponte ad se commeantes uberrimo congiario prosequebatur; cf. Cic. Att. x 7, 3: Sen. Ep. 29, 5: Quintil. vi 3, 52: Mart. iii 7,2, Centum miselli iam valete quadrantes | anteambulonis congiarium (= sportula) lassi.

: mechanicus and machinator are both found answering to the Gr. μηχανοποιός. According to Daremberg-Saglio (iii 1663) machinatores were Roman citizens, generally military engineers, while the term mechanici was originally applied to foreigners, slaves or freedmen, mainly Greeks who brought in with them the designation mechanicus (μηχανικός), which occurs in ante-class. and post-Aug. writers (first in Lucilius of an equilibrist, petaurista, who performed by the aid of mechanical appliances; later of architects and engineers of various kinds).
: mechanical contrivances for the conveyance of columns are described in Vitruvius x 2 and illustrated in Daremberg-Saglio iii 1467.
: for the restitutio Capitolii see c. 8, 5.

: Ihm reads plebiculam, which has better support but seems a doubtful form, perhaps due to a confusion with plebicola. The diminutive was probably used by Vespasian in a merely pitying way; but elsewhere it is contemptuous, e.g. Cic. Att. i 16, illa contionalis hirudo aerarii, misera ac ieiuna plebecula: ib. xvi 8: Hor. Ep. ii 1, 186, his nam plebecula gaudet: Pers. iv 6. Wilkins, on Hor. l.c., suggests that Suetonius puts the word in the mouth of Vespasian as "a specimen of the rough language of the low-born emperor."
: by allowing only manual labour to be used, and so giving more employment.

: at the games to celebrate the original dedication of this theatre Augustus met with a slight mishap: Aug. 43, 5, commissione (i.e. at the opening) ludorum, quibus theatrum Marcelli dedicabat, evenit ut laxatis sellae curulis compagibus caderet supinus.

: Marcellus, son of Octavia sister of Augustus, and adopted son of Augustus, died in 23 B.C., at the age of 20; cf. Verg. Aen. vi 883 sqq., Prop. iii 18. In 44 в.с. Julius Caesar had projected and laid the foundations of a huge theatre (it afterwards held 10,000) which Augustus completed and called after Marcellus; cf. Iul. 44, 1, destinabat .. extruere theatrum summae magnitudinis Tarpeio monti accubans: Dio xliii 49, θέατρόν τέ τι κατὰ τὸν Πομπήιον (i.e. as Pompey had done) οἰκοδομῆσαι ἐθελήσας προκατεβάλετο μέν, οὐκ ἐξετέλεσε δέ. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν ὁ Αὔγουστος μετὰ ταῦτα ἐκποιήσας ἀπὸ Μάρκου Μαρκέλλου τοῦ ἀδελφιδοῦ ἐπωνόμασε: Mon.
