Ancyr. 21, Theatrum ad aedem Apollinis in solo magna ex parte a privatis empto feci, quod sub nomine M. Marcelli generi mei esset: Suet. Aug. 29, 4, quaedam etiam opera sub nomine alieno . . fecit, ut .. theatrum Marcelli. The building was so far advanced in 17 B.C. that there was a performance given in it at the Ludi Saeculares, and it was finished and dedicated in 13 B.с. (Dio liv 26) or 11 в.с. (Plin. N.H. viii 65). It suffered damage in 69 A.D. at the storming and burning of the Capitol by the Vitellians. Martial (x 51, 11) mentions it among the most conspicuous buildings of Rome. For its subsequent history and the extant remains in the Via del Teatro di Marcello (between the S.W. end of the Capitoline and the Tiber) see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 516 sqq.

: acroāma (ἀκρόαμα) means a thing heard, especially music, also plays, recitations, entertainments of any kind. The performer or "artiste” was also called acroama (e.g. Cic. Sest. 116, of an actor: Nep. Att. 14, of an anagnostes or reader); cf. the description of the dinners of Augustus, Aug. 74, ad communionem sermonis tacentes vel summissim fabulantes provocabat, et aut acromata et histriones aut etiam triviales ex circo ludios (i.e. strolling players from the circus) interponebat ac frequentius aretalogos (i.e. story-tellers). Pliny, Ep. vi 31, 13, mentions acroamata at Trajan's dinner-parties. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 337; Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 176.

: the MSS. have appellari, apellari, apelli. The reading in the text is a correction by Bücheler. Apollinari is read in Ed. Rom. ii and most subsequent editions; Roth and Preud'homme adopt Politian's Apellari; but nothing is known of any actor named Apollinaris or Apellaris. Apelles may possibly be the Apelles of Ascalon, a famous tragic actor, who was at first an intimate friend and favourite of the emperor Caligula (Dio lix 5), but later, as Suetonius tells us, he had a painful experience of Caligula's eccentricity: Calig. 33, Inter varios iocos, cum assistens simulacro Iovis Apellen tragoedum consuluisset uter illi maior videretur, cunctantem flagellis discidit conlaudans subinde vocem deprecantis quasi etiam in gemitu praedulcem. Apelles is referred to in Petron. Satyr. 64 as a peerless actor: Quando parem habui nisi unum ("the one and only'") Apelletem? The difficulty lies in assuming that this Apelles was still acting in the reign of Vespasian, 30 years after his maltreatment by Caligula.

: Terpnus was a famous citharoedus who taught Nero to play upon the cithara and to sing to it (Ner. 20, 1). He was one of those in the train of Nero on his musical tour to the Greek contests (see Vesp. 4, 4) and competed unsuccessfully against the emperor (Dio lxiii 8). Apollonius of Tyana, according to Philostratus (v 7), spoke scornfully of Nero's doffing the robes of Augustus and Julius in order to don those of a Terpnus at the festivals in Greece. Diodoro: Diodorus also was defeated by Nero at the Greek musical contests. He had the honour of riding with Nero in the triumphal car when the emperor entered Rome after his "victories" in Greece (Dio lxiii 20). =
: praeter; see on c. 24.

: in Ner. 53 we read of the scaenicae coronae which Nero won by his victories on the stage. The custom of rewarding actors with golden crowns must have been common in the later days of the Republic, as Plutarch (Cat. min. 46) says that Cato cut down the expenses of official theatrical entertainments by giving the players crowns not of gold but of wild olive like the prizes at Olympia. Varro (L.L. v 178) mentions "corollae in scaena dari solitae cum placuerant actores," but does not specify the material. Pliny (N.H. xxxiv 94) states that actors' crowns of bronze, if dyed with ox-gall, present the appearance of gold. Sometimes a successful actor was awarded a corollarium, which was a wreath of bronze leaves silvered or gilded (cf. Plin. N.H. xxi 5: Merrill on Plin. Ep. vii 24). A golden olive-crown was the prize at the musical contest (agon) held by Domitian at his Alban villa (cf. Stat. Silv. iii 5, 28, etc.). See Dom. 4, 4.

: "gave dinner parties"; cf. Aug. 74, convivabatur assidue nec umquam nisi recta: Iul. 48, convivatum assidue per provincias: Dom. 21, convivabatur frequenter ac large, sed paene raptim: Claud. 32, convivia agitavit et ampla et assidua: Tit. 7, 2, convivia instituit iucunda magis quam profusa.

: sc. cenâ, a regular formal dinner of successive courses (fercula, lit. 'trays'"). The smallest number of courses was three, viz. the gustatio (hors d'oeuvres), cena, and secunda mensa (dessert). At times Augustus had six (Aug. 74) and Juvenal (i 94) mentions fercula septem, these numbers being made up by subdividing the second of the three old courses (the cena) into prima cena, altera cena, tertia cena, etc. A cena recta was opposed to a mere sportula or distribution of portions of food to clients; cf. Mart. viii 50, 10, promissa est nobis sportula, recta data est. See on Dom. 7, 1, sportulas publicas sustulit revocata rectarum cenarum consuetudine.

: this form of the adv. occurs in Pompon. Atell. 161, verrem sume dapsile; Naevius (com. 39 R.) has dapsiliter suos amicos alit; Lucilius (xxx 55 M.) uses the comparative, qui invitavit dapsilius se. The adj. dapsilis (δαψιλής) is found in Plautus, e.g. Aulul. 167, dotes dapsiles (dapsilas, Nonius), and in post-Aug. authors. See Neue - Wagener, Formenlehre ii 150, 687.

: "market-vendors"; cf. Iul. 26, 2, quae ad epulum pertinerent, quamvis macellariis ablocata ("let out on contract"), etiam domesticatim apparabat. The subst. is found earlier in Varr. R.R. iii 2, 11; 4, 2. Macellum (μάκελλον) is connected with the Hebr. mikhela, makhela ""enclosure.'" The first macellum at Rome was built in 179 в.с., and was replaced under Augustus by the macellum Liviae. In order to enforce his sumptuary laws, Julius Caesar had guards placed to prevent the sale of forbidden dainties in the macellum (Iul. 43), and Tiberius proposed that the prices in the macellum should be revised annually by the senate, to check profiteering, e.g. the sale of mullets (mulli) at 10,000 sesterces apiece (Tib. 34).

: apophoreta (ἀποφορητά) was the word used for the presents which guests received at table to take home with them, especially during the festival of the Saturnalia (Dec. 17-23). The name is familiar as the title of the 14th book of Martial's Epigrams, which consists of distichs, like mottoes, to accompany such presents, which were either cheap (e.g. nuts) or costly (e.g. works of art); in the introductory epigram Martial associates them with the Saturnalia. Augustus gave these presents; cf. Aug. 75, Saturnalibus, et si quando alias libuisset, modo munera dividebat, vestem et aurum et argentum, etc. Tiberius sent Claudius "quadraginta aureos in Saturnalia et Sigillaria” (Claud. 5). Caligula gave 2,000,000 sesterces "in apophoretis" to the charioteer Eutychus (Calig. 55). The Schol. on Juv. vi 202 says that apophoreta were given at weddings: solebant enim antea per nuptias recedentibus dulcia (sweetmeats or cakes) erogare pro apophoretis.

: = singulis Kalendis Martiis. For the change of constr. from Saturnalibus to per Kal. Mart. cf. Iul. 16, 1, vi ac per arma: Sall. Iug. 7, per vim atque insidiis: Tac. H. ii 77, per fastidium ac contumacia. See also App. i. § 15. d. On the 1st of March, "the New Year's day of the Roman religious calendar," the matrons celebrated the festival of the Matronalia in honour of Juno Lucina whose temple on the Esquiline was dedicated on that day, probably in 379 B.C. (see Warde Fowler, Rom. Fest. p. 38). Ovid (Fast. iii 229 sqq.) describes the origin and nature of the festival; cf. Hor. C. iii 8, Martiis caelebs quid agam Kalendis? For the custom of making presents to women at the Matronalia cf. Juv. ix 53, munera femineis tractat secreta Kalendis: Plaut. Mil. 690, da mihi, vir, Kalendis: Tibullus (Lygdamus) iii 1: Mart. v 84 (where Martial describes the Martiae Kalendae as the women's Saturnalia). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 571 sq.
: see on c. 16, 1.

div.p: § 2. Alexandrini: Dio (lxvi 8) says that the Alexandrians taunted Vespasian with being avaricious enough to exact even so petty a sum as six obols (about 9d.), a taunt to which Vesp. replied by promptly levying six obols from each of the inhabitants of the city. Dio also says that they regarded Vesp. as ignorant of how to act like a Caesar (Καισαρεύειν) i.e. to be prodigally lavish like Nero. The Alexandrians were notorious for their pungent criticisms of their rulers; cf. Herodian iv 9, 2, πεφύκασι δέ πως εἶναι φιλοσκώμμονες, καὶ λέγειν εὐστόχως ὑπογραφὰς ἢ παιδιάς, ἀπορριπτοῦντες ἐς τοὺς ὑπερέχοντας πολλὰ χαρίεντα μὲν αὐτοῖς δοκοῦντα, λυπηρὰ δὲ τοῖς σκωφθεῖσι: Sen. Cons. ad Helv. 19, itaque loquax et ingeniosa in contumelias praefectorum provincia, in qua etiam qui vitaverunt culpam, non effugerunt infamiam. For Vespasian's new taxation at Alexandria see on c. 16, 1. Dio

p.note: : this reading was restored by Torrentius for cybiotanten of the MSS. Strabo (xvii 796) says that after the expulsion of Ptolemy Auletes in 58 B.C. the Alexandrians made his daughter Berenice queen, and as husband for her they brought in from Syria a certain Cybiosactes (Κυβιοσάκτης τις) who claimed descent from the royal house of Syria; Berenice, however, murdered him in a few days, οὐ φέρουσα τὸ βάναυσον καὶ τὸ ἀνελεύθερον (cum eius sordes illiberalitatemque ferre non posset). (xxxix 57) gives the name of Berenice's husband as Seleucus; it is doubtful whether he was a son or a bastard son of Antiochus X (see Pauly-Wissowa, s.v. Seleukos). Sturz, Dial. Mac. et Alex. 77, explains κυβιοσάκτης as "salsamentarius, qui salsamenta componit et vendit.” κύβιον (cybium) was the flesh of the pelamys, or tunny-fish, cut up into dice-shaped pieces and salted (Plin. N.H. xxxii 146, 151; Athen. iii 116, 118); σάττειν properly meant “onus iumento imponere," as is done by itinerant vendors, and so κυβιοσάκτης is the same as ταριχέμπορος or ταριχοπώλης (Casaubon on Strab. l.c.). salsamentarii, salt-fish vendors, were held in contempt at Rome; cf. Auct. ad Herenn. iv 54, Suet. vit. Horat. 1.
: as an actor's name this is found frequently in inscriptions (Pauly-Wissowa, vi 2078).

: the director and principal actor in the company (grex) which performed a mimus or loosely constructed character-sketch of common life. These mimi were notorious for their vulgarity and immorality; see Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 113 sqq. The number of the company varied with the piece, and female parts were played by women. The one word mimus is used both for the actor and for the piece. The term archimimus occurs also in Sen. frag. 36, doctus archimimus, senex iam decrepitus, cotidie in Capitolio mimum agebat: Porphyr. (on Hor. S. ii 6, 7'2), archimimus iucunde et molliter et saltaret et eloqueretur: Dig. xxxviii 1, 25: C.I.L. iii 7343, etc. The fem. archimima is also found, C.I.L. vi 10107.

: this seems to be the only passage where we are told that it was customary for a mask of the deceased to be worn at his funeral by an actor, though we often hear of the imagines or wax- 2G masks of distinguished ancestors (see on c. 1, 1) being worn in the funeral procession (e.g. Polyb. vi 53, Plin. N.H. xxxv 6). In the illustrations which we have of Etruscan funeral processions the deceased is depicted as playing an active part, and according to Martha, Art étrusque pp. 417 sqq., the deceased was represented in the procession by a mannequin or an actor (Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1383). In a triumphal procession an actor attired in all the splendour of the triumphator provided amusement to the populace by his imitations of the victorious general trampling or dancing(ἐπορχούμενος, insultans) on his foes (App. Рип. 66).

: the pompa funebris or funeral procession was organised by the funeral-marshals (dissignatores) after the fashion of the pоmра circensis or pompa triumphalis. It was headed by musicians (tibicines, tubicines, siticines, cornicines), followed in the old days by praeficae or women chanting dirges (naeniae), who were later replaced by choirs of men. After them came dancers and actors; then the wearers of the imagines, each attired in the robe of the office held by the ancestor whom he represented, and driving in a car of state preceded by the appropriate number of lictors. After them came bearers of crowns, spoils, and other records of victories and triumphs won by the deceased. The procession was closed by torch-bearers and lictors with fasces reversed; these pre-. ceded the bier which in the case of emperors was borne by magistrates and senators (Suet. Iul. 84, Aug. 100). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 353 sqq.
: = centiens centena milia sestertium, 10,000,000 sesterces, about £85,000. Nero was buried at a cost of 200,000 sesterces (Ner. 50).

: apparently the Romans did not regard as unseemly at an emperor's funeral such an exhibition of the licence which had become familiar on the stage. In the later days of the Republic mimi were allowed great freedom in the way of political allusion (cf. Cic. Att. xiv 3, populi ἐπισημασίαν et mimorum dicta perscribito). Laberius revenged himself on the dictator Caesar, for compelling him to act in his own mimes, by the two famous lines “Porro Quirites! libertatem perdimus'' and "Necesse est multos timeat quem multi timent" (Macrob. Sat. ii 7). The audience were quick to detect allusions to the alleged effeminacy of Augustus and the debauchery of Tiberius at Capri (Suet. Aug. 68, Tib. 45). Caligula buried alive a composer of Atellanae for a double entendre reflecting on him (Calig. 27). Nero's poisoning of Claudius, his attempt to drown Agrippina, and likewise the harshness and avarice of Galba were hinted at upon the stage (Ner. 39, Galb. 13). Helvidius Priscus was executed by Domitian for making his farce (exodium) entitled “Paris and Oenone" a satire on the emperor's divorce (Dom. 10, 4). Further examples are given by Friedlaender (l.c.).

: cf. Tib. 75, 1, morte eius ita laetatus est populus, ut ad primum nuntium discurrentes “Tiberium in Tiberium!”” clamitarent. The body of the emperor Elagabalus was thrown into the Tiber (Lamprid. Heliog. c. 17). See also Vitell. 17, 2.

: quadratus as applied to the build of men or other animals meant well-proportioned, not too long or too short, and not too plump or too spare; this is shown by Celsus ii 1, corpus habilissimum quadratum est, neque gracile neque obesum; nam longa statura, ut in iuventute decora est, sic matura senectute conficitur, gracile corpus infirmum, obesum hebes est. Columella (vii 12) says that a dog for guarding a farmhouse (villaticus canis) should be “quadratus potius quam longus aut brevis"; while a dog for guarding cattle (pecuarius canis) should possess a "status longior productiorque quam brevis aut etiam quadratus.” The Greek τετράγωνος is used metaph. of those who stand four-square, well-balanced in body and mind. •
: "with well-knit limbs"; cf. Plin. Ep. vii 24, compacto corpore et robusto: Pallad. iv 11, 2, (sint boves) cervice torosa atque compacta.

: "wits"; cf. Domitius Marsus (ap. Quintil. vi 3, 105): Urbanus homo erit, cuius multa bene dicta responsaque erunt; et qui in sermonibus, circulis, conviviis, item in contionibus, omni denique loco ridicule commodeque dicet. The opposite of urbanitas is rusticitas: Quintil. vi 3, 17, urbanitas . qua quidem significari video sermonem praeferentem in verbis et sono et usu proprium quendam gustum urbis et sumptam ex conversatione doctorum tacitam eruditionem, denique cui contraria sit rusticitas. Gr. ἀστεῖος opp. to ἄγροικος.
: see on Dom. 6, 2.

: cf. Cic. Phil. ii 17, 42, At vero adhibes ioci causa magistrum, suffragio tuo et compotorum tuorum rhetorem, cui concessisti ut in te quae vellet diceret, salsum omnino hominem, sed materia facilis est in te et in tuos dicta dicere. Cicero uses dicta dicere "to utter witticisms (mots)" also in Planc. 85, de or. ii 244; so dicax (from dico) "witty." in does not mean "against," but “on” “concerning"; see Holden on Cic. Off. i 28.

: the same jest on a person who had a strained look occurs in Mart. iii 89: Utere lactucis, et mollibus utere malvis: | nam faciem durum, Phoebe, cacantis habes (cf. id. x 48, 7, Exoneraturas ventrem mihi villica malvas | attulit).
: but he was gouty, for Dio (lxvi 17) says that his last illness was not his "accustomed gout" but a fever (νοσήσας οὐ τῇ ποδάγρᾳ τῇ συνήθει ἀλλὰ πυρετοῖς). •

: fricare, fricatio, frictio, and their compounds are very often used of massage, friction, either dry or with unguents which are rubbed in; see Thes. Ling. Lat., where abundant instances are cited from Pliny N.H. and medical writers like Celsus, Serenus Sammonicus, and Scribonius Largus. =

: certo finitoque numero (Baumg.-Cr.); cf. Cels. ii 14, neque audiendi sunt qui numero finiunt, quoties aliquis perfricandus sit: id enim ex viribus hominis colligendum est; et si is perinfirmus est, potest 2G2 satis esse quinquagies, si robustior, potest ducenties esse faciendum; inter utrumque deinde, prout vires sunt.

: in the last century of the Republic the Romans played their games of ball in the open space of the Campus Martius (Hor. Sat. i 6, 126, Sen. Ep. 104), but under the Empire they preferred a closed-in court for the purpose. These ball-courts formed part of every gymnasium and were adjuncts of the various public baths at Rome. Private mansions possessed them, and the younger Pliny had a sphaeristerium (σφαιριστήριον) close to the baths in both his elaborate country-houses (Plin. Ep. ii 17, 12: ▼6, 27). The players stripped for the game; Pliny mentions an apodyterium or dressing-room in connexion with the sphaeristerium. inediam unius diei: cf. Cels. vii 7, 4, abstinentia ("fasting'") unius diei. The curative value of abstinence from food (λιμός, νηστεία, abstinentia, inedia) is mentioned in the medical writers from Hippocrates on; e.g. Cels. ii 16, neque ulla res magis adiuvat laborantem quam tempestiva abstinentia. Hippocrates declared that privation (ἔνδεια) is the mother of health (ὑγιείας μητήρ). Protracted inedia was a common means of suicide under the Empire, e.g. in the case of Silius Italicus (Plin. Ep. iii 7); cf. Suet. Aug. 53, 3, inedia mori destinantem . ad vitam revocavit: Tib. 53, 2, mori inedia destinanti, per vim ore diducto, infulciri cibum iussit.

: interponere is used in Celsus of introducing at intervals certain changes of treatment, diet, etc.; e.g. iii 6, poteritque a balneo etiam pinguius aut dulcius dari vinum; poterit semel aut bis interponi Graecum salsum.

: ordo denotes the systematic portioning out of each day between the successive officia which have to be discharged; cf. Juv. 1 127, ipse dies pulchro distinguitur ordine rerum: Plin. Ep. iii 1 (of the life of Spurinna), nihil est illo vitae genere distinctius (i.e. better distributed) parva haec, parva, si non cotidie fiant, ordine quodam ac velut orbe circumagit. “Ordinare diem” and “disponere diem” were used for the methodical arrangement of one's day.

: so [Aur. Vict.] Εpit. 9, Institutum vero uniforme omni imperio tenuit. Vigilare de nocte publicisque actibus absolutis caros admittere, dum salutatur calceamenta sumens et regium vestitum. Post autem negotiis, quaecumque advenissent, auditis exerceri vectatione, deinde requiescere, postremo ubi lavisset, remissiore animo convivium curabat.

: "while it was still night." On this temporal use of de see Kühner-Stegmann, i 498, where de die and de nocte are explained "vom Tage her, von der Nacht her = noch bei Tage, am hellen Tage, noch in der Nacht, in der Nacht"; cf. Ter. Ad. 840, Hor. Ep. i 2, 32, ut iugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones. officiorum: officia here is practically equivalent to "officials," a meaning which we find more definitely in later Latin; e.g. [Treb. Poll.] Gall. 17, cum iret ad hortos omnia Palatina officia sequebantur. The concrete use of officium appears in the younger Pliny; e.g. Ep. iii 12, erunt officia antelucana (i.e. callers, salutatores, abroad before dawn), in quae incidere impune ne Catoni quidem licuit: Pan. 76, ipsius officium (‘suite'') tam modicum; cf. Juv. x 44, praecedentia longi | agminis officia ('attentive clients''): Apul. Met. iv 31, marinum obsequium = dii marini obsequentes. Abstracts like servitium, remigium, ministerium, are often used in a concrete sense; see Draeger, Hist. Synt. i² 22-24.

: ''summaries," "condensed reports." Seneca (Ep. 39) condemns breviarium as a barbarism: vide, ne plus profutura sit ratio ordinaria quam haec, quae nunc vulgo breviarium dicitur, olim cum Latine loqueremur, summarium vocabatur. Suetonius uses it also in Aug. 101, breviarium totius imperii (called rationarium imperii in Aug. 28, 1): Galb. 12, 3 dispensatori breviarium rationum offerenti: Gramm. 10, Ateius Sallustium breviario rerum omnium Romanarum instruxit; cf. Plin. N.H. vii 97, xviii 230, and the “Breviarium Historiae Romanae" by Eutropius. Cicero (Att. xiii 8, etc.) uses epitome (ἐπιτομή) for an abridgement.

: Dio (lxvi 10) describes the accessibility of Vespasian. The door of his palace in the Sallustine Gardens stood open all day long; no one was denied admission, senator or plebeian. His intimate friends were admitted even while he was still in bed. The elder Pliny used to visit him before dawn: Plin. Ep. iii 5, ante lucem ibat ad Vespasianum imperatorem, nam ille quoque noctibus utebatur. Philostratus (vit. Apollon. v 31) describes Vespasian, while still at Alexandria, as engaged on his correspondence long before dawn. Einhard in his Life of Charlemagne (c. 24) imitates Suetonius very closely: cum calciaretur et amiciretur, non tantum amicos admittebat, verum etiam, si comes palatii litem aliquam esse diceret, quae sine eius iussu definiri non posset, lite cognita sententiam dixit. See Introd. ii ad fin.

: persons of rank were usually assisted in their toilet by numerous attendant slaves (see Marquardt, Privatl. 145); cubicularii would put on their robes, and calciatores their shoes. Pliny (Ep. iii 16) mentions the argument used by Arria when imploring the soldiers to allow her to go on board the ship which was to bear her husband Thrasea Paetus as a prisoner to Rome: “nempe enim,” inquit, “daturi estis consulari viro servolos aliquos, quorum e manu cibum capiat, a quibus vestiatur, a quibus calcietur: omnia sola praestabo.”
: the only part of amicio used by the best writers is amictus (sum). post decisa .. ..

: cf. Hor. Ep. i 7, 56 sqq., praeconem ... et ludis et post decisa negotia Campo, a passage which gaudentem shows that decidere negotia could be used in the general sense of transacting or completing any business, and not merely in the limited legal sense of deciding or settling a case (e.g. Capitol. M. Antonin. Phil. 10, multis praetoriis et consularibus privatis decidenda negotia delegavit): it is in the latter sense that the words of Suet. are understood in [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, quoted above.

: gestatio, which is a post-Aug. word, was used especially of taking exercise either by being carried in a litter (lectica) or driving in a carriage (cf. Galb. 8, 1). The word denoted not merely the exercise itself but also the part of the grounds of Roman villas where the gestatio took place (cf. Plin. Ep. ii 17, 13; v 6, 17). Seneca refers to the advantages of gestatio as a form of exercise; Ep. 15, gestatio et corpus concutit et In studio non officit: possis legere, possis dictare, possis loqui, possis audire. (Claudius even played at dice; Suet. Claud. 33, 2, solitus etiam in gestatione aleam ludere, ita essedo alveoque adaptatis ne lusus confunderetur.) Ep. 55 Seneca also mentions the tired feeling produced by the motion: a gestatione venio non minus fatigatus quam si tantum ambulassemi quantum sedi. Medical writers recommend gestatio; e.g. Cels. ii 15, gestatio longis morbis aptissima est genera autem gestationis plura sunt: lenissima est navi vel in portu vel in flumine, vehementior vel in alto, vel lectica, etiamnum acrior vehiculo.
: i.e. the siesta (meridiatio).

: the form pallaca (= Gr. παλλακή) is very rare, the only other example cited being Plin. N.H. xxxv 86, dilectam sibi (i.e. Alexander the Great) e pallacis suis praecipue, nomine Pancasten. The usual Lat. word for a mistress or concubine is paelex (pellex), the derivation of which is uncertain; see Walde, Lat. Etym. Wörterb.
: see on c. 3.

: i.e. from the private apartment where he had been resting. For secreto see on Oth. 3, 1. balneum tricliniumque: bathing was a regular preliminary to dining, e.g. Plin. Ep. vi 20, mox balneum, cena, somnus inquietus et brevis. The usual time for the bath was the eighth hour or a little later; see on Dom. 21. ea momenta.. ad aliquid petendum
: cf. Ov. Pont. iii 1, 129, eligito tempus, captatum saepe, rogandi: Liv. xxxiii 35, temporum opportunitates captasse ad rebellandum.
: for super cenam see on Tit. 8, 1; for the position of autem see on Dom. 13, 33; for et autem followed by et cf. Aug. 73, Et forensia autem et calceos habuit ad subitos casus parata.

: this reading has been reasonably suspected, and the variant super aleas (so Ts; super alias, PO) was approved by Casaubon and read by Burman; Graevius, on the ground that the pl. aleas is indefensible, suggested aleam. The only example of the pl. of alea given in the Thes. Ling. Lat. is Amm. xiv 6, 25, pugnaciter aleis certant. Preud 'homme marks off the words et semper alias comissimus as a parenthesis.

: com(m)unissimus (Ts) is read by the editors before Roth; cf. Claud. 21, 5, nec ullo spectaculi genere communior ("more familiar'") aut remissior erat. Torrentius preferred the reading cum amicis given by one of his MSS.

: i.e. he settled many matters by dismissing them with a bon mot; cf. Hor. Sat. i 10, 14, ridiculum acri | fortius et melius magnas plerumque secat res: Cic. de or. ii 236, odiosas res saepe, quas argumentis dilui non facile est, ioco risuque dissolvit. Vespasian could take a joke as well as make one: ἔσκωπτε δημοτικῶς, καὶ ἀντεσκώπτετο ἡδέως (Dio lxvi 11).

: this phrase for "obscene expressions" is very obscure. It occurs also in Gell. N.A. ix 10, non praetextatis, sed puris honestisque verbis, and in Macrob. Sat. ii 1, 9, impudica et praetextata verba. The first of the two explanations given by Festus (p. 245 M.) is rather on the "lucus a non lucendo" principle: praetextum (al. praetextatum) sermonem quidam putant dici, quod praetextatis (i.e. boys who have not yet assumed the toga virilis) nefas sit obsceno verbo uti; alii, quod nubentibus, depositis praetextis, a multitudine puerorum obscena (i.e. Fescennina) clamentur. Freund explains praetextata verba as velata verba "verblümte (i.e. disguised in flowery language) Worte": Forcellini says "praetextata verba esse ea, quibus aliquid praefari vel praetexi debet honoris causa, quemadmodum obscenis dictis 'honos sit auribus' praetexere solemne fuit." Juvenal (ii 170), describing Armenian envoys who had been initiated in evil practices at Rome, has the line "Sic praetextatos referunt Artaxata mores," which the Schol. explains "mores quos filii senatorum intra urbem habent, obsides in suis patriis redeuntes reportant, quos ceteri apud se ephebi discant'"; and praetextata verba is prob. to be understood either of the foul language used by such young libertines, or (as Gronovius on Gell. l.c. suggests) of the language which the seducers of youth employed (verba quibus ad nequitiam sollicitarentur).
: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, ferebat patienter amicorum motus, contumeliis eorum, ut erat facetissimus, iocularibus respondens.

: Lucius Mestrius Florus took part in the first battle of Betriacum in 69 A.D. as an unwilling follower of Otho. It is uncertain in what year he was consul. He was proconsul of Asia under Domitian (prob. in 83/4), as is shown by coins of Smyrna and an inscription at Ephesus (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. ii p. 370). Plutarch made his acquaintance in literary circles at Rome, and Florus accompanied him through Cisalpine Gaul, showing him over the plain of Betriacum; cf. Plut. Oth. 14. Florus is introduced by Plutarch in his Quaestiones Conviviales (1,9; 3, 3-5; 5, 7. 10; 7, 1. 2. 4. 6; 8, 1. 2. 10) as giving banquets and taking part in discussions at table, the author describing him as an antiquarian (φιλάρχαιος).

div.p: "plaustra" potius quam "plostra'': the emperor's speech displayed rusticitas in this pronunciation of the word for wagons. Lindsay (Lat. Lang. p. 40) says: “o for au is a feature of the Umbrian language (e.g. ote, Lat. aut) and other dialects, and was preserved in 'rustic' Latin and even in the Latin of the streets of Rome Cicero's rival Clodius was the first of the gens to change the name Claudius to the plebeian form Clodius, no doubt with the view of conciliating the mob. Cicero himself in his letters often uses the more homely forms with o, e.g. loreolam, pollulum, oricula, while plodo is quoted from his 'De Gloria' by Diomede." Cf. Priscian i 52, au transit in o productam more antiquo, ut “lotus” pro lautus, “plostrum” pro plaustrum, “cotes” pro cautes; sicut etiam pro o, au, ut “austrum” pro ostrum, “ausculum” pro osculum, frequentissime hoc faciebant antiqui. “Plostrum” and “plostellum,” as the vulgar forms, are read in Hor. Sat. i 6, 42: ii 3, 247, but in the Odes and Epistles of Hor. “plaustrum” is the form favoured by the MSS. (cf. Wilkins on Εp. ii 2, 74).
"Flaurum": Vespasian scored by substituting for "Florus" (from flos) the form "Flaurus" which at once suggests φλαῦρος (vilis, inutilis, nequam).

p.note: : cf. Tib. 21, 2, expugnatum precibus uxoris: Iul. 1, 3, Sullam, cum deprecantibus .. aliquamdiu denegasset, atque illi pertinaciter contenderent, expugnatum tandem proclamasse, etc.: Liv. xxxvii 56, 9, senatum omni modo expugnaturum pertinaciam legatorum.
: in a causal sense; see on Tit. 5, 1.

: cf. Dom. 3, 1, Paridis histrionis amore deperditam: Plaut. Cist. 132, is amore misere hanc deperit mulierculam: Catull. 35, 12, quae illum deperit impotente amore. So too deperire (without amore) = perdite amare “to love to distraction" "to be dying with love for'"; e.g. Plaut. Bacch. 470, meretricem indigne deperit; cf. Prop. ii 30, 29, (Iuppiter) ut Semela est combustus, ut est deperditus Io, where Io is the accus.

: the MSS. vary, as usual, between suo and sui; in some the word is omitted altogether, and Modderman (Lectiones Suetonianae р. 67) suggests that this is due to the fact that the reading in the archetype was amore se deperiret, a construction which the copyist failed to understand.

: this verb is frequently used de feminis ad stuprum ductis (e.g. Tib. 45, Calig. 25, 2, Cic. Verr. v 31, Hor. S. ii 5, 77, Ov. Am. iii 12, 11); so perductor for a pander or pimp (Plaut., Cic., etc.). Casaubon proposed perducta and Burman perducta ei, making Vespasian the payee and not the payer, on the ground that the penurious emperor would never have paid 400,000 sesterces for the favours of a lady who was only too anxious to grant them; but, as Ernesti pointed out, perducta requires the further change of expugnatus to expugnato, and Vespasian's conduct would have been so unutterably sordid that Suetonius would have mentioned it in c. 16 and not here. Vespasian was extravagant in matters of love (cf. c. 21 where plurimae pallacae of his are mentioned), and it is unnecessary to accuse him of behaving like the gallant captain Pyrgopolinices whose minimum fee was a talentum Philippum (Plaut. Mil. 1061).
: about £3,400. Vesp. bestowed the same amount on an actor, c. 19, 1. The variant quadraginta (GTQ) is read by Burman and Ernesti.

: the steward raised the question "quem ad modum summam rationibus vis inferri?” Cf. Tit. 8, 1. For the use of the pres. ptc. in the sense of a perf. or of a Greek aorist ptc. cf. Iul. 65, ac subinde observandum se admonens repente interdiu vel nocte se subtrahebat: ib. 73, Catullum.. satisfacientem eadem die adhibuit cenae: Galb. 5, 2, revocante: ib. 10, cohortantibus: ib. 11, supervenientibus. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 757.

: the dispensator ("payer out, lit. "weigher out'") was the steward who had charge of the accounts (hence he was called at times a rationibus) and made the payments; cf. Galb. 12, 3: Ner. 44, 1: Aug. 67, 1. He was nearly invariably a slave or freedman, and the value of the position (dispensatio, c. 23, 2) is shown by the story in Oth. 5, 2 that Otho extorted a million sesterces from a slave whom he had recommended as dispensator to Galba.

: dat. case; cf. the phrase ferre alicui expensum "to debit" (referre alicui acceptum “to credit"). Baumg.-Cr. explains it as the abl. (= Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἐρασθέντος). Marcilius suggested that in adamato there is a play on adhamato (“hooked"). The compound adamare, which is first found in Cicero, is nearly always used in the perfect forms (for rare exceptions see Thes. Ling. Lat.). It is a stronger word than amare; cf. Sen. Ep. 71, 5, si virtutem adamaveris, amare enim parum est. The meaning of illicit love which it has in our passage is found also in Ov. A.A. ii 109, Sit licet antiquo Nireus adamatus Homero: Plin. N.H. viii 157, xxxvi 22: Petron. Satyr. 110, etc.

: the MSS. vary between et de (Ihm), et ut de, and ut de. The correction ut et de, suggested by Preud'homme and defended by Alexander, seems absolutely required by the use of the imperfect utebatur; Suetonius gives two instances of what was a general habit of Vespasian. a a

: if the text is not corrupt, natus here is to be interpreted in the light of the meaning that natura sometimes has, viz. the natural parts (e.g. Cic. N.D. iii 22, 55: Div. ii 70, 145), improbe being used in the sense of enormiter; cf. Charis. i 102, 1, Chilones improbius labrati ('blubber-lipped''): Marc. Emp. 31, ad eos, quibus intestinum improbe prominet. Casaubon, however, maintained that improbe natus means ὁ κακῶς πεφυκώς, "homo deformi et turpi proceritate corporis," and that ἔγχοs "hic dicitur de corpore producto ad instar perticae longuriive (i.e. like a long staff or pole)"; so too Salmasius. Marcilius took improbe natus as 'natura improbus, i.e. impudens," and explained the comparison with spear in curious way: “Impudentiam huiusce Longini Vespasianus argute cum hastae vibratione comparavit, quia impudenter petens, et instans atque urgens, quasi hastam vibrare videtur atque intentare.'" Among the corrections suggested for nato are mutoniato and vasato (both = magna mentula instructo); these give the sense required, but neither explains the corruption. Suetonius may have written improbiusque venato (ve- being lost by haplography). vena is often used for membrum virile (e.g. Mart. iv 66, 12: vi 49, 2), and though venatus does not occur elsewhere, Suet. has several participial adjs. in -atus not found earlier, e.g. cycladatus, discalciatus, fistulatus, infulatus, sagulatus, sericatus, tessellatus; cf. also pedatus (Oth. 12, 1) which means lit. "furnished with feet." μακρὰ . . . ἔγχος: Hom. Il. vii 213, νέρθε δὲ ποσσὶν | ἤϊε μακρὰ βιβάς, κ.τ.λ., describing Ajax about to give battle to Hector. The equivocal sense in which Vespasian was using ἔyxos has its parallel in the play on the word δόρυ by Diogenes the Cynic quoted by Diog. Laert. (vi 2, 53), and in hasta = mentula.

: this freedman of Vespasian is not mentioned elsewhere, but Friedlaender plausibly suggests that it is with reference to him that Martial chooses the name Cerylus in i 67, Liber homo es nimium, dicis mihi, Ceryle, semper. | In te quis dicit, Ceryle, liber homo es?

: Vespasian occupied the position of a patronus in relation to his freedman Cerylus. The rights of the patronus in the estate of his freedman are described fully by Roby, Rom. Priv. Law i 270 sqq. When the freedman had no natural children born since his manumission, the patron was entitled to one moiety of the estate. If he left no own heirs (sui heredes) or natural children at all, the patron succeeded to the whole estate. Under the Lex Papia (in the reign of Augustus), if the freedman left fewer than three children, the patron was to have one equal share (pars virilis), i.e. one-third if there were two children, a moiety if he left only one, provided the estate exceeded 100,000 sesterces. The amount due to Vespasian on the death of Cerylus would be collected by the officials of the fiscus (see on c. 16, 3). The use of ob with the gerund or gerundive is found in early Latin (Cato R.R., etc.); in Cic. frequently with pecuniam accipere or dare (ob rem iudicandam, ob ius dicendum, ob innocentem condemnandum, etc.); in Sall. (Iug. 89, 102), and Tac. (A. i 79, iv 31, xi 5). See KühnerStegmann, i 750.

: for se ferre in the sense of "to give oneself out as" "pass oneself off as," cf. Vell. Pat. i 11, 1, qui se Philippum regiaeque stirpis ferebat, cum esset ultimae: Tac. H. ii 72, extiterat quidam Scribonianum se Camerinum ferens: iv 10, proditor corruptorque amicitiae, cuius se magistrum ferebat.

: it is not easy to see why Cerylus chose the name "Laches," as it was one of the stock names for slaves in Greek comedy; cf. Amm. Marc. xxviii 4, 27, Cum mutuum illi quid petunt, soccos et Miconas videbis et Lachetas (i.e. they employ the wheedling style of slaves in comedy): Dio Chrys. Orat. 74, οὐ κατὰ Λάχητα, οὐδὲ κατὰ Σίμωνα. ὦ Λάχης ... Κηρύλος: the opening words, ὦ Λάχης, Λάχης, are from an unknown play of Menander (frag. 921, Kock); the second line, ἐπὰν . . ἔσει, is from the Θεοφορουμένη of Menander (frag. 223, 2, Kock), and Vespasian added the words σὺ Κηρύλος, his meaning being that in dealing with the estate of Cerylus the fiscus would treat him as a freedman in spite of his claim to be freeborn and his change of name.

: adfectare, like ζηλοῦν, was a tech. rhetorical term for aiming at a certain effect in speech or writing. It is very frequent in Quintilian, e.g. xi 1, 30, adfectata scurrilitas. Cf. the use of captare in Hor. Sat. i 4, 82, qui captat risus hominum, famamque dicacis.

: diluere as a rhet. term means "to weaken the force of an opponent's argument or a charge brought," and it was widely used in the general sense of extenuare or minuere in such phrases as diluere infamiam, dedecus, nefas, peccata, etc. For cavillatione see on Tit. 8, 2.

: the object of transferret is invidiam (not lucra) and the verb here means 'to make use of for a new purpose"; cf. Quintil. vi 2, 30, hoc animi vitium ad utilitatem non transferemus? In Tac. A. ii 65 "transferre invidiam" is used quite differently of transferring odium from oneself to another.

div.p: §2. dispensationem: see on dispensatore, c. 22. exacta pecunia: cf. Oth. 5, 2, servo Caesaris pro impetrata dispensatione decies sestertium expresserat.

p.note: : "appointed,” lit. "assigned him the rank or position (ordo)"; cf. Iul. 76, 3, magistratus in plures annos ordinavit (for which in Vitell. 11, 2, comitia in decem annos ordinavit, seque perpetuum consulem); so of appointing to commands, Aug. 46, equestrem militiam petentes etiam ex commendatione publica cuiusque oppidi ordinabat. This use of the verb does not seem to occur earlier, and Suetonius is also the first to use ordinatio for "appointment to office." He frequently uses ordinare in its more usual sense of arranging or putting in order; e.g. Iul. 56, 7, ordinare bibliothecas (= digerere bibliothecas, Iul. 44): Galb. 7, 1, electus ad ordinandam provinciam inquietam: Aug. 31, annum (i.e. the calendar) a Divo Iulio ordinatum, sed postea neglegentia conturbatum atque confusum, rursus ad pristinam rationem redegit.

: in ancient times shoes were not put on mules or horses except when a bad stretch of road had to be traversed or when their hoofs were weak, and the shoes were never fastened by nails but by strings or straps (lemnisci, fasciolae, Veget. i 26), no farrier being needed to fix them. The shoe (solea, ὑπόδημα) was generally of iron, e.g. Catull. xvii 26, ferream ut soleam (derelinquit) tenaci in voragine mula; Nero's mules had shoes of silver (Ner. 30) and Poppaea's had shoes of gold (Plin. N.H. xxxiii 140). calciare (calceare) is the word used by Palladius, Pliny, Vegetius, etc., for putting on the shoes. See Reinach's article "Mulomedicus" in Daremberg-Saglio. non

div.p: §3. urinae vectigal: Dio lxvi 14, πρὸς τὸν Τίτον ἀγανακτοῦντα τῷ τοῦ οὔρου τέλει, ὁ καὶ αὐτὸ μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων κατεδείχθη, εἶπε, λαβὼν ἐξ αὐτοῦ χρυσοῦς πεπορισμένους καὶ δείξας αὐτῷ, “ Ἰδού, τέκνον, εἴ τι ὄζουσιν." At Rome, at least as early as the 2nd cent. B.c., public urinals were placed in alleys (angiportus); Macrobius, Sat. iii 16, 15, quotes from C. Titius, a contemporary of Lucilius, "dum eunt, nulla est in angiporto amphora quam impleant.” The receptacles were amphorae or dolia (cf. Lucr. iv 1026, Mart. xii 48, 8). Fullers (fullones) and tanners (coriarii), who used large quantities of urine in their trades, were probably taxed by Vespasian for the right of placing these receptacles and emptying them. This is the explanation given by Beroaldus, and is much more probable than the alternative assumption that the public were charged for the use of the amphorae in the same way as, according to one interpretation of Juv. iii 38, they were charged for the use of the foricae or public jakes. It is by no means certain that foricae in Juv. bears this meaning; the Schol. also explains it as shops near the Forum, and this is accepted as correct by Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 280.

p.note: : Casaubon suggests that this was done because the sense of smell was used by moneychangers and others as a means of testing the genuineness of metals; cf. Aristot. de mirabil. 1088, Arrian Epict. Dissert. i 20.
: Juvenal is referring to this story in his famous words lucri bonus est odor ex re | qualibet (xiv 204).
: Dio (lxvi 14) states the sum as 250,000 denarii (= 1,000,000 sesterces), about £8,500.
: like the Colossus of Nero, see on c. 18; the same expression occurs in Plin. N.H. xxxiv 39 and 78 (cf. xxxv 51, Nero iusserat colosseum se pingi).

: the MSS. vary between poneret (MGS) and ponerent. Suetonius has iubere ut in Tib. 22 (lectis codicillis quibus ut id faceret iubebatur), and the subjunctive with ut omitted in Vitell. 14, 4 (edictum quo iubebat urbe mathematici excederent); 'generally he uses iubere with the acc. and inf. Ernesti and Burman read ponere, arguing that the constr. legatos iussit ponerent is not found till a much later period. Bentley made the same correction, and it is adopted by Ihm. Bentley however is inconsistent, as in Ter. Andr. 412 he would read: Erus me relictis rebus iussit Pamphilum | hodie observarem. Alexander (op. cit. p. 18) also points out that the passive constr. in Suet. Tib. 22 (quoted above) implies an active ‘‘lectis codicillis qui eum iusserunt ut id faceret,” i.e. with an accusative preceding and a subjunctive following. Roth conjectured ponere et (adopted in Preud'homme's text), the best correction, if any were needed.
: like the hand of a beggar; cf. Aug. 91, 2, stipem quotannis die certo emendicabat a populo, cavam manum asses porrigentibus praebens: Aristoph. Eq. 1083, ἔμβαλε κυλλῇ (sc. χειρί).

: the pile of money was to be the statue resting on his hand as base. For basis cf. Dom. 15, 2, a basi statuae triumphalis: Aug. 31, 1, sub Palatini Apollinis basi. On the basis were inscribed the name and honours; cf. Plin. Ep. iii 6, 5, iube basim fieri, ex quo voles marmore, quae nomen meum honoresque capiat. The Greek origin of the word basis (βάσις) is preserved in the case-forms like baseos (gen.) and basin (acc.) which are found occasionally (see Thes. Ling. Lat.).

div.p: § 4. ne in metu quidem mortis abstinuit iocis: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, seriis ioca, quibus delectabatur, admiscens interiit. Cf. the spirit of playfulness (τὸ παιγνιώδες) shown by Theramenes when drinking the hemlock (Xen. Hell. ii 3, 56).

p.note: : the same portents of his death are mentioned in Dio lxvi 17, ἐγεγόνει δὲ σημεῖα αὐτῷ φέροντα εἰς τοῦτο, ὅ τε ἀστὴρ κομήτης ἐπὶ πολὺ φαντασθείς, καὶ τὸ μνημεῖον τὸ τοῦ Αὐγούστου αὐτόματον ἀνοιχθέν.

: in 28 B.C. Augustus built in the northern part of the Campus Martius a tomb for members of the house of the Caesars. It was called the Mausoleum Augusti after the tomb built for the Carian prince Mausolus (ob. 353 в.с.) by his wife Artemisia (cf. Aug. 100, Strab. v 236, Dio lviii 22). In shape it was circular with a base of white marble about 300 ft. in circumference and 60 ft. in height, on which rose a mound of earth covered with evergreens, the interior being divided into sepulchral chambers to contain the ashes. A bronze statue of Augustus crowned the whole. Tacitus calls it the tumulus Augusti or tumulus Iuliorum (Ann. iii 4, xvi 6). The first whose ashes were laid there was the young Marcellus (23 B.C.); then Agrippa (12 B.c.); Drusus, brother of Tiberius (9 B.C.); Lucius and Gaius, adopted sons of Augustus (2 and 4 A.D.); Augustus (14 A.D.); Germanicus (20 A.D., died in 19); Livia (29 A.D.); Tiberius (37 A.D.). Caligula transferred to it the ashes of his mother and his brother (Calig. 15), but was not himself buried there. Claudius, Britannicus, and Vespasian were probably entombed in it, as were Nero's wife Poppaea and the emperor Nerva. The other members of the Julio-Claudian and the Flavian houses were, with few exceptions, laid elsewhere (see Jordan-Huelsen Topogr. Rom i 3, 614 sqq.). Dio (lxix 23) says that by Hadrian's time the Mausoleum of Augustus was filled, and Hadrian built another on the other side of the Tiber, the Mausoleum Hadriani (mod. Castello di S. Angelo).
: so before Nero's death: de Mausoleo, sponte foribus patefactis, exaudita vox est nomine eum cientis (Ner. 46, 2).

: the appearance of a comet betokened a ruler's death; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 41, taetrum sidus regnis quod crinitum vocatur: Suet. Ner. 36, 1, stella crinita, quae summis potestatibus exitium portendere vulgo putatur, per continuas noctes oriri coeperat: Claud. 46, praesagia mortis eius praecipua fuerunt exortus crinitae stellae, etc.: Verg. G. i 489 (describing portents at the death of Julius Caesar), non alias totiens arsere cometae: Shakespeare Jul. Caes. ii 2, When beggars die there are no comets seen; The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes. Seneca (N.Q. vi 3, 3) first uses crinitum sidus as a translation of κομήτης (ἀστήρ); the luminous tail of the comet was compared to floating hair (κόμη, crinis). diri

: daughter of M. Iunius Silanus (cons. 19 A.D.) and of Aemilia Lepida. Her name Calvina was derived from her paternal grandmother Domitia Calvina (Mommsen, Ephem. Epigr. i 64). She is mentioned in Tac. A. xii 4 as the "decora et procax soror" of L. Iunius Silanus and daughter-in-law of L. Vitellius (censor 48 A.D.), being wedded to L. Vitellius brother of the emperor Aulus (see Vitell. 3, 1). A charge was trumped up against her of having incestuous relations with her brother Silanus, and he was driven to suicide in 49 A.D., while she was banished from Italy (Tac. A. xii 8). Ten years later she was restored from exile by Nero (A. xiv 12).

: she was a great-great-granddaughter of Augustus, and, as such, might be buried in the Mausoleum Augusti. Her mother Aemilia Lepida was a daughter of Aemilius Paulus and of Julia, who was a granddaughter of Augustus.

: this verb is very frequently used of the application of portents; e.g. Phaedr. iii 3, 6, ad consulendos currit maerens hariolos; | hic pertinere ad domini respondet caput: Val. Max. i 6, haruspices ad salutem imperatoris pertinere dixerunt.

: in contrast to Vespasian who was bald; cf. Dio lxvi 17, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς περὶ τοῦ κομήτου τι διαλαλοῦντας, “ Οὐκ ἔμοιγε,” εἶπεν, “ἀλλὰ τῷ τῶν Πάρθων βασιλεῖ προσημαίνει· ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ κομᾷ (comatus est), ἐγὼ δὲ φαλακρός (calvus) εἰμι.” The Parthians, the successors of the Persians, wore the same flowing locks (τὸ ἄφετον καὶ ἀνειμένον τῆς κόμης, Suid. s.v. Λεόννατος: Hdt. vi 19, τῶν Περσέων ἐόντων κομητέων). In [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, 18 it is the Persian king whom Vespasian is said to have mentioned: cum crinitum sidus apparuisset, “Istud,” inquit, "ad regem Persarum pertinet, cui capillus effusior." The king of Parthia at Vespasian's death was Vologaesus, successor to the Vologaesus mentioned in c. 6 who must have died before June 78 as from that time a new image appears on the coinage (Prosop. Imp. Rom. i 476; Gardner, Parthian Coinage p. 76).

: Dio (l.c.) says that it was when Vespasian believed that he was going to die (ἐπειδὴ ἐπίστευσεν ὅτι τελευτήσει) that he said “ Θεὸς ἤδη γίγνομαι.”" Accessio (more rarely accessus) is regularly used by post-Aug. writers for a "coming on" or "attack" of any malady, especially an intermittent fever; the abatement of the attack is decessio (decessus) or remissio. Cicero uses accedere in the same way: Att. vii 2, alteram quartanam (sc. febrim) dixit decessisse et alteram leviorem accedere. Greek medical writers have εἰσβολή, προσβολή, ἐπίληψις, ἐπισημασία, and παροξυσμός in the sense of accessio.

: some of the later MSS. have ut (so edd. princ., vulg.) or ne. Many corrections have been proposed: vah (Graevius), nae (Gronovius), at (Burman), eu (Modderman); but vae is rightly defended by Ernesti, who says: Non modo iocus est in eo quod pro ‘morior” dixit “Deus fio," sed etiam acumen in eo quod dolentis voce utitur in re, quae, si proprie diceretur, felicitas esset.

: referring to the deification of the Roman emperors after death, expressed by such phrases as inter divos referre (Aug. 97,2): in numerum deorum referre (Claud. 45): caelum decernere (Tac. A. i 73): caelestes honores decernere (A. xii 69). The honour was decreed by the senate on the motion of the reigning emperor. Vespasian's deification is mentioned by Pliny (Pan. 11), when congratulating Trajan on his reasons for deifying Nerva: Quem tu .. templis honestasti, non imitatus illos qui hoc idem, sed alia mente, fecerunt. Dicavit caelo Tiberius Augustum, sed ut maiestatis crimen induceret, Claudium Nero, sed ut inrideret, Vespasianum Titus, Domitianus Titum, sed ille, ut dei filius, hic, ut frater videretur. Tu sideribus patrem intulisti, non ad metum civium, non in contumeliam. numinum, non in honorem tuum, sed quia deum credis. Vespasian's worship was in the care of the collegium Flavialium (Dom. 4, 4). Tiberius, Caligula, Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius were not deified, and the senate was not cowed into granting the honour to Domitian (see Dom. 23). Imperial deification, or apotheosis, is delightfully satirised in Seneca's Apocolocyntosis (“Pumpkinification") of Claudius. Nero, with grim humour, used to call mushrooms (boleti) the food of the gods (deorum cibus) after they had been used to poison Claudius (Dom. 14, 1, n.).
: in 79 A.D.; see on c. 8, 1.
: where Pompey also was stricken with fever; cf. Juv. x 283, provida Pompeio dederat Campania febres.

: slight attacks, touches of fever or ague accompanied by shivering; cf. Sen. Ep. 53, 6, levis aliquem motiuncula decipit, sed cum crevit et vera febris exarsit, etc. Celsus (iii 5) uses motio for an ague-fit. Cicero has commotiuncula in Att. xii 11, commotiunculis συμπάσχω; cf. xiv 5, leviter commotus ("slightly indisposed'').

: a Sabine village about 7 miles from Vespasian's native place Reate. There was a small lake there (mod. Lago di Contigliano) which Varro called the umbilicus Italiae as being in the centre of the peninsula (Plin. N.H. iii 17). Close to it were springs, sulphureous and others, and the Romans went there for "cures" either by drinking the waters or by bathing in them. There is an epigram (Anth. Pal. ix 349) addressed by Leonidas to Vespasian at Aquae Cutiliae on his birthday: Ὑδατά σοι Κοτίλεια γενέθλιον ἦμαρ ὁρῶντι, | Καῖσαρ, ἐπιβλύζοι σωρὸν ἀκεσφορίης, | ὄφρα σε κόσμος ἅπας πάππον τρισὶν αὐγάζηται, | ὡς πατέρα τρισσῆς εἴσιδεν εὐτοκίης. Titus, like his father, died at Cutiliae; see Tit. 11.
: see c. 1, 2. This

: cf. Galb. 4, 3, Tusculum, ubi aestivare consuerat. verb is almost entirely post-Aug.; the only earlier writer who uses it is Varro, e.g. R.R. ii 2, 9, mihi greges in Apulia hibernabant, qui in Reatinis aestivabant. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1.

: the extreme coldness of the springs at Cutiliae and their curative powers are mentioned in Plin. N.H. xxxi 10, Iuxta Romam Albulae aquae volneribus medentur egelidae; sed Cutiliae in Sabinis gelidissimae suctu quodam corpora invadunt ut prope morsus videri possit, aptissimae stomacho, nervis, universo corpori: Vitruv. viii 3, Est autem aquae frigidae genus nitrosum, uti Pinnae Vestinae, Cutiliis aliisque locis similibus, quae potionibus depurgat per alvumque transeundo etiam strumarum minuit tumores: Celsus iv 5 (on stomachic disorders), consistere in frigidis medicatisque fontibus, quales Cutiliarum sunt, salutare est.

: cf. Liv. xxviii 46, Punicum exercitum super morbum etiam fames affecit. The use of super in the sense of praeter begins in prose with Livy and is common in later writers. Suetonius has it repeatedly, and often follows it with etiam, quoque, or ct.

: a regular phrase in medical writers; so too venter solutus. In describing the last illness of Augustus, Suetonius (Aug. 97, 3) says: causam valitudinis contraxit ex profluvio alvi. Dio (lxvi 17), while stating as an ascertained fact that Vesp. died of fever at the Sabine springs, adds that there were some, including the future emperor Hadrian, who falsely asserted that he was poisoned at a banquet by Titus. Tacitus (A. xii 67, xiii 15) mentions "soluta alvus” as an effect of the poison administered to the emperor Claudius and to Britannicus.

: (Aur. Vict.] Epit. 9, deinde ventris eluvie fessus, et assurgens, ‘“Stantem,” ait, “imperatorem excedere terris decet'': Dio lxvi 17, τῶν δὲ ἰατρῶν ἐπιτιμώντων ὅτι τῇ τε ἄλλῃ διαίτῃ ὁμοίᾳ νοσῶν ἐχρῆτο, καὶ πάντα τὰ προσήκοντα τῇ ἀρχῇ ἔπραττε, “ Τὸν αὐτοκράτορα” ἔφη “ ἑστῶτα δεῖ ἀποθνήσκειν.” Dio (lxix 18) attributes a like utterance to Turbo, prefect of the praetorian guard in Hadrian's reign, who, when advised by the emperor to take a rest when ill, replied: “Tὸν ἔπαρχον (praefectum) ἑστῶτα ἀποθνήσκειν δεῖ.” Cf. Sen. Ep. 82, 21, quis post hanc (contionem) dubitet se infestis ingerere mucronibus et stans mori (where stans is opp. to fugiens): id. Ep. 37, 2, recto tibi invictoque moriendum est. Seneca is always inculcating the Stoic doctrine that the "wise” man should die in harness (in actu mori).

: niti could be used by itself = "to make an effort Holland to rise"; cf. Sall. Iug. 101, niti modo ac statim concidere. strangely takes nititur in the same sense as nitens in c. 20, and translates: "As he was rising therefore and straining still to ease his body."
: June 23.

: a very careless expression, though the meaning is clear; he was aged (natus) 69 yrs. 7 mths. and 7 days, but in (agens) his 70th year. The variant gerens is preferred by Graevius, Gronovius, Marcilius, Oudendorp, and Bremi. See on Dom. 1, 1, adulescentiae tempus gessisse fertur.

: septimum is to be taken with mensem as well as with diem; see App. i § 16. (d). Dio (lxvi 17) says that Vespasian lived 69 yrs. 8 mths. (Zonaras adds "and 8 days"), and reigned 10 yrs. all but 6 days. He was born on Nov. 17, 9 A.D. (see c. 2, 1), and died on June 23, 79 A.D.; so that the calculation of his age by Suetonius as 69 yrs. 7 mths. 7 days is accurate. He reigned from July 1, 69 A.D., when he was first proclaimed imperator at Alexandria (c. 6, 3), to June 23, 79 A.D., i.e. 10 yrs. all but 8 days. See also on c. 25.

: ''horoscope"; see on Tit. 9, 2. Cf. Eutrop. vii 20, Genituram filiorum ita cognitam habuit, ut, cum multae contra eum coniurationes fierent, quas patefactas ingenti dissimulatione contempsit, in senatu dixerit,

p.mentioned: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem
p.note: : Aur. Vict. Caes. 9, divinis deditus, quorum vera plerisque negotiis compererat, successores fidebat liberos Titum ac Domitianum fore.

: Dio (lxvi 16) describes how Julius Sabinus, a Gaul who had taken part in the unsuccessful effort of Classicus to establish an Imperium Galliarum in 70 A.D., and who styled himself a Caesar as being descended from a bastard son of Julius Caesar, was brought to Rome in 79 after being nine years in hiding and was put to death by Vespasian's orders along with his wife Epponina. He mentions at the same time the conspiracy of Caecina Alienus and Eprius Marcellus, on both of whom the emperor had lavished favours. For Caecina Alienus and his fate see on Tit. 6, 2. Eprius Marcellus exercised great power both as an orator (cf. Tac. Dial. 5. 8. 13) and informer (delator) in the reign of Nero. It was he who secured the condemnation of Paetus Thrasea. At the beginning of Vespasian's reign he was impeached by Helvidius Priscus, son-in-law of Thrasea, but escaped through his influence with Mucianus and Domitian. He enjoyed the friendship of Vespasian and was proconsul of Asia (70- 73 A.D.). When he was condemned by the senate for conspiring with Caecina against the emperor in the later years of his reign, he committed suicide (Tac. A. xii 4, xiii 33, xvi 23, etc.; H. ii 53, iv 6-8).

p.mentioned: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem
p.note: : Dio lxvi 12, “Ἐμὲ μὲν υἱὸς διαδέξεται ἢ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος.” Dio says that the words followed a display of defiant insolence by Helvidius Priscus in the senate; see on c. 15. The remark of Vespasian is much more appropriate if, as Suet. says, it was made "post assiduas in se coniurationes" and so, presumably, towards the end of his reign. There is no evidence that Priscus (executed in 73) organised any conspiracy, though his denunciations of the empire were revolutionary. Rostovtzeff (Social and Economic Hist. Rom. Emp. c. iv n. 4) thinks that Priscus had been advocating in the senate the selection as emperor of the best man of the senatorial class, taking the Stoic and Cynic point of view, and that Vesp. would not listen to the suggestion and uttered these words which mean that the reestablishment of the Republic would be better than the method suggested by Priscus.

: "in a dream," cf. Iul. 7, 2:81, 3: Tib. 74: Claud. 37, 1: Ner. 7, 1:46, 1: Oth. 7, 2: Vesp. 5, 7:7, 2; so in Val. Max., Tac., etc. Cic. has in quiete and secundum quietem ("after going to sleep''); Val. Max. also uses inter quietem.

: stătēra was used either in the general sense of a scales or balance (libra, trutina) or in the special sense of a steelyard. The mention of the two scales (lances) shows that the former is the meaning here, as in many other passages, e.g. Petron. Satyr. 35, stateram in cuius altera parte scriblita erat, in altera placenta; see Wilkins on Cic. de or. ii 159, aurificis statera. Vitruvius (x 3, 4) describes statera as a steelyard with a beam or yard (scapus) marked by points (puncta), the hanging weight (aequipondium) moving along the scapus, and the object weighed being placed in a scale (lancula).

: Augustus at first dwelt in the modest town house of Hortensius, the orator, on the Palatine (Aug. 72, 1). When this was struck by lightning, he gave the site for the stately temple to Apollo (Aug. 29, 3), and close to it he built a palace for himself. Tiberius built a second palace near that of Augustus (see on Vitell. 15, 3, Tiberiana domus), and in official documents the designation of the imperial buildings on the Palatine continued to be Domus Augustana et Tiberiana or Domus Palatina; cf. Dom. 15, 2. In popular speech and gradually in literature Palatium, the name of the Palatine hill, came to be used for the palace of the Caesars (e.g. Galb. 18, 1: Vitell. 15, 2); see Jordan-Huelsen, Topogr. Rom i 3, 64, where the double use of Quirinale in Italian is cited as a parallel.

: the examen was the tongue or needle which worked in an eye (agina) or opening in the upper part of the balance and showed whether the two scales were in equipoise; cf. Verg. A. xii 725, Iuppiter ipse duas aequato examine lances | sustinet: Pers. i 6, examenque improbum in illa | castiges trutina.
: Titus and Domitian.
: see on c. 16, 3.
: approximately 27 years. (41-54 A.D.); Nero 14 (54-68); Vespasian 10 Domitian 15 (81-96). Claudius reigned 13 years (69-79); Titus 2 (79-81);

: by adding these words Suetonius presumably means that the two periods, when calculated accurately in years, months, and days would exactly correspond. He does not himself furnish us with the precise length of each reign, and the figures which we derive from other sources vary considerably. Claudius reigned 13 yrs. 2 m. 20 d. (Dio, Zonar., Joseph.). Nero reigned 13 yrs. 8 m. (Dio; Zonaras adding "all but two days''); 13 yrs. 8 d. (Joseph.). Vespasian (see on c. 24) reigned 10 yrs. all but 6 days (Dio); 11 yrs. 11 m. 22 d. (Clem. Alex., who mentions that some say 11 yrs. precisely); 10 yrs. 8 d. (Cedrenus); 9 yrs. 7 m. 12 d. (Epiphanius). Titus reigned 2 yrs. 2 m. 20 d. (Suet., Dio, Zonar.; for other figures see on Tit. 11). Domitian reigned 15 yrs. 5 d. (Dio, Zonar., Eutrop.). 2 H
